7 killed as auto-rickshaw collides head-on with container truck in Jharkhand
An auto-rickshaw collided head-on with a container truck in Latehar district, killing seven people and injuring several others. Police and local residents launched rescue operations as officials worked to identify the victims and investigate the crash.
At least seven people were killed and several others injured after an auto-rickshaw collided head-on with a container truck in Jharkhand's Latehar district on Saturday evening, police said.
Rescue operations were underway, with the injured being shifted to hospital.
The accident occurred in the Derh Tangwa Ghat area under the Chandwa police station limits. According to preliminary information, the auto-rickshaw was travelling from Chandwa when it collided with an oncoming container truck.
Local residents said the impact of the collision was so severe that several passengers travelling in the auto-rickshaw were trapped beneath the container. The crash triggered panic in the area, with villagers rushing to the spot and alerting the police and district administration.
POLICE LAUNCH RESCUE OPERATION
Upon receiving the information, Chandwa Police Station in-charge Manoranjan Prasad Singh, along with police personnel, reached the accident site and launched rescue and relief operations. Police, assisted by local residents, worked to extricate those trapped in the wreckage and shift the injured to nearby hospitals for treatment.
Officials said seven people died on the spot, while several others sustained injuries. The condition of the injured was not immediately known.
The administration is in the process of identifying the deceased and injured. Authorities said the exact number of people travelling in the auto-rickshaw and the identities of the victims are being verified.
Police have begun an investigation into the cause of the accident. The circumstances that led to the head-on collision are yet to be ascertained.
The accident briefly disrupted traffic in the area as rescue teams cleared the damaged vehicles from the road. Further details are awaited as officials continue rescue operations and gather information about the victims.
Police said a detailed investigation will be carried out to determine the sequence of events leading to the fatal crash.

Morocco arrests 111 migrants headed to Spain's Ceuta as sides step up crackdown
Moroccan police used tear gas to disperse groups gathered at border, Spanish media reports
Moroccan police arrested at least 111 people on Saturday as they tried to enter Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, amid tightened security on both sides of the border after social media posts called for another mass migrant crossing.
The attempted crossing came two weeks after more than 72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta, sparking tensions within the European Union and fuelling anti-immigration rhetoric among far-right parties worldwide. At least 96 people died in the attempt to reach European soil.
A source in Morocco's Interior Ministry told Reuters those detained included 109 migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two Moroccan citizens arrested in or around Fnideq, the Moroccan city opposite Ceuta.
According to Spanish news agency EFE, Moroccan police used tear gas to disperse groups of migrants gathered on hills about three kilometres from the border. Reuters later saw hundreds of police officers, some in riot gear and others in plain clothes, returning from the hills outside Fnideq.
EFE and Spanish state broadcaster TVE said Morocco's Interior Ministry ordered their journalists to leave Fnideq immediately, without providing an explanation.
In Ceuta, Spanish soldiers guarded supermarkets while police heavily patrolled the enclave's main streets. The city was calmer than in the days after the deadly crossing attempt on July 30.
Madrid has since installed a maritime barrier and deployed more than 500 additional police from mainland Spain, raising the total in Ceuta to more than 1,600. The Interior Ministry said the reinforcements would remain for as long as needed.
"We'll continue to deploy whatever personnel are necessary to restore normality as soon as possible and prevent events like those of July 30 from happening again," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Thursday.
About 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta, the minister said. Reuters saw hundreds sheltering from scorching heat under makeshift bamboo shelters on the urban beach of El Trampolin.
Grande-Marlaska said migrants who entered irregularly would not be allowed to stay in the enclave, travel to mainland Spain or obtain legal status, except in rare cases involving extreme vulnerability. Those without a right to remain would be returned to Morocco, he said.
Earlier this week, Rabat said it was monitoring "the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin" calling for a mass crossing on Aug. 15, warning it would prosecute organizers and participants.
A Reuters witness saw reinforced security near the border, including police vans with wire shields and road checkpoints. Local media reported similar measures near Spain's other North African enclave, Melilla.
Authorities prevented several groups from boarding trains and buses to northern Morocco in cities such as Casablanca, Fez and Kenitra.
However, witnesses told Reuters that some migrants from sub-Saharan Africa were bypassing security checkpoints by taking mountain routes towards Fnideq.
One witness said the schools in Fnideq had been turned into accommodation for security forces deployed near the border.
'Don't cross now, my brothers'
Many of the young people who entered Ceuta on July 30 were fishing, swimming or washing at Tarajal beach on Friday.
Driss Sadik, a 22-year-old from Fez who said he swam for five hours to reach Ceuta, urged others not to follow his example.
"The important thing I would advise people trying to cross: Don't cross now, my brothers. You're only going to suffer," he told Reuters.
The warning was echoed by Adil Jamil, 17.
"Those who enter aren't going to benefit from anything. There will just be more and more of us, and they won't find a solution for all," he said.
Jamil said that the mass border crossings were "planned by the people" who pick a date, gather in Fnideq and cross together to find strength in numbers.
"If I had stayed with my parents, I would've died slowly. But if I risk my life, arrive and build my future ... it will be better," he said.

Spidey’s Sense for Success
The masked web-slinger has been setting box-office records for decades, even as the popularity of superhero movies wanes.
This has been a terrific year for movie theaters. Cinemas are on course for their best financial year since before the coronavirus pandemic, powered by large-scale hits such as The Odyssey and surprise small-budget smashes, particularly Obsession and Backrooms. Fears about the decline of the big-screen experience amid the rise of at-home streaming seem to have begun dissipating. But one theatrical stalwart is showing serious signs of weakness: the superhero movie, which helped keep blockbusters afloat for most of the 2010s. Marvel’s most anticipated title last year, The Fantastic Four: First Steps—which reintroduced the fan-favorite comic-book team—failed to meet the studio’s lofty expectations; this June’s DC Comics adaptation of Supergirl was an out-and-out bomb.
By those metrics, one might have predicted a similar slump for this summer’s new Spider-Man sequel, subtitled Brand New Day. Instead, it has broken nearly every box-office record imaginable.
That the film has been able to defy mounting superhero fatigue may seem unexpected. After all, Brand New Day is the fourth Spider-Man entry set in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, which owns the rights to the character; it’s Tom Holland’s seventh time playing the character. Whereas its predecessor, 2021’s No Way Home, sold itself on bringing back heroes and villains from prior Spider-Man entries, Brand New Day promised a general reset. Its story also feels smaller, the action confined to the hero’s hometown of New York City, where he faces off with more street-level villains. Given the public’s declining appetite for the MCU—long gone are the days when an installment starring a relatively unknown character could make more than $1 billion worldwide—Brand New Day’s streamlined focus seemed like an audience gamble.
Not so: The movie earned $360 million domestically during its opening weekend, shattering a record set by Avengers: Endgame in 2019. Endgame was the grand conclusion of Marvel’s initial saga, featuring Spider-Man alongside every other popular character in the company’s wheelhouse. Yet Brand New Day, with its far less cataclysmic stakes, could be the first-ever film to make $1 billion in the United States and Canada alone; if it doesn’t break the all-time worldwide box-office record held by Avatar ($2.9 billion), it will at least come close. Its popularity is proof that for some costumed do-gooders, the exhaustion with superheroes just doesn’t apply. Maybe the simplest rule of thumb is that although audiences are losing interest in most comic-book adaptations, Spider-Man will always endure.
He initially set a famous box-office milestone back in 2002, when Spider-Man—the character’s major-feature debut, starring Tobey Maguire—grossed more than $110 million domestically during its opening weekend. Since then, even as other actors have assumed the role (including Andrew Garfield and an animated version voiced by Shameik Moore), Spider-Man has remained the most consistent of comic-book movie stars. Sony, which owns the film rights to the Spider-Man franchise, has attempted to build offshoot storylines that don’t feature him but has consistently failed; though the Venom trilogy did well enough, the spin-offs Morbius, Madame Web, and Kraven the Hunter were commercial failures. (Critics hated all of them too.) Yet Spider-Man himself has proved indestructible to theatergoers: The 11 films in which he stars have made nearly $11 billion worldwide.
Brand New Day’s colossal success can’t just be attributed to the hero’s appeal, however. The genius of the co-creators Stan Lee and Steve Ditko’s comic-book invention was that he was more grounded and familiar than DC Comics’ godlike figures, such as Superman and Wonder Woman, or the multibillionaire Batman. Spider-Man, in his original incarnation, was really just a nerdy teen named Peter Parker who readers could relate to, and the installments starring Holland have replicated that zippy, youthful energy. Spider-Man’s brand has also been savvily extended to fans of all ages: Projects such as the wildly popular cartoon Spidey and His Amazing Friends appeal to preschoolers, featuring villains including the Green Goblin and Doctor Octopus downgraded from homicidal to simply mischievous; the studio Insomniac Games’ three video games focused on the character are best sellers.
Beyond that, the star power of Holland and Zendaya, who plays Spider-Man’s girlfriend, MJ, is on a level few other young actors can claim. They both feature in the summer’s other biggest hit, Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, and although they largely keep their real-life relationship private, it adds to the authenticity of their romance on-screen. Zendaya in particular has proved exceptionally good at getting young viewers to show up for more daring movies, such as this spring’s The Drama; comparatively, something as broadly crowd-pleasing as Brand New Day is a layup.
The film’s achievements will likely not be taken for granted. Marvel’s next movie, Avengers: Doomsday, will be released in December and stands to benefit from the hype around Brand New Day. The studio is also soft-rebooting the franchise following next year’s Avengers: Secret Wars, in part by leaning on another well-known superhero team—the X-Men, one of whom is deployed as Brand New Day’s surprise antagonist. The industry will probably never return to producing the relentless glut of comic-book adaptations that buttressed the past decade-plus in Hollywood—which is a good thing, because a diversity of genres and cinematic experiences is the wisest thing to have on offer. Perhaps Brand New Day could kick off a more stable new phase for superheroes. No matter what, Spider-Man will keep on swinging.

Manipur CM stresses peace, normalcy for development on Independence Day
With the deployment of new police vehicles, security forces can now reach far-flung places in Manipur to monitor the law and order
Manipur chief minister Yummam Khemchand Singh in his speech on the 80th Independence Day on Saturday stressed on restoring peace and normalcy in the state to bring development.
“Peace and normalcy will be the backbone to bring development in Manipur as a first step and peace and development need to go in parallel,” Khemchand said.
The CM said the Manipur government has continued its peace efforts and added 477 police vehicles. With the deployment of new police vehicles, security forces can now reach far-flung places in Manipur to monitor the law and order , he said.
Deep Dive
Singh also condemned the killing of two civilians and the injury of two others in an alleged ambush on Friday at Langka village, Kangpokpi district. “The government will book the culprits involved in the crime according to the law of the land,” he said.
Unknown individuals killed two farmers and injured two others in an alleged ambush on a group of farmers in Langka village, Manipur’s Kangpokpi district on Friday.
Naga bodies, including the United Naga Council (UNC), a Naga apex civil body, imposed a 24-hour total shutdown in solidarity with the victim families, effective from 11 p.m. on August 14 to 11 p.m. on August 15, across Naga-inhabited areas of Manipur. Additionally, the Liangmai Naga Council, Manipur also imposed an emergency total shutdown across Liangmai-Naga inhabited areas of Manipur on Friday.
Meanwhile, Manipur governor Ajay Kumar Bhalla extended greetings to the people of Manipur on the occasion of the 80th Independence Day in a message, and called for renewed efforts to strengthen national unity, uphold the Constitution and ensure peace and social harmony.
“As we celebrate this historic occasion, let us renew our resolve to strengthen national unity, uphold the Constitution, and contribute wholeheartedly to the progress and prosperity of our nation,” the governor said.
He urged citizens to work towards building a “peaceful, inclusive, and developed India” while ensuring that Manipur continues to move forward on the path of stability, growth and social harmony.
Coordinating Committee (CorCom), an apex coalition of six banned underground outfits in Manipur, imposed a total general strike and boycott of India’s Independence Day. The six banned outfits comprise the Kangleipak Communist Party (KCP), Kanglei Yawol Kanna Lup (KYKL), People’s Revolutionary Party of Kangleipak (PREPAK), PREPAK-Progressive, Revolutionary People’s Front (RPF) and United National Liberation Front (UNLF).
CorCom claimed the 1949 annexation as a violation of international law and Article 2(4) of the United Nations Charter.
The shutdown has paralysed Imphal City, as markets, business establishment, transports were shutdown.
Manipur has been in ethnic unrest since May 3, 2023 following Kuki-Zo and Meitei conflict claiming over 260 lives, and leaving more than 60,000 displaced.

With the revelation that ICE will spend up to $20 million by March on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to subdue an individual, according to a notice published earlier this week by the Department of Homeland Security, it's worth looking at how this apparel, designated as a non-lethal tool for law enforcement, actually works.
These shock gloves go by the unsubtle acronym of GLOVE (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter), and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies, based in Lexington, Kentucky. The GLOVE, previously used in jails and police departments in the US, looks and functions like a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate an electrical mode.
Classified as a CD3 (Conductive Distraction and De-escalation Device), the gloves don't work like stun guns or Tasers, which shoot out probes or use high voltages to cause neuromuscular incapacitation that overrides the central nervous system. Instead, the GLOVE works using Neuro-Peripheral Interference (NPI), essentially shocking the skin to bombard the sensory nerves and temporarily short-circuit the brain's focus.
Compliant Technologies did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.
When activated via a one-second press on a wrist switch, conductive pads embedded on the palm and undersides of the fingers of the gloves can transmit high-frequency electrical pulses directly to the wearer’s point of contact on a subject. A rechargeable battery and microprocessor module tucked inside a zippered pouch on the cuff powers the entire system.
The electrical pulse overstimulates nerve endings in the subject's peripheral nervous system, resulting in pain that inhibits coordinated muscle movement, but without causing systemic muscle lockup. The pain induced is localized to just the area touched by the glove's conductive pads. The manufacturer claims the gloves result in a subject's compliance in less than three seconds and leave no burns, marks, or scars.
Because the current flows only between the contact pads on the device and across the subject's skin, the officer wearing the GLOVE, as well as any assisting officers holding the subject, should not feel electrical shocks. The gloves, capable of operating between 14 and 122 degrees Fahrenheit, come in three versions: Gen 3, 4, and 5. Maximum voltage is capped at 380 V for all, and the minimum voltage for Gen 3 and 4 is 210 V, which rises to 324 V for Gen 5.
Maximum stimulation time on Gen 3 and 4 models is a sobering two hours, though that drops to 90 minutes for Gen 5. The battery is apparently good for 2,000 charge/discharge cycles, and can recharge to full in 2 hours. Four LED lights on the gloves display the current charge level, each noting 25 percent battery increments.
Gen 4 and 5 of GLOVE both include mechanisms that record “activation events,” tracking the date, hour, minute, and skin contact time for audit trails and after-action reporting. Gen 4 stores this data on a removable microSD card, while Gen 5 does away with this in favor of built-in internal memory, accessed via a USB-C cable.
There's a test function on the gloves, too, where operators can verify they are working by tapping an active pad against their own forearm to feel a minor electrical pulse. According to the manuals, GLOVE users must be certified and then recertified every other year to continue using the device.
GLOVE, which can only be sold to verified professional entities such as the military, correctional facilities, and law enforcement agencies—has some clear usage recommendations in Compliant Technologies' instruction manuals:
- No more than two GLOVE units (or, in other words, one pair) should be used simultaneously on a single subject.
- Continuous shocks should not exceed 15 seconds.
- Operators must target arms and legs, while strictly avoiding the head, face, throat, chest, and groin.
- The gloves should not be used on the elderly, young children, pregnant individuals, or people with severe disabilities.
- The technology must not be used to counter verbal defiance, as punishment, or for torture.
Crucially, the GLOVE has limitations, chief among them that for the device to work effectively and deliver its restraining pain shock, it must come into contact with the subject's bare skin. According to Compliant Technologies, the gloves won't work through dry clothing or thick hair. The gloves will work, however, if the subject is wearing thin, wet clothing, such as soaked T-shirts or blouses. The GLOVE also does not like being dunked in water and will likely be rendered inoperable if this happens.
Michael Crowley, a senior researcher at Omega Research Foundation—an organization that tracks human rights abuses committed across the world by people using police, security, and military equipment—is concerned that the GLOVE. is seemingly designed not to restrain or incapacitate, but to hurt.
“CD3 technology inflicts pain," Crowley says. "The company talks about it as a de-escalation solution, but the whole idea of it is to get control or influence somebody through pain. Omega considers it to be an inherently abusive technology that should not be manufactured, sold, or used by law enforcement officials, including ICE.”

Mumbai: Western Railway is preparing to deploy 20 or more contractual personnel at each of its busiest suburban stations to tackle peak-hour crowds, while around 10 staff will be stationed at less-crowded stations. The special teams will focus on crowd movement, platform safety and ensuring AC local train doors close on time, in a move aimed at reducing avoidable delays on the suburban network.
Busy Stations To Get Dedicated Staff For Crowd Movement And Safety
The teams are proposed for crowded stations such as Dadar, Andheri, Santacruz, Borivali, Virar and Nalasopara. Their responsibilities will include regulating passenger movement, preventing crowding at platforms, foot overbridges and staircases, diverting commuters when required and providing assistance during emergencies. A major focus will be the period immediately before and after trains arrive and depart, when passenger movement becomes particularly heavy.
Western Railway officials are also linking the deployment to the punctuality of AC local services. During peak hours, overcrowding near automatic doors often prevents them from closing on time, forcing trains to remain at platforms for longer than scheduled. Railway officials believe that reducing even a few seconds of additional halting time at multiple stations could help prevent a chain reaction of delays.
Railway Officials Say Seconds Saved Can Improve Overall Timeliness
“Even a few seconds saved at each station can help maintain punctuality across the entire route. Special personnel will also reduce the pressure on the security department,” a senior Western Railway official said.
The personnel will be hired on a contractual basis, with departmental-level approval already received. While the busiest stations will get 20 or more staff each, stations with comparatively lower passenger footfall will receive around 10 personnel.
Dedicated Crowd Teams To Ease Pressure On Railway Security Personnel
The move is significant as the railway's existing security personnel often have to handle multiple responsibilities, including passenger safety, crowd management and security-related duties. By creating dedicated teams for crowd control, Western Railway expects to improve passenger movement at key stations while allowing its security staff to concentrate on their primary responsibilities.
The deployment is expected to be implemented shortly, with the railway administration now working on the next stage of the process.

A study conducted in rural areas of Kozhikode district has found that 174 people per a population of 1,000 (17.4%) required outpatient (OP) medical treatment within a recall period of 15 days and 19 people per a population of 1,000 required (1.9%) inpatient (IP) medical treatment within a recall period of a year for their various illnesses.
It also revealed that the utilisation of private healthcare facilities was higher for both OP and IP care. Out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) was higher in private facilities compared with public facilities for both OP and IP services. A substantial proportion of households were covered under government health insurance schemes. The OOPE, however, remained considerable among both insured and uninsured households.
The study titled ‘Morbidity and out-of-pocket expenditure among rural households of Kozhikode district, Kerala’ was published in Healthline Journal, a peer-reviewed publication of the Indian Association of Social and Preventive Medicine, on July 23, 2026. It was conducted by T. Jayakrishnan, Head of the Department of Community Medicine, P. Sruthi Krishna, Assistant Professor, Community Medicine, and Anjali Lakshmanan and Ahana Salim, junior resident doctors, at KMCT Medical College, Mukkom, Kozhikode.
The community-based cross sectional study was conducted among 700 households and a sample size of 2,371 in a select grama panchayat in the district. Of the total population, 413 illnesses requiring OP treatment were reported over a period of 15 days, corresponding to a rate of 174 per 1,000 population. Most frequently reported causes of OP morbidities were infectious diseases (76.9%) which included viral fever, respiratory tract infections, mumps, chickenpox, and viral hepatitis. Accidents and injuries constituted 7.6%.
As many as 83.1% sought care from any health facilities, while 16.9% managed themselves through self-medication. A total of 53.4% sought care from private facilities, while 46.6% approached public facilities. The median expenditure OOPE for OP care was ₹145 and ₹700 in public and private facilities, respectively. In public facilities, cost of medicines (₹500) accounted for the highest share and in private facilities, it was for investigations (₹1,150).
Over a one-year period, 44 incidents requiring IP treatment were reported with an incident rate of 19 per 1,000 population. Of this, 77% were admitted in private facilities and only 23% were in public facilities. The cause of hospitalisation in 43.1% of the cases were non-communicable diseases and 34.4% were infectious diseases. The median expenditure OOPE for IP care was ₹600 and ₹5,050 in public and private facilities, respectively. In public facilities, cost of medicines accounted for the highest expenditure.
Out of 663 households, 494 were enrolled in any form of health insurance schemes while 25.4% had no such coverage. The most commonly availed scheme was Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, covering 60.3% of the population. The participants who were covered under health insurance schemes, including those belonging to BPL families, had an OOPE of ₹2,625 for IP care, compared to ₹4,250 among those who did not have it. Although the OOPE was relatively lower for the insured belonging to the BPL category, they still incurred substantial expenditure, indicating that they also suffer high financial burden and are not fully protected.
The OOPE for IP care in the private sector was ₹5,050, which was less than that of previous studies, possibly because patients were admitted for minor illnesses or discharged within a day to comply with insurance claim requirements.
The authors of the study said that the preference for private OP care was a sign of increased privatisation in healthcare which may be driven by many causes like increasing health aspirations, reduced waiting times, perceived better quality of care and greater flexibility in service delivery. The lower hospitalisation rate seen in the present study may not reflect a true reduction in morbidity but could be attributed to reduced affordability, where individuals delayed or avoided hospital admission due to financial constraints.

Telangana cabinet okays ₹200-crore scheme for conversion of fuel autos into electric vehicles
The Telangana cabinet, chaired by chief minister A Revanth Reddy, on Friday approved a ₹200 crore scheme to convert petrol and diesel-powered auto rickshaws into electric vehicles within core Hyderabad capital region in a move to reduce automobile pollution and transform Hyderabad into a green city
The Telangana cabinet, chaired by chief minister A Revanth Reddy, on Friday approved a ₹200 crore scheme to convert petrol and diesel-powered auto rickshaws into electric vehicles within core Hyderabad capital region in a move to reduce automobile pollution and transform Hyderabad into a green city.
Disclosing this to reporters after the cabinet meeting, state information and public relations minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy said there were currently around 18,766 petrol and diesel autos operating in the Core Urban Region (CURE) area of Hyderabad.
“Under the proposed scheme, eligible auto drivers will be provided a subsidy of up to ₹1.50 lakh per vehicle to facilitate the transition to electric autos,” the minister said, adding the decision was taken as part of the state government’s efforts to reduce vehicular emissions and promote cleaner transportation in Hyderabad.
The cabinet also decided to encourage farmers to cultivate seven identified varieties of fine-grain paddy during the Kharif season and provide a bonus of ₹500 per quintal specifically for these seven varieties of fine paddy this year.
“The government will undertake a widespread awareness campaign through gram panchayat buildings and Rythu Vedikas across the State to encourage farmers to increase cultivation of these varieties,” the minister said.
The cabinet approved bringing all the existing Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs), Advanced Training Centres (ATCs) and polytechnic colleges under the jurisdiction of the newly-formed Young India Skills University.
“At present, these institutions function under the Technical Education Department. The cabinet decided that they would be removed from the purview of the Telangana Education Act and brought under the Young India Skills University framework,” Srinivas Reddy said.
He said the move was aimed at integrating the State’s technical and vocational education infrastructure with the skills university.
The cabinet gave its approval for establishing Young India Integrated Residential School complexes in seven assembly constituencies — Adilabad, Nirmal, Mudhole, Boath, Sirpur, Gajwel and Dubbaka.
He said the state government had proposed establishing Young India Integrated Residential School complexes in 113 assembly constituencies. With the seven schools approved on Friday, permissions have now been granted for 86 school complexes, he said.
The cabinet also decided to extend the deadline for applications under the Hyderabad Industrial Lands Transformation (HILT) policy, which seeks to facilitate the relocation of polluting industries operating within Hyderabad city limits to areas on the city’s outskirts.
In response to requests from applicants, the government extended the application deadline by another three months, allowing applications to be submitted until October 31.
The cabinet has tentatively decided to hold the Telangana Rising Global Summit 2.0 on December 7, 8 and 9 this year. A sub-committee headed by deputy chief minister Bhatti Vikramarka and ministers Duddilla Sridhar Babu, N Uttam Kumar Reddy and Vivek Venkataswamy, would be constituted to organise the event.
He said the upcoming summit will be organised around the theme ‘Invest Telangana’ with focus on projecting Telangana as a major global destination for investments in sectors such as defence, aerospace and pharmaceuticals. The government also plans to unveil the Future City plan during the summit, he said.

A wave of blanket and seemingly arbitrary restrictions is sweeping Instagram in India, with posts and accounts being taken down or restricted, particularly content related to the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests, political satire and any kind of criticism of the ruling dispensation.
The takedowns have exposed an opaque and largely unaccountable process, with users given little to no meaningful avenue to appeal the removal or restriction of their posts and pages. Meta’s explanations often lead to a loop of generic messages citing “local legal requirements” or “automated systems”. While India is identified as the location of the restriction, the platform offers little clarity on what triggered the decision or why specific content was targeted, including through Meta’s Transparency Centre.
The timing of this state-ordered censorship frenzy is difficult to ignore. It comes immediately atter a youth-led movement whose whose unprecedented reach and mobilisation were driven largely by social media, with Instagram playing a central role. The platform helped transform CJP from a satire page into a nationwide movement, amplifying dissent and mobilising young people at a scale that ultimately forced the government to concede to some of its core demands.
For many creators affected by the takedowns, their work on Instagram is a primary source of income and professional engagement. Alt News spoke to several users, including content creators, comedians, satirists and journalists, caught up in this expanding censorship drive.
ALSO READ: Government orders trigger sweeping Instagram censorship days after CJP protest
Anjali Priya, an Instagram creator with more than 104,000 followers, is among those affected. Priya’s content spans politics, entertainment and other issues, typically combining personal commentary with factual references.
On August 1, Priya uploaded a video featuring a photo of Prime Minister Narendra Modi from his address to young protesters, in which he “forgave them” for using expletives during the Chalo Sansad protest in Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on July 20.
In the satirical video, Priya, using a cat filter, asked when Modi would give the opportunity to the citizens to forgive him, urging him to take accountability for the police brutality that occurred against students during the July 20 march, which led to hundreds being severely injured and hospitalised.
The video received nearly two million views before Instagram notified Priya that it had been restricted in India. Meta said the action was taken by an “automated system pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021”.
A similar restriction was imposed on her July 24 carousel meme post calling for the PM’s resignation. The platform cited a legal request based on local laws.
The restricted post is shown below:
Speaking to Alt News, Priya describes the restrictions of her posts as nothing short of a ‘digital emergency’. “I used to read about the emergency, but the BJP government’s actions have made me experience a taste of what it was like,” she said. “This is a digital emergency. We don’t need to go 50 years back to understand it — we are living through it right now.”
‘Censorship on Censorship’
Sneha Pan, the administrator of the Instagram page Moviemaniacs.co.in, told Alt News that a video uploaded on her page on July 28 had been restricted in India. The video addressed the increasing censorship surrounding Indian cinema, particularly highlighting the case of the recent film, ‘Satluj’, based on the life and murder of human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra. Originally titled ‘Punjab ’95’, the film was subjected to prolonged scrutiny by the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), which sought multiple changes before clearing it. The dispute contributed to a three-year delay in its release, and after eventually making it to a streaming platform, the film was swiftly taken down, adding another chapter to its troubled journey with censorship.
On July 29, Pan received a notification from Meta indicating that the post was unavailable in India, in accordance with India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (IT Rules).
The “How we made this decision” section said: “Our technology found that your post is affected by a request and took action. We are legally required to restrict access to your post in certain locations.” It also included the message: “We have taken this action based on local legal requirements.”
Pan calls the restrictions “deeply troubling” and highlights the irony in this particular case as hard to miss: “I was talking about censorship, and now the conversation about that censorship itself has been censored.”
‘Meta doesn’t want to annoy the government’
Sunil Sharma, a satirist who runs the Instagram account Rofl Gandhi2.0, with around 130,000 followers, alleged that a comment mocking Modi’s Bengal campaign post was removed after he shared it on his Instagram story in April.
On May 21, Sharma posted a video featuring Rahul Gandhi and Modi, with the former quipping that while the country was “going through hell”, the latter was asking why “Melody” was so “chocolatey” — referring to the viral social media phenomenon from back in May, when the Indian PM gifted Italian PM Giorgia Meloni a packet of Melody toffees during his visit to Italy. Sharma’s post played on the joke of the famous Melody chocolate’s advertising line: “Melody itni chocolatey kiyu hai?” This video was made unavailable in India on July 21.
Another video, posted in April, satirising Modi and Donald Trump, was restricted on July 31.
Sharma had commented, “Pyaz kya chez hai beta, hum toh desh bhi kha jate hai” [What is an onion, son? We even eat the country] on a post by Modi, featuring another viral moment when the Prime Minister had ‘jhalmuri’ during his visit to Kolkata as part of the West Bengal election campaign. While the comment was eventually deleted from the post, he had shared the comment on his own Instagram story, which was removed by the platform on April 19.
“I think Meta just wants to survive in India, as it is a big market owing to WhatsApp. Because of WhatsApp, Meta is not taking risks. They don’t want to annoy the government. Instagram has been a democratic platform, but now they want to reset the algorithm to promote right-wing content more,” Sharma opined.
‘Suppressing the Voice of Democracy’
Journalist Sachin Gupta, on August 1, uploaded a video reporting on the alleged violence by Kanwariyas on the streets of Uttarakhand in the presence of police. The video was removed on August 3 with a similar message: a government or law-enforcement request under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act.
Gupta told Alt News that an FIR had been registered in the case and that police were taking further action. “How can you then label a video related to that case as fake or misleading?” he asked, calling the restriction “nothing short of an attempt to suppress the voice of democracy.”
“Government wants to completely control social media,” Gupta said. “Journalism within media houses is already under government control. Now, even the few journalists who can express their views through social media are being targeted, and attempts are being made to control them as well.”
‘No Transparency For The User’
Shrishti Khanna is an educator by profession and a political content creator who speaks on issues like Palestinian genocide, local Indian politics, Hindutva and the RSS-BJP playbook. With around 104,000 Instagram followers, Khanna’s account was banned in India on July 7 following a government request under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act.
Sharing details of her long censorship battle with Alt News, Khanna said that she received no notification from either Meta or the government, and only discovered that her account was restricted in India after her followers and friends intimated that her account was not visible to them. Khanna was compelled to create a back-up account.
However, this was not the first time her account had been suspended. On June 9, Instagram suspended her account for alleged copyright infringement — something Khanna described as a tactic allegedly used by the BJP IT cell to target accounts posting politically sensitive content. Meta later acknowledged the suspension as an error and restored the account after Khanna appealed. As of today, her main account remains suspended.
Her X account was also locked on June 11. The only explanation she received was that following a review, X had determined that her account had violated its rules.
Khanna said a writ petition challenging the Instagram ban is currently before the Delhi High Court. Since the restriction was issued at the government’s request, she said, there is no way to appeal through the platform. “One has to take it to court if they want to appeal or challenge it, or even find out on what grounds the account was banned, because there is no transparency offered to the user,” she said.
Khanna said she is receiving legal assistance from the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), which had also supported her during her earlier suspensions.
Video on Police Lathicharge Taken Down
Varnika Dhawan, a 21-year-old content creator with approximately 56,000 followers on Instagram, uploaded a satirical video on July 24, in collaboration with a fellow creator and satirist, Nitesh Kumar Tiwari. In the video, they took a jibe at the politicians who have allegations of rape and molestation against them and how the government allegedly treats them with garlands and respect.
This video garnered around 8.3 million views, after which it was restricted in India following a similar message: “local legal requirements” or “a request from the government”
On July 22, Dhawan uploaded another video featuring a 9-year-old boy who was allegedly a victim of the lathi charge by the Delhi police during the July 20 march. This video amassed around 2.1 million views, but on August 5, it was restricted in India.
On the same day, Dhawan posted a video questioning the reason for the restriction of the second video. The caption asked: “9-year-old kid beaten by police, the video is a violation of local laws, beating up wasn’t a violation of any laws?”
View this post on Instagram
‘They are Restricting only Viral Videos’
Nitesh Kumar Tiwari, who posts satire through the Instagram page peter_paarkar2.0, also faced similar restrictions. On August 1, he uploaded an image mocking the fiasco over youth using expletives during the protest against the politicians and the ruling government. This post was also restricted in India.
Speaking to Alt News, Tiwari noted that censorship is not being implemented simply based on content. He observed, “They are restricting videos only after they go viral. My video received around 8.3 million views before it was restricted. After a few days, both Varnika and I reuploaded our videos and they are still live on our pages.”
Four videos from the Instagram account sakhi.bandhu have been restricted in India. In the first video, the user is seen playfully interacting with a policeman.
The second video shows a van loaded with food for police personnel, garnering approximately 4.3 million views.
The third video features the user singing along with other protesters and received around 634,000 views.
The last video includes a statement from Mohammed Junaid — a prominent face who volunteered and served free food and drinking water to the protesters during the CJP protest.
Another one of their videos, which depicted how the user was mishandled by the police during the protest, was taken down from Instagram.
Following these repeated bans, Sakhi uploaded a video asking Instagram for an explanation. “I cannot understand what kind of community guidelines these reels are violating that they are being censored,” they said.
Sakhi further mentioned that they have been targeted in various ways on the platform and have reported the same to Meta, but in vain. “Till date, no action has been taken regarding my…but the reels I upload, which depict reality on the ground, are getting restricted and removed.”
Alt News has written to Meta seeking clarity on the basis for the restrictions, including whether it independently reviews government requests and the criteria it applies. We also asked them about the number of such restrictions since July 20 and the appeal process, including how long reviews take and who conducts them. This story will be updated if we get a response from the platform.

Ireland is becoming a global leader in the field of innovation in harnessing digital technologies as a tool to address various barriers for access to care. In alignment with WHO, Ireland recognizes the importance of mobilizing assistive technology to help the 2.5 billion people in need globally, including older persons, people with disabilities, and those living with health conditions. This includes ensuring equitable access to assistive products such as glasses, hearing aids, walking aids, wheelchairs, prosthetics, and communication and memory devices.
In March 2024, Anne Rabbitte, T.D., Ireland’s Minister of State with special responsibility for disabilities at the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, agreed to a €12.5 million donor agreement between the Government of Ireland and WHO, aimed at accelerating affordability and availability of assistive technology for those in need.
The cooperation has been building throughout the years. Back in 2022, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, TD, launched the Global report on assistive technology, along with the Director-General of WHO and the Executive Director of UNICEF. The Taoiseach highlighted the importance of international cooperation to ensure more equitable access to assistive technology, in order to achieve a society where everyone is included and enabled to live their best life.
Minister Rabbitte stated that: “Ireland has identified the serious need to invest in public health systems alongside the WHO. The present risk of rising health needs coupled with a decreasing pool of health and social care professionals globally reveals an urgent need for all of us to act now. Ireland’s contribution aligns with the recommendations of the Global Report on Assistive Technology and supports a five-year initiative towards achieving national health system models that include assistive technology. The programme will explore and demonstrate how digital technology can facilitate people-centred services, assistive technology policy, improve the affordability and appropriateness of assistive products, enable effective provision systems, and boost the capacity of health personnel to identify, screen, refer and provide assistive technology for all those in need.”
Health personnel in Tanzania participating in on-line training on assistive products, as part of an overall program aimed at provision of simple assistive products through community and primary health care facilities - making products such as walking aids and reading glasses more readily available for people within their local area. Digital technology was instrumental in facilitating efficient learning through the platform, and enabling support for health workers from their mentors through communication apps after the training. Credit: WHO/Kylie Shae
With an ageing global population and a rise in noncommunicable diseases, an estimated 3.5 billion people will need assistive technology by 2050. Dr Yukiko Nakatani, WHO Assistant Director-General, Access to Medicines and Health Products, welcomes this important contribution from Ireland and their leadership in the digital initiative. She said: “The 2018 World Health Assembly resolution on assistive technology calls upon WHO to take the necessary steps to promote equitable access to assistive technology in our endeavour to build a more inclusive world. Our partnership with the Government of Ireland will support WHO in achieving our mission to ensure health for all, everywhere, with assistive technologies as an important enabler of well-being, inclusion, and participation.”
Through Ireland’s contribution, and in collaboration with its broad network of partners, WHO will develop evidence-based guidance for Member States on strengthening access to assistive technology through understanding, prioritising and stimulating increased innovation and use of digital solutions. The work will also involve national, regional, and global projects that test digital solutions designed to address persistent access barriers such as: digital platforms that empower users with information about assistive technology and how to access it; digital tracking of products to manage supply; and online training and support for health workers. The results and lessons learned will help countries expand their knowledge, skills, and capacities in the provision of assistive technology as an integral component of Universal Health Care.
‘Leaving no one behind’ means ensuring that people with disabilities, the older population, those affected by chronic diseases and everyone who needs assistive technology are included in society and able to live healthy and dignified lives.
* * * *
Click below to find out what is assistive technology, who needs it, and how it improves lives
Assistive technology is an umbrella term for external products used by individuals to help maintain or improve their bodily functions. Common examples are wheelchairs, glasses, prosthetic limbs, white canes, and hearing aids as well as digital solutions such as speech recognition or time management software. Assistive technology helps people in all aspects of their lives, including in education, employment, fitness, leisure and other everyday activities such as self-care, cooking and reading.
Most people will need assistive technology at some point in their lives, especially as they age. While some may require assistive technology temporarily, such as after an accident or illness, others may require it for a longer period or throughout their lifespan. It is commonly needed by older people, children and adults with disabilities, people who have been injured or who have a health condition such as diabetes, stroke and dementia.
Equitable access is key
Improving access to assistive technology enables the inclusion and participation of users in their family, community and all areas of society, including the political, economic and social spheres. Assistive technology positively impacts a person, their family and friends, and has broader socioeconomic benefits. For example:
- early provision of hearing aids for young children supports their development of language and communication skills, limiting negative impacts on their education, future employment and community participation;
- provision of appropriate wheelchairs facilitates mobility, improving individuals’ access to education and employment while reducing healthcare costs due to a reduction in secondary complications such as pressure sores and contractures;
- therapeutic footwear for diabetes reduces the incidence of foot ulcers, preventing amputations and the associated impact on individuals and burden on health-care systems; and
- timely provision of assistive technology for older people can improve their independence and safety as well as enable them to live at home for as long as possible.

Purchased a smartphone, laptop or tablet via loan financing? What happens if you miss an EMI? Can the lender lock your phone or block access to the device? According to a study by Home Credit Finance, the single biggest reason for borrowing in 2025 remained the purchase of smartphones and home appliances.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has laid out some guidelines for lenders on recovery of loans, and whether they can block or lock the device that has been purchased via EMI financing. This new framework will come into effect from January 1, 2027.
The new framework governing loan recovery practices comes on the back of increasing complaints from borrowers who have alleged harassment in the recovery process. This harassment has in the past taken the form of intimidation through social media and also the use of abusive language.
In 2024, RBI asked lenders to stop the practice of locking phones of borrowers in case of default. Lenders were doing this using an app that was installed at the time of the loan issuance.
In May this year, the RBI had released a draft framework that outlined proposed norms on the "Conduct of Regulated Entities in Recovery of Loans and Engagement of Recovery Agents". The central bank had invited comments from stakeholders. 
The final norms have now been released.
What do the new rules mean for you? What are your rights as a borrower and what does a loan default for EMI-financed devices mean for you? We break it down:
RBI’s new rules: Can your phone be locked?
RBI has clearly told lenders that they cannot disable the borrower’s mobile phone, laptop or tablet in cases of loans taken for home, car or other personal loans. The restrictions to use can only come in place for devices that have been financed via loans.
"A bank shall not deploy any technology-based mechanism...which restricts or disables any of the functionalities of a mobile device of a borrower such as mobile phone, tablet and laptop as a recovery tool, except to recover its loan dues arising out from financing of such a device," RBI has said.
RBI’s New EMI Device Rules: What Lenders Can Do
Even in such cases the restrictions have to be gradual and with certain rules in place. Let’s take a look at what the lender can and can’t do:
What the lender can do:
Lenders have been allowed to impose gradual restrictions on the devices after 30 days of the payment being overdue.
So, to begin with if your EMI is overdue for less than 30 days then the lender cannot do anything to the device. The lender is required to send you a formal notice.
If the loan remains overdue between 30-60 days, then the gradual restrictions can be introduced.
The full contractual restrictions can only be imposed after the loan has been overdue for more than 60 days.
If a device locking software is eventually used, it can only be one that is certified by the original equipment manufacturer or the operating system provider.
RBI’s New EMI Device Rules: What Lenders Can't Do
But outgoing and incoming calls cannot be stopped.
SMS, Emergency SOS and any restrictions that impact work or employment are not allowed.
Lenders cannot access details on the borrower's phone such as contacts, photos, call logs, location history or even SMSes.
Borrowers should also be aware that once the loan payment is received by the lender, the device has to be unlocked within an hour. Any delay in unlocking at the lender’s end will entail a Rs 250 per hour compensation for the borrower, up to the loan amount.
Additionally, no uncertified recovery agents will be allowed to interact with the borrowers for the loan.
What do the new rules mean for you?
The biggest takeaway for loan borrowers is that your device can’t be blocked for non-payment of EMIs. Also, if at all any restrictions come into place, they can only be if the loan has financed that particular device. The loan agreement needs to clearly state these conditions.
“A missed EMI can no longer make your phone go dark. From 1 January 2027, the default is that lenders cannot lock or disable a device to recover dues at all. The sole exception is a device bought on that specific loan, and only if the agreement says so, notice is given, and functionality is curbed gradually. A defaulted car loan, personal loan or credit card can never touch your phone,” explains Vivek Iyer, Partner and Financial Services Risk Advisory Leader, Grant Thornton Bharat.
RBI’s New EMI Device Rules: Know Borrower Rights
So the next important thing to note is this: always read the terms and conditions of the loan agreement when opting for an EMI-financed device.
“Read the agreement for how it treats remote access and default remedies. The restriction is unenforceable unless written in expressly. Borrow only from regulated lenders, since every safeguard depends on it,” Vivek Iyer recommends.
“Set up auto-debit, because 30 days now starts a formal pathway. And insist on written notice. That is your evidence for both the graded-step rule and any compensation claim,” Iyer adds.
According to Adhil Shetty, CEO of Bankbazaar.com, the new framework brings greater clarity to how lenders can use technology for recovery of dues on EMI-financed purchases.
“It allows action against genuine defaults while placing clearer limits on how that action can be taken. A key safeguard is that a lender cannot restrict a device that was not financed through the loan. For borrowers, the broader impact is greater clarity around their rights and privacy. This should create a better balance between a lender's need to recover dues and a borrower's right to fair treatment,” he tells TOI.
The Bankbazaar CEO also advocates carefully reading the term agreements instead of just focusing on the monthly EMI figure.
Why India borrowed in 2025 (Source: Home Credit Finance Report)
“Consumers should look beyond the monthly EMI and understand the financing terms before committing to a purchase. They should check whether the agreement allows device-based recovery and understand the consequences of missing payments,” he tells TOI.
Yet another important point to note is that while the RBI’s rules safeguard the privacy and rights of individuals, they do not remove the repayment obligation.
“The EMI should therefore be comfortably affordable and the recovery terms understood before taking the loan,” Shetty says.
Some steps also need attention after you have repaid the loan.
Santosh Agarwal, CEO of Paisabazaar suggests that on successful repayment of the loan, borrowers should get the access relinquished and disable any technology mechanism at the earliest.
“It is important for borrowers to retain all repayment proof and contact the lender for unlocking their devices,” she tells TOI.

Arteta not worried about Arsenal contract talks
- Published
Mikel Arteta has said that supporters "don't have to worry about" his future at Arsenal as he wants to extend his contract and the time left on his deal is "not an issue".
The Gunners boss is into the final 12 months of his agreement that he signed in 2024 but says he is relaxed about formal talks taking place regarding a renewal.
Arteta has been in charge of Arsenal since 2019 and led the club to their first Premier League title in 22 years last season.
Arsenal face Manchester City in the Community Shield on Sunday (15:00 BST) and Arteta was asked in his news conference about the concern some supporters may have given he is yet to agreed a new deal before the 2026-27 campaign kicks off.
"No, they don't have to worry about any of that because I want to be here, I'm extremely happy," Arteta said.
"I feel very grateful to work with the people that I work with and whenever we have the possibility we will resolve that and that's it."
The Gunners are attempting to build on their success of last season and strengthen their squad in the transfer window.
They were unsuccessful in their pursuit of Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr but have signed midfielder Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle, Greece international winger Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge and made Piero Hincapie's loan move from Bayern Leverkusen into a permanent transfer for a combined £143.5m.
Goalkeeper Illan Meslier has also arrived on a free transfer from Leeds United while, from last season's squad, Leandro Trossard, Jakub Kiwior and Christian Norgaard have been moved on.
The Gunners remain interested in Aston Villa's Ezri Konsa or Jarell Quansah of Bayer Leverkusen as a further defensive reinforcement in the market following injuries to William Saliba and Jurrien Timber.
With the transfer window open until 1 September, the feeling at the club is that finalising a contract can come at a quieter period in the season.
"There's always another priority I think and that's the way we've been treating it. Arteta added.
"I think because everybody feels comfortable that the time on the contract is not going to be an issue.
"I think because my will certainly is to be here and I'm very happy here.
"And my feeling from the club is is the same one so I think that's why everybody doing it things in a really organic way."
Arsenal also reached the Champions League final last season where they were beaten by Paris St-Germain and Arteta has repeatedly spoken of his ambition since that loss to take the Gunners to next level.
"I'm not going to talk about any individuals, obviously what I can tell you is the ambition of the club." Arteta said.
"It's big that we want to improve the squad, we want to evolve the squad in order to achieve that.
"We have obviously detected some areas that they can be strengthened and that's what we are trying to do."

A Texas oil company with ties to Donald Trump just landed a dozen shipping containers of drilling equipment on Greenland's remote eastern coast. They never got permission.
Greenland's government issued a "strong warning" that no approval had been granted. But Greenland Energy, a company set up last year with chairman Larry Swets enjoying access to Trump's inner circle, pushed forward anyway.
A company representative named Robert Price told residents at a community meeting in June that they had permission to bring equipment ashore. That was false. Greenland's resources ministry confirmed there are "no actually active permissions for any exploration activity." When caught, the company blamed "enthusiasm" for the confusion. Then the next month, locals watched a tug pull a barge to shore and unload containers.
(Facebook user Jim Heath)
"An American company lands equipment on foreign soil without permission, lies about having approval, and the sitting president posts memes threatening to take the whole island. Trump is making the USA a villain in real time," the post ended.
Similar versions of the claim spread elsewhere. One Instagram video alleged Trump was "having an oil company that he is linked to go and start drilling in Greenland" and that "experts are saying across the Internet that this is what looks to be essentially an invasion without an invasion." One article's headline went further, claiming that "Trump's oil company begins drilling in Greenland without consulting authorities." Snopes readers also contacted us about the story and searched our website for information about it.
In short, there was some truth to the claims. However, they often made both the company's actions and its ties to Trump sound stronger than the evidence showed. It was true that in late July 2026, the equipment connected to the planned oil project was moved without the required authorization, which led Greenland's government to issue a warning. But, as of this writing, the drilling had not started and the exploration licenses were still valid. Also, we found no evidence that Trump owned or controlled Greenland Energy.
For those reasons, we rated this claim a mixture of true, false and undetermined information.
Snopes reached out to Greenland Energy, Greenlandic authorities and the White House for comment and will update this story if we receive responses.
Origin of the rumor and what actually happened
Social media claims stemmed from genuine reporting about a planned oil exploration project in Jameson Land in eastern Greenland. Questions about the project already surfaced in July 2026, when The Guardian reported that Greenland Energy representative Robert Price told residents the company had permission to bring equipment ashore, while Greenland's resources ministry said there were no active permissions for exploration activities or preparations.
At the end of July, Danish news outlet Danwatch reported that equipment linked to the project was moved to Nerlerit Inaat without the required authorization. Greenland's government confirmed the move and issued a "strong warning," saying future logistical activities had to be approved in advance.
Later, The Guardian reported on Aug. 8 that a "Trump-linked" oil firm was preparing to drill. Importantly, the article said the company was preparing for drilling, and not that drilling had already started.
Did the company start drilling without permission?
The incident that prompted Greenland's warning was not unauthorized drilling, but the movement of equipment connected to the project without the necessary approval. Greenland's Ministry of Trade and Mineral Resources said the license holder "did not have the necessary approvals from the mineral resources authority in place before initiating this operation," according to a Google translation of its statement.
The project's actual drilling rig did not arrive in Greenland. Stampede Drilling, the Canadian contractor hired for the project, said it would not take the rig ashore unless all required regulatory approvals were in place.
But that does not mean the entire project lacks a legal basis. Greenland stopped issuing new oil and gas licenses in 2021, but the three licenses covering the Jameson Land project were issued in 2015 and 2018 and remain valid through the end of 2028. Those licenses do not automatically authorize drilling, which still requires separate approvals from the authorities.
Moreover, Greenland Energy does not itself currently hold those licenses. Greenland's government said the company "incorrectly informed the public" that it was the license holder. The licenses are in fact held by White Flame Energy A/S, while Greenland Energy is involved as an investor and operator of the project.
As of August 2026, drilling had not started. On Aug. 12, Greenlandic authorities said the required regulatory process could not be completed in time for the planned drilling campaign, including the assessment of its environmental and social impact. The government and company said drilling could now begin no earlier than winter 2027.
How is the company connected to Trump?
We found no evidence that Trump owns, controls or has directly invested in the company. Therefore, calling Greenland Energy "Trump's oil company" is unsupported. The "Trump-linked" description appears to come mainly from connections between people involved with the company and Trump or his administration.
For instance, as The Guardian reported, Greenland Energy hired Envoy Media — a company founded by television personality Phil McGraw. McGraw supported Trump during the 2024 election and Trump later appointed him to his Religious Liberty Commission. The company also appointed Carol Craig to its board. Craig leads Sidus Space, which has received work connected to the Trump administration's Golden Dome missile defense initiative.
The Guardian pointed to investor Kenneth Griffin, a major Republican donor who voted for Trump in 2024 and contributed to his inauguration. The outlet also reported that some Greenland Energy shareholders discussed hoping for a public endorsement from Trump that could boost the company's stock price. Snopes was unable to independently verify the posts from the shareholder Telegram group cited by the newspaper.
There was also some direct contact with the Trump administration. Greenland Energy CEO Robert Price told Greenlandic broadcaster KNR that he and company chairman Larry Swets met Trump's special envoy to Greenland, Jeff Landry, at a conference in Nuuk in May and discussed the project. However, Price said the company did not receive any promises of political support from the administration and denied having any broader relationship with Landry or Trump's circle.
Still, none of those connections showed that Trump was behind the project. The Guardian reported Greenland Energy representative Robert Price, when asked whether Swets had close relations with Trump, replied, "Not that I know of." Swets also said the oil project was not connected to the prospect of U.S. annexation of Greenland.
Greenland is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark and is strategically important because of its Arctic location and natural resources. Trump has repeatedly said he wants the United States to acquire Greenland and has at times floated the possibility of using military force.
Bottom line
All in all, it was true that in late July 2026, equipment connected to the Jameson Land oil project was moved without the required authorization, and Greenland's government issued a warning over it. The company also had some indirect connections to Trump and his administration. However, as of this writing, it had not yet started drilling. Also, Trump does not own the company, and we found no evidence that he directly instructed it to carry out its activities in Greenland. The project itself is based on legally valid exploration licenses, although separate activities still need approval.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated numerous rumors surrounding Trump's interest in Greenland.

In conversation with Clare Binns, managing director of Picturehouse Cinemas, at the Edinburgh Film Festival’s inaugural UK Film Conference BFI CEO Ben Roberts was candid from the outset about the problems of working for a major public-funding body. Having previously worked for numerous UK distribution and sales outfits, Roberts admitted that he had been warned against taking the job as Director of the BFI Film Fund in 2012. “Various people said to me, ‘Everyone will hate you and you’ll never work again,’” he laughed. “So, there was definitely that sense going in — that these jobs are quite challenging, because you can make a lot of enemies. The fact is you turn most people down in that job. You just do, because the numbers are stacked against you.”
Roberts now has more than just the Film Fund at his disposal, dispensing sums in the region of £150 million in a three-year cycle, and, in his interview, he outlined a case for a future of British film that would include the whole process, from script to screen — which includes supporting exhibition, distribution, archival work, festivals and education. “The BFI does a unique job of having some money to support filmmakers,” he said, “which can be very easily [measured]: Yes or no. Yes, you got it. No, you didn’t get it. But there are so many other things that the BFI does to try to make the conditions for making and releasing films in the UK possible.”
Watch on Deadline
Roberts conceded that the BFI system can seem like a bureaucracy but defended the amount of paperwork. “It’s lottery money,” he said, “so you have to run everything in a very open way. We’re different to the BBC or Film4 in the fact that we can’t have a conversation with one of you in this room, and when you tell me about your project — and we like the sound of it — say, ‘Come in for a meeting, let’s give you some money.’ We can’t work like that because we have to run an open process. And then, within that, we establish some goals about what we might be looking for.” (In a shorter version of this comment, Roberts quipped, “Look, everyone has to fill out a form. Get over it!”)
Another preconception about the BFI, he said, is that it favors worthy projects that tick politically correct boxes. “Principally, you’re looking for something that feels worthy of ‘good cause’ money, because national lottery money is ‘good cause’ money. So, you’re looking for something that really needs that money — something that the market is probably not going to obviously fund, but that’s still pretty broad. And then there’s obviously, as there should be, a qualitative assessment as well. Is it good? Does it read well? Is the team that’s making it — even if they’re early in their career — clear on what they want to achieve? Have they made anything that would suggest that raw talent is there? An old colleague of mine, when I first joined the film fund said, ‘It’s not social work.’ Which is really important, actually, because it’s not social work.”
On the subject of artistic quality, Roberts also suggested that the metric for success should not be limited to two of the most common, which tend to prioritize the role of the director and the importance of box-office. “You could have a film that might not make money, but an actor in that film might be identified. We often sometimes forget to talk about the actors that have been discovered, or platformed, through lottery funded or publicly funded films and gone on to be huge stars. Tom Holland’s second film was How I Live Now, directed by the great Kevin McDonald and was funded with lottery money. And that was putting him on a particular path. Olivia Colman’s first standout work that moved her from sketch comedy to dramatic feature film was Paddy Considine’s Tyrannosaur. So, I think there are many markers of success in a film.”
Warming to his theme, Roberts pushed back at the sometimes-combative relationship between artists and those dishing out public funds. “I do think I should be given a hard time,” he said. “But it’s a two-way street. We get quite frustrated by the quality of original thought sometimes, original ideas. And there is plenty of opportunity for filmmakers to start to demonstrate their original thoughts and their skills without needing to wait for the very highly prized and highly won lottery money… I think it can be a misconception that a lot of money needs to be spent in order to create something that’s got value.”
He did concede, however, that “there are some things I think we haven’t been great at in the UK as an independent sector. For instance, I don’t think we’re great at comedy. Obviously, the Edinburgh Film Festival opened with a really strong, lottery-backed comedy this year, The Incomer. I’m not saying we don’t do it, but I think it takes real skill to do it well. We know audiences love horror, and I think that we pull our punches sometimes in horror, as well as comedy, in independent film. Someone said to me recently, ‘I’ve got a horror project.’ I said, ‘Is it scary?’ He said, ‘It’s more of a mood.’ But we don’t want mood. Go for it. Go for it a little bit more. There are a few areas where sometimes we sort of polish off the edges of genres that punch through a bit harder.”
Both Binns and Roberts commented on the recent renaissance of cinemagoing among young people, as well as an uptick in attendances since Covid, but Roberts was particularly keen to get to potential audiences as soon as possible. “There are lots of ways that we try to open up pathways for young people,” he said. “But the missing piece — and it’s really, really important — is having film firmly in the classroom. I mean, teaching film as a storytelling medium, particularly a time when — on a sort of crude level — I would say that watching is the new reading for a lot of people. So, how you develop really good interpretation skills, literacy skills, how you can create your own communication channels healthily and creatively is really important right now.”
