Trump’s 2024 photo op comes back to haunt Republicans in the midterms
Most of the items Trump displayed at Bedminster are now pricier, some by a lot
Two years after Donald Trump staged a press conference in New Jersey where he stood alongside basic household groceries to attack Democratic inflation, food costs continue to climb.
At his Bedminster golf club on August 15, 2024, he stood amidst displays stacked with meat, fruit, cereal, milk and standard pantry items while laying the blame for steep grocery price hikes on the Biden administration. The event, featuring charts illustrating rising costs, targeted Democratic nominee Kamala Harris while emphasizing Trump’s primary claim: that he was uniquely equipped to curb inflation and ease the cost of living.
Fast forward two years, and elevated prices at the pump and the supermarket continue to strain family finances, making living costs the dominant concern for the electorate.
The disparity between his promises to lower costs and the daily reality for shoppers has emerged as a critical weakness for the Republican Party leading into November's midterm elections.
According to Reuters/Ipsos polling, voters currently favor Democrats over Republicans by a slim margin on economic stewardship, marking the first time in almost ten years that Democrats have held this advantage.
Sheila Carney, a 68-year-old Trump voter, voiced her frustration with a curse word while loading $70 worth of groceries into her trunk near Trump's Bedminster facility. The haul was minimal, consisting of a bit of meat, laundry detergent and a 12-pack of iced tea.
For Carney, that checkout total demonstrated that the cost-of-living struggles Trump has on occasion brushed off as a Democratic "hoax" are very real for working families.
"This is real. He can say it's not, but it is," said Carney, a hospital administration assistant who has postponed her retirement to help clear her son's student loan debt. "He hasn't brought anything down."
An examination by Reuters covering 26 food categories monitored by the Bureau of Labor Statistics—and displayed during Trump’s Bedminster presentation—shows that prices have increased by 3.4% during the initial 19 months of his second term.
While that rate is under one-fourth of the increase registered over the equivalent stretch of former President Joe Biden’s term, it misses Trump’s goal of bringing prices down, as sharp price surges for beef, coffee and apples have outweighed price reductions in goods like butter and eggs.
A White House official cited figures released Wednesday showing minimal growth in U.S. consumer prices from June to July as proof that inflationary pressure is stabilizing.
"The July CPI report is further proof that President Trump’s long-term agenda is delivering: prescription drug and auto insurance costs continue to fall, real wages are rising, and beef prices have cooled while other household essentials like eggs, poultry, and dairy remain low," the official said.
LACK OF ENTHUSIASM
Carney, a registered Republican, noted that elevated supermarket and fuel costs stemming from the conflict with Iran have driven her toward enough disillusionment that she may skip the upcoming midterms, mirroring broader polling trends that show weaker voter enthusiasm among Republicans compared to Democrats.
Carney was among 17 independent and Republican voters surveyed by Reuters in New Jersey's 7th Congressional District, a competitive area encompassing Bedminster where turnout among undecided voters could decide the outcome. The contest features Republican incumbent Tom Kean against Democratic challenger Rebecca Bennett, who has made economic frustration a centerpiece of her campaign.
Over half of those surveyed indicated they were undecided or leaning toward Bennett. Although food inflation was a major concern, grievances regarding Kean frequently focused on his multi-month absence from public appearances earlier in the year, an absence he linked to depression.
These economic perspectives align with comments from other Trump supporters interviewed in recent months who, despite backing the president, report that ongoing financial strain has weakened their motivation to turn out in November. Such hesitation creates an added headwind for Republicans and puts greater pressure on their voter mobilization efforts.
Francesco Trebbi, a professor of public policy at the University of California, Berkeley, recently co-authored a study demonstrating that Trump received higher support during the 2024 election in counties where inflation overtook wage gains, undercutting consumer buying power.
Because real wage growth remains sluggish and behind overall economic expansion, Trebbi suggested that dynamic could invert this November.
"I expect the same anti-incumbent shift to happen in 2026, this time possibly weakening Republicans," he said, noting that weekly grocery trips serve as a "psychologically salient" reminder of household budget constraints. "Each time one does it, it is the equivalent of a campaign ad against the incumbent."
TRUMP SUPPORT
Presidents have limited influence over inflation, which stems from complex economic variables and is primarily managed by the Federal Reserve. A significant portion of Republicans remain inclined to grant Trump leeway, even as tariff policies and the military conflict in Iran add upward pressure to prices.
Bonnie Chandler, 64, intends to back Kean, and said she believes some companies are intentionally maintaining high prices to damage Trump politically. She said the rise of progressive figures within the Democratic Party rules out supporting Democratic nominees.
"I'm going to vote Republican. I'm not a woke person. I'm not a communist. I'm not a socialist," she said.
Lauren DeGirolamo, a 34-year-old Trump voter, noted that priorities like border security and education carry greater weight for her than food costs, which she considers to have leveled off under Trump following sharp rises under the Biden administration.
"I feel grocery prices are pretty much at level with where they were during Biden. I know some of the key things that I look for - eggs - have gone down," she said, confirming her plan to vote Republican in November.
Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics indicates egg prices have dropped almost 40% under Trump, marking a market stabilization after avian flu outbreaks drove a sharp price hike that originated during the Biden presidency. Eggs are one of six categories out of 26 to experience price drops since 2025, alongside bacon, butter, and cooking fats and oils.
However, the majority of the products featured during Trump’s Bedminster showcase have grown more expensive, several by substantial margins. Raw beef has surged 19.2%, fresh fish and seafood 8.6%, apples 14%, and coffee roughly 23%.
HITTING CLOSE TO HOME
A Reuters/Ipsos survey completed earlier this month revealed that Trump's net approval rating on managing the cost of living stood at -47%, down sharply from -6% when his term began. This marks his lowest score by a broad margin, far behind his standing on the general economy (-35%) and immigration (-16%).
Bennett told Reuters that, if victorious, her priorities would include reversing Trump's tariffs, seeking an end to the Iran conflict, and restoring food stamp funding to assist households struggling with grocery bills.
The challenge is personal, according to Bennett, a military veteran and married mother of two daughters.
"This is not an abstract concept to me," she said. "For example, beef is very expensive, so we don't buy beef anymore."
Whether Kean—whose campaign team did not reply to inquiries for comment—can retain his district could depend on voters like Margaret Derkach, a traditional Republican leaning voter who is contemplating changing her ballot if financial burdens do not ease.
"The cost of living, as far as homes, apartments and food - the necessities - they have gone up. It's shocking, shocking," said Derkach, 84, speaking after a trip to discount supermarket Aldi.
While acknowledging that Trump "inherited a mess" from Biden, Derkach added, "I am undecided right now. I have to see."

Tarling's team withdraws as Volta a Portugal resumes
- Published
Finlay Tarling's team, NSN Development, have withdrawn from the remaining stages of the Volta a Portugal following the British cyclist's death.
The 19-year-old died following an accident during the eighth stage of the race on Friday.
Organisers confirmed the race will continue with the penultimate stage on Saturday, while tributes will be held for Tarling before the start.
In a statement, the Volta said it had been a "tragic day for cycling" and the race would be held in an "atmosphere of profound mourning".
It added that "as a sign of respect and mourning" the main sponsors of the event had agreed to cancel all activities for the remaining two stages.
"The race continues. There will be a sporting competition, but not a party... This Saturday, the Volta rides for Finlay."
Welshman Tarling was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8km route from Melgaco to Fafe on Friday.
In a statement provided to local media, Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said there had been "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle" and that an investigation was under way.
"Following Fin Tarling's tragic passing on Friday, the NSN Development Team has withdrawn from the remaining Volta a Portugal stages," NSN said in a statement on Saturday morning.
"With the full support of Fin's parents, the WorldTour team will race on at Czech Tour and the Arctic Race of Norway. We will continue to hold Fin in our hearts as we race in his honor, doing what he loved most.
"We want to thank everyone in the cycling community and beyond for the incredible support at this difficult time."
Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.
He looked to be following in the footsteps of his older brother Josh as a time trial specialist.
He finished in third in the under-23 men's individual time trial at the British Championships in June and competed in the Tour of Britain just under 12 months ago.
"This is not the time for speculation about the circumstances of the accident. The incident is being investigated by the GNR Command, which is responsible for rigorously establishing the facts," the Volta added.
"We all remain deeply shaken.
"Cycling is a sport that involves risks, but we are never prepared for a tragedy of this magnitude. Finlay lost his life. A family lost a son. A team lost a team-mate. Cycling lost one of its own. It is a tragedy that transcends the competition itself."

As rain lashed the Pir Panjal mountains before dawn on 19 July, Haji Mohammad Latief stepped outside his home in Murrah, a remote mountain village in Indian-administered Kashmir. His daughter had asked him to move the family’s car to a safer place as the rain got heavier.
“I had only just parked it,” Latief recalled. “When I turned around, I saw the water coming.” Minutes later, a cloudburst sent mud, boulders and water crashing down the hillside.
Latief, 48, had spent years building the house, where five generations of his Gujjar family lived together. Within minutes, the torrent swallowed it, trapping eight family members inside. He survived only because he had stepped outside. By dawn, everything he had built lay in rubble.
When the Guardian reached Murrah four days later, electricity, roads and mobile networks were cut off. Floodwaters had washed away roads and footbridges, leaving the only way into the village a 90-minute walk through rain and landslide debris. Residents carried sacks of flour, cooking gas cylinders and medicines across the broken crossing.
Murrah is perched high in the Pir Panjal range above the town of Bafliaz, in Poonch district, about 125 miles (200km) south-west of Srinagar, Kashmir’s main city. The village is home to mostly Gujjars, one of the largest pastoralist communities in the Himalayas, whose livelihoods have long depended on livestock, farming and seasonal migration through the mountains.
The hillside remained too unstable for excavators to reach. Soldiers, disaster response teams and local volunteers searched the debris by hand while others combed the swollen Suran River for the missing.
Latief now lives in the house of his brother, Mohd Bashir, just above the landslide. Inside, women gathered to mourn while men quietly received visitors offering condolences. Verses from the Qur’an echoed through the house.
“I built that house for my family,” Latief said, holding up pictures of his 16-year-old son Sajjad Ahmed, an aspiring cricketer, whose body was still missing. Days before the disaster, the family recorded videos together.
As mourners gathered, news spread that another body had been found several miles down the river; the room fell silent as another funeral procession passed through the village.
Among those searching was Mohammad Razak, 45, who had spent four days combing the river with a team of volunteers. “We’ve been searching every bend of the river,” he said. “We’re still hoping we’ll find them.”
Murrah was among the worst-hit places after a series of cloudbursts, flash floods and landslides swept Jammu and Kashmir this month, killing at least 28 people. Scientists say rising temperatures are increasing the likelihood of short, intense rainfall events across the western Himalayas. In steep mountainous terrain, these rains can trigger rapid flooding and landslides, putting remote communities at increased risk. For mountain communities, the climate crisis is also exacerbating longstanding geographical and social vulnerabilities.
The destruction stretched far beyond Murrah. About 30 miles away in Rajouri, the Manawar Tawi River burst its banks, washing away roads, dozens of vehicles and the town’s main Bela bus station.
Low-lying settlements along the riverbank were submerged in mud and debris. Several houses collapsed across the Pir Panjal mountains, livestock were swept away and hundreds of families were displaced.
About 180 miles north, in Gurez Valley near the line of control with Pakistan-administered Kashmir, residents say they are seeing the same pattern. A cloudburst in Achoora village on 20 July damaged the crops of 11 families and blocked the valley’s only road.
Residents say increasingly erratic rainfall is disrupting farming and making traditional livelihoods more precarious. It followed a series of cloudbursts that hit Gurez and neighbouring Tulail over the past month, damaging homes, farmland, bridges, and roads.
“People knew when the snow would come and when to plant crops,” said Aamir Asghar Khan, 26, a resident of Achoora. “Nothing seems predictable any more. The rain is getting more intense every year, and the frequent cloudbursts are threatening our livelihoods.”
Heavy rainfall also triggered devastating floods and landslides in Ladakh and across the border in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, reinforcing concerns that increasingly erratic weather is affecting communities across the western Himalayas.
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (Icimod) said the western Himalayas were experiencing frequent bursts of intense rainfall capable of triggering floods, landslides and cloudbursts. Accelerating glacier melt is likely to increase flood risks in the short term before reducing water availability in coming decades.
“The challenge our mountain communities face is twofold – too much water at times and too little at others,” an expert from Icimod said. “Adaptation requires work on both fronts, managing flood risk and water scarcity together.”
ICIMOD said priorities included expanding community-based early warning systems, installing more weather stations in high-altitude areas, restoring damaged watersheds and designing roads and other infrastructure for future weather conditions rather than historical weather patterns.
Dr Suheel Rasool Mir, a Kashmir-based sociologist who studies Indigenous communities in Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, said pastoral communities were among the first to bear the consequences of erratic weather as their livelihoods relied directly on forests, rivers, grazing lands and seasonal migration.
“For Gujjar, Bakarwal and Dard-Shin communities, these disasters are not simply natural hazards,” he said. “As climate extremes become more frequent, they lose not only homes and livestock but also the ecological knowledge and ancestral livelihoods that have sustained them for generations.”
For Latief back in Murrah, only one hope remained. “I just want to find them,” he said. “Then we can bury our family together.”

Lalduhoma said that the scheme aimed at going beyond financial assistance by enhancing skills, creating livelihood opportunities and supporting the economic development of individuals, families and the state.
Highlighting measures aimed at promoting entrepreneurship, Lalduhoma said the government has launched a ₹20 crore Mizoram Bana Kaih Venture Capital Fund to help young people establish businesses and become self-reliant.

A ₹30.13 crore project sanctioned by the Ministry of DoNER for a ginger processing unit in Champhai is expected to increase the value of processed produce and boost farmers' incomes, he said.

Under the National Mission on Edible Oils, oil palm cultivation has covered 1,607 hectares, while farmers have sold 7,225 metric tonnes of produce worth ₹10.53 crore.

On fiscal reforms, Lalduhoma said Mizoram's tax collection had reached ₹1,278.55 crore in 2025-26, while reforms, including GST 2.0, were helping widen and streamline revenue collection.
Lalduhoma said that his government was also expanding rural infrastructure and social welfare programmes.
Mizoram is among the first states preparing to implement VB-GRAM , with ₹611.65 crore earmarked for its launch, he said.
Under VVP-II, 109 border villages are being covered, while 273 new computer-equipped libraries have been established in rural areas.
Under PMAY-Gramin, 25,433 houses have been completed, he said.
To strengthen food security, the government has distributed benefits under the Mizoram State Special Ration Package to 29,000 families and stocked over 1,67 lakh quintals of rice as monsoon reserve for 2026-27, the chief minister said.

Taliban leaders mark 5 years in power in Afghanistan as UN official warns of crisis
Taliban rulers have celebrated the fifth anniversary of their return to power in Afghanistan
KABUL, Afghanistan -- Taliban rulers and other officials gathered at Afghanistan’s traditional Loya Jirga assembly hall on Saturday to celebrate the fifth anniversary of their return to power, touting having brought stability and an end to conflict after decades of upheaval.
A top United Nations official, however, warned of a grave human rights crisis in the country where girls above the age of 12 are denied an education.
The Taliban seized power on Aug. 15, 2021, as the U.S. and other NATO troops withdrew following a costly two-decade war. The U.S. withdrawal led to chaos at Kabul airport as crowds of people tried to flee the country in desperation.
Soon after taking power, the Taliban administration imposed a ban on girls’ education beyond the sixth grade and later also banned higher education for women, despite having pledged before the takeover that women would be allowed access to education, employment and public participation.
Women have also been banned from public spaces such as gyms and parks, from taking part in sports and traveling to distant locations without a male guardian.
At the Loya Jirga, high-ranking officials were joined by some foreign representatives and thousands of ordinary citizens for speeches marking what they said was Afghanistan's liberation from American forces.
The Taliban government remains isolated internationally, with Russia being the only country to have recognized it formally.
“We pray to Almighty God to forever protect our homeland from occupation, aggression, wars, and insecurity, and to enable our people to enjoy peace, tranquility, and prosperity under the auspices of the Sharia-based government,” the Taliban government’s deputy spokesman, Hamdullah Fitrat, said during the ceremony.
There were no women present.
Celebrations were also held in provinces across Afghanistan, where Taliban flags and posters emblazoned with slogans in praise of the Taliban’s return to power were displayed along major roads and marketplaces.
In a video message, Richard Bennett, the U.N. special rapporteur on the human rights situation in Afghanistan, said the country was undergoing a deep human rights crisis.
“While the era of war has ended, it’s questionable whether there’s real peace, and the human rights situation has steadily deteriorated, most dramatically for women and girls,” Bennett said. “My mandate has concluded that this system amounts to the crime against humanity of gender persecution.”
“The crisis extends well beyond gender discrimination, even beyond gender apartheid,” he continued. “Across Afghanistan we continue to document arbitrary arrests, torture and ill treatment, extrajudicial killings, corporal punishment, enforced disappearances, restrictions on freedom of expression, attacks on journalists and human rights defenders, persecution of ethnic and religious minorities, discrimination against LGBT plus persons, and the reduction of civic space.”
Bennett warned the international community against “normalizing” the Taliban’s policies, saying it would legitimize the discrimination and tell “victims their suffering is negotiable.”
In an interview with The Associated Press this week, Molvi Hayatullah Mahajar Farahi, deputy minister in the Taliban government for broadcasting at the Ministry of Information and Culture, said despite “challenges and difficulties” the administration has in the past five years delivered security, infrastructure and created jobs.
Farahi, when asked, did not address the issue of the education of girls and women but said “the level of investment made in universities surpasses anything seen in the past."
The U.N. agency on education and culture, UNESCO, estimates that some 2.4 million girls have been excluded from secondary education.
The world body’s agency on women’s rights, U.N. Women, said this week that women and girls are facing the harshest restriction in the world and that the bans are damaging Afghanistan’s future, with the lack of teachers, doctors, nurses and midwives threatening the country’s social and economic foundations.

India’s AI story has grown beyond building an Indian equivalent of ChatGPT. The current phase is about building the infrastructure, data and applications that can make AI work for India and give Indian companies an edge in markets beyond the country. The government is already doing its bit. The IndiaAI Mission, with an outlay of roughly ₹10,300 Cr, is backing around 20 indigenous sovereign AI model proposals, spanning 12 large and eight small language models. It is also building a public dataset platform and offering subsidised access to GPUs for startups, tackling two of the biggest constraints facing India’s AI ambitions: data and compute. But the more interesting signs are emerging outside the government programme. A new generation of AI founders is moving beyond the race to build yet another general-purpose model and tackling problems that require deeper domain expertise. Some are building the data infrastructure needed to teach machines how the physical world works. Others are developing sovereign inference platforms, AI systems that can operate across India’s many languages, and tools tailored to the quirks of Indian enterprises and consumers. This shift matters because India’s AI advantage may not come from building the biggest model, but from building systems around AI that are difficult to replicate — proprietary datasets, local-language capabilities, domain-specific intelligence, and applications designed around problems that Western AI companies have historically overlooked. The opportunity is already drawing capital. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, H1 2026, Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn in the first six months of 2026, nearly four times the amount raised during the same period last year. The funding boom, however, is only one part of the story. The more telling signal is where founders are choosing to deploy that capital. As India marks its 80th Independence Day, we are back with yet another edition of Inc42’s AI Startups To Watch. This edition of the AI Startups To Watch offers a glimpse into what India’s next AI layer could look like — from the data needed to train machines on the physical world and AI-powered cinematic content to enterprise productivity, deeptech healthcare and education. These are not simply startups using AI as a feature. They are attempting to build businesses around some of the hardest problems that emerge when AI moves from the laboratory into the real world. With that thought, here are the five emerging ventures that made it to the eleventh edition of Inc42’s AI Startups To Watch. Editor's Note: This is not a ranking. The startups featured here are a curated selection by the Inc42 editorial team and are listed alphabetically. Clairva | Contextual Intelligence For World Models As AI moves from understanding language to operating in the physical world, the training data behind these systems is changing. A robot learning to navigate a kitchen or a world model trying to understand human movement cannot learn everything it needs from text and internet images. Clairva converts real-world video into structured behavioural signals that models can use for training, fine-tuning and evaluation. Founded in 2025 by Sunil Nair, Dushyant Verma and Sabari Raju, the startup sits at the intersection of AI training data, multimodal AI and embodied AI. Its pipeline structures elements such as movement, object interaction, task sequence, gesture, speech and cultural context, combined with consent, licensing, provenance and usage-right information. The output is a model-ready dataset whose origin, permissions and structure are known. Clairva is deliberately building deep supply in markets where AI training data remains thin: India, Southeast Asia and the wider Global South. It follows a B2B model, licensing datasets to AI labs, robotics companies and multimodal developers, and recently raised $500,000 in pre-seed funding led by Venture Catalysts. The startup is targeting a combination of markets. Among them, the AI training dataset market is projected to reach $16.3 Bn by 2033, while the embodied AI market is forecast to hit $23.06 Bn by 2030. Coreworks | Offering AI-Powered Business Intelligence Founders, marketers and analysts often spend days assembling presentations, only to have a number questioned in a meeting without being able to trace where it came from. Coreworks is building a platform that connects directly to a company's data and generates a finished report or presentation, with every figure traceable to its source. Founded in 2025 by Prashant Kumar and Pavan Sondur, the platform reads data semantically, surfaces the metrics and trends that matter, and produces an editable deck in minutes rather than days. Each metric links to the exact formula, cell, or row behind it, so updating the source automatically updates the output. Users can upload their own brand deck so the output matches their design language. The startup is targeting the report and presentation automation space, targeting India's augmented analytics market, which is estimated to reach $2.89 Bn by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 17.6%. It is positioning itself as an alternative to the manual process of assembling and verifying board-ready decks from raw spreadsheets. eNLife Research | AI-Powered Early Detection For Neurodegenerative Diseases Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's are often detected only after symptoms appear, when treatment options have narrowed. India-based eNLife Research is combining biomarker research with AI-powered analytics to build an end-to-end pipeline from detection to personalised intervention. Founded in 2025 by Deepak Kumaran Nair, Jojo Jacob and Anish Mathew, the research organisation works across biomarker discovery, early detection systems, nanoscale precision therapeutics and personalised treatment protocols based on individual genetic and biomarker profiles. Its technology platform combines multiple biomarker modalities with AI analytics for early detection and risk assessment, targeting 95% accuracy and a 24-hour turnaround for results. eNLife's diagnostics are built on blood-based and neuroimaging biomarkers alongside large population studies, going beyond conventional scans to enable early detection. It is working towards accessible, affordable diagnostics that can be deployed in routine healthcare years before symptoms appear. The platform says it has more than 28 publications, over 1,700 study participants, six active studies and 15-plus collaborations. eNLife Research is capitalising on the growing push for early diagnosis in neurology, focusing on India's Alzheimer's disease diagnostics market, which is projected to reach $600.2 Mn by 2033. Kalpnk | An AI-First Filmmaking Studio Filmmaking has long been a slow and expensive process, with commercials taking weeks to produce and costs that put premium content out of reach for many brands and storytellers. Kalpnk is a studio using AI workflows to create cinematic content, from brand visuals and commercials to short-form reels and AI films. Founded in 2025 by Sameer Talawdekar, Aayush Raj and Manav Soni, the studio is led by filmmakers and writers, with AI enhancing their vision across ideation, moodboards, images, animation, editing, sound and music. It produces high-impact 10- 15-second brand reels, premium commercials and pitch decks and storyboards for studios. Kalpnk says it delivers a finished commercial in about five days on average, cutting production time by around 85% and cost by roughly 70%. The studio operates on a cloud-based, global-commission model, targeting brands and storytellers seeking faster, more flexible production. It operates in the AI-generated video market that is becoming an increasingly attractive option for brands in India. The market is projected to grow from about $31.8 Mn in 2025 to $142 Mn by 2033. UpKraft | AI-Powered Extracurricular Learning Music, dance and other extracurricular skills are often taught inconsistently at home or in communities, with little structure or visible progress. UpKraft is building structured extracurricular learning at home, in housing societies and in schools, led by expert tutors and powered by AI. Founded in 2025 by Tejasvi Singh Kushwah, Varun Mangal and Kritika Varandani, the platform covers guitar, piano, drums, violin, vocals, dance and fitness, with certified and vetted instructors, level-based learning paths and clear progress tracking. Its AI Practice Studio provides real-time feedback to help learners fix practice gaps. For tutors, UpKraft offers an all-in-one toolkit covering student enrolment, a 2,000+ song library, payments, scheduling and automated parent updates. For schools and academies, it provides admin tools, an AI practice companion and global resources, supporting classroom, hybrid or remote teaching. The startup is targeting the structured extracurricular learning and edtech space, serving learners, tutors, academies and schools while expanding into certification-aligned music education. UpKraft is targeting the after-school and extracurricular program market, which was valued at about 34.46 Bn in 2026 and is projected to reach $62.38 Bn by 2033. If you’ve followed mental health topics on TikTok or Instagram lately, you have probably heard the term emotional regulation. But emotional regulation isn’t just a trendy buzzword. It’s a nuanced concept that psychologists like me have been studying for decades.
At its core, emotional regulation is how well someone can manage their emotions – whether positive ones like excitement and joy, or negative or more uncomfortable ones like jealousy and anger.
I study emotional regulation – which scientists refer to as simply “emotion regulation” – within the context of relationships, including understanding how children learn to regulate their own emotions. The goal of healthy emotional regulation is not to erase difficult feelings, but to be able to manage those feeling more effectively so they do not become overwhelming.
Emotional regulation versus temperament
People often confuse emotional regulation with temperament, which is your natural, inborn style for how you approach or react to the world. Psychologists describe three different types of temperament that a person can have: easy and flexible; active, outgoing and excitable; or cautious and quiet. Temperament is genetically and biologically driven – in other words, it is something you are born with.
Emotional regulation, on the other hand, isn’t something people either have or don’t have. It is a set of skills that develops over time, beginning in childhood as children learn from and interact with the people around them. And like other skills, emotional regulation can be strengthened with instruction and practice.
There are two types of emotional regulation: self-regulation, or managing your own emotions, and co-regulation, which involves helping others manage their emotions. Both are important in romantic relationships, at work and in parenting.
Co-regulation is especially important as a way to help kids respond to intense feelings.
Taming emotional cycles
Emotions don’t exist on their own. They are part of an ongoing conversation between your mind, your body and your behavior. The way you think affects how your body responds, your body’s reactions influence how you feel, and your feelings shape what you do.
For example, imagine someone cuts you off in traffic. Within moments, several things happen at once. You may feel a surge of rage as your heart starts racing, your palms begin to sweat, and thoughts like “What a #$% jerk!” flash through your mind. Those reactions may lead you to respond by rolling your eyes, swearing at the steering wheel or flipping off the driver.
Each of these reactions influences the others, creating an emotional cycle that can escalate or de-escalate, depending on how you respond. Understanding this cycle is important because changing just one part of it can shift the entire emotional experience.
Responding instead of reacting
Everyone engages in emotional regulation throughout the day – whether consciously or not. Healthy emotional regulation allows people to use their emotions as valuable sources of information rather than letting them take over their lives or ruin their day.
Emotions can signal that something feels threatening, unfair, exciting, disappointing or important, prompting you to pause and consider what might have triggered the reaction.
In the traffic example above, anger may be a clue that you perceived the other driver’s behavior as dangerous or disrespectful. Your emotion doesn’t mean your interpretation is wrong or right, but it does provide useful information about how you are experiencing the situation, which can help you decide how to respond.
Many people use emotional regulation strategies intentionally during the day to deal with uncomfortable or intense emotions. These include taking a walk, venting to a friend or shooting hoops. Or they might include less healthy options, such as doomscrolling, being irritable with loved ones or pouring that third glass of wine.
Multiple factors, such as life stressors – even sleep quality – can make it harder for people to regulate or contain tough emotions, increasing the risk of less-than-healthy coping strategies.
When emotional regulation falls short
We psychologists can’t talk about emotional regulation without talking about its opposite state – emotional dysregulation. That’s when you are not able to successfully use coping skills to deal with tough feelings, and those feelings then interfere with your ability to function.
Instead of using strategies that might serve as life rafts for when the seas of daily life become difficult, the waves wash over you – which can feel like you are drowning in the intensity of these feelings.
Yet it isn’t the emotion itself that’s the problem. Rather, it’s how you interpret the emotion, the story you tell yourself about it, and how you respond to it. When emotions become difficult to manage and begin interfering with how you think, act or function, that’s emotion dysregulation.
Prolonged emotion dysregulation has profound costs that extend far beyond how you feel in the moment.
Emotional dysregulation can affect a person’s physical health, including heart and immune system functioning, disrupt sleep, contribute to mental health problems and make it more difficult to be present and responsive in your relationships. It can also impair your memory, concentration and performance in everyday activities – not to mention your finances.
Research suggests that learning to address emotional dysregulation early on can reduce the risk of long-term consequences, including serious mental health conditions such as major mood disorders and borderline personality disorder.
Emotional regulation can be learned
Learning emotional regulation strategies begins with identifying your feelings and building a vocabulary to describe them. You can’t regulate what you can’t name.
Children learn emotional regulation skills by watching people around them. Parents and other caregivers can help their children by serving as an “emotional container,” naming emotions and modeling how to express them in a healthy way.
In the moment, emotional regulation strategies can include breathing or mindfulness techniques that help calm the body’s nervous system and turn down the intensity of emotions.
Longer term, skills from cognitive-behavioral therapy, one of the most effective forms of talk therapy for anxiety and depression, can help. These skills include learning to view difficult experiences as opportunities for growth, questioning unhelpful thoughts instead of automatically believing them, and accepting emotions without letting them take over.
Rather than trying to avoid or eliminate difficult feelings, the goal is to notice them and recognize that your emotions are not always accurate reflections of reality – in other words, that feelings are not facts. Then you can choose how to respond.
Talking through difficult emotions with someone you trust can help you feel understood, gain perspective and make it easier to respond thoughtfully rather than react impulsively.
Taking care of your body also supports emotional regulation. Getting enough sleep, eating a balanced diet and moving your body regularly helps your brain function at its best, making it easier to manage stress, think clearly and respond thoughtfully.
For healthy long-term emotional regulation skills, practicing matters. Just like working out your biceps in the gym, if you use these skills consistently, your capacity for responding can grow.
Jessica Griffin, Associate Professor of Psychiatry and Peditrics, UMass Chan Medical School

Beijing retains commercial interests in Venezuela even as analysts see Washington curbing its political and strategic influence

Teresa Elena Frontadoin Washington
Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez’s tribute to Fidel Castro has drawn a blistering rebuke from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, highlighting the political tensions surrounding Caracas’ rapprochement with Washington even as China seeks to preserve its economic interests in the South American country.
Rodriguez marked the centenary of the late Cuban leader’s birth this week by praising Castro as a figure who “transcends time” and invoking his commitment to sovereignty, social justice and Latin American unity.
Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants and a long-time critic of the communist government in Havana, responded sharply.
“Fidel Castro was a complete failure at everything except destroying Cuba and impoverishing, jailing and murdering his own people,” Rubio wrote on social media.
The exchange came as Chinese President Xi Jinping also commemorated Castro’s centenary, praising his contribution to relations between Beijing and Havana and describing him as a founder and promoter of China-Cuba ties.
But analysts said Rodriguez’s embrace of Castro should not necessarily be read as evidence that Venezuela is returning to the geopolitical alignment that characterised the Nicolas Maduro era.

Newly declassified accounts of Operation Sindoor have shed light on the immediate military response to the April 22, 2026, terror attack in Pahalgam and the events that followed, with senior Indian military officers and National Security Adviser Ajit Doval recalling the brutality of the attack and the decision-making that culminated in India's retaliatory operation.
Lt Gen Rajiv Ghai, who served as the Director General of Military Operations (DGMO) during Operation Sindoor, recalled receiving a call from the Corps Commander in Kashmir informing him that something had happened in the Baisaran Valley near Pahalgam. He said he immediately realised that the incident was unlike a routine terror attack.
The attack took place on April 22, when Army Chief General Upendra Dwivedi was attending a seminar for retiring officers. According to the account, the Chief was discreetly informed by the DGMO that a terrorist attack had taken place in Pahalgam.
Following the incident, the Army immediately mobilised a nearby unit and a Quick Reaction Team to reach the site. However, the absence of a motorable road between Pahalgam and Baisaran meant that the troops had to cover the final stretch on foot, taking around 30–40 minutes.
As soldiers made their way towards the site, reports of the scale of the attack began emerging. The commanding officer of an infantry battalion described the scene as one in which "dead bodies" were scattered across the area.
Colonel Ashish Upreti, VSM, said the incident appeared markedly different from conventional terror attacks. Recalling the scene, he described it as an "execution", asserting that victims were segregated on the basis of religion before Hindu men were targeted and killed.
"It wasn't a normal terror attack," Upreti said, describing the killings as a "cold-blooded" execution carried out in front of the victims' families. He added that he had never witnessed violence of such a "gory" nature in his military career.
The DGMO also described the killings as deliberate and carried out using automatic weapons, including AK-47 rifles.
National security analyst Nitin Gokhale said the attack represented a departure from earlier instances of terrorism, in which militants had generally targeted people indiscriminately. "The attackers in Pahalgam identified victims based on their religion and specifically targeted Hindu men," he added.
The brutality of the attack also deeply affected India's national security leadership. NSA Ajit Doval recalled the emotional impact of the killings, particularly the attack on families who had travelled to Pahalgam as tourists.
Doval said he felt particularly distressed thinking about a young couple who had gone to Pahalgam expecting a normal holiday, only for the husband to be killed while his wife remained at the scene.
Recalling the terrorists' message, Doval said the attackers told the victim's wife to "go and tell Modi to do whatever he can".
The accounts provide a detailed picture of the situation faced by Indian security forces immediately after the Pahalgam attack and the sense of urgency that followed within the military and national security establishment.
The revelations come in the context of Operation Sindoor, India's subsequent military response to the terror attack, and offer insight into the experiences of officers involved in assessing the attack, reaching the affected area and formulating the response.

This Ontario farm uses bees for relaxation therapy. Is it a buzzkill for stress?
Visitors to Comber-area farm say bee bed therapy helped them relax; research on mental health impact limited
Half a million bees are buzzing in a southwestern Ontario farm to offer visitors a way to help them relax and reduce stress.
Inside a small hut on Diana Graham's 28-hectare Comber-area farm, where she runs Bees and Bloom Wellness, four beehives are underneath each of two wooden beds, with screens separating the insects from clients who lie over them to experience bee bed therapy.
Graham and others who offer the therapy say it can be beneficial in reducing anxiety and stress.
But there’s still a dearth of scientific evidence around it.
Graham said sleeping while surrounded by bees is therapeutic, and her visitors have reported feeling “amazed” and “breathing better” after spending time in the presence of bee pheromones. She said it’s built perfectly safe, so the insects can’t sting her clients.
“The pheromones from the bees help with your immune system, lungs and their buzz, the frequencies, helps with anxiety, depression, PTSD, sleep disorders and overall health,” Graham told CBC News.
“Your anxiety will go down because the hum of these bees is absolutely amazing.”
The air inside the cabin is rich with honey and beeswax scents. Graham said it adds to the wellness.
There are a handful of such centres across Canada.
Visitors say time at bee farm helped them relax
Christine Brady of Petrolia, a town southeast of Sarnia, is among visitors to Graham’s farm who were contacted to talk about their experiences there.
Brady, who recently was at the farm with her mother and recommends the therapy, said she's elated there's a bee bed facility in Ontario.
Before she came across Graham's far, Brady said, she could only find one in Italy.
“I just went there to kind of zone out and relax. It was just more for the vibration, the smell and the frequency of the bees,” she said.
“I probably got into an almost meditative trance. You kind of go into that mental zone where you're aware, but you have kind of gone within.”
Annette Bourassa of Barrie, Ont., visited Graham's farm a couple of weeks ago and plans to go again with her friends in the fall.
“It was incredible. I can see the benefits of doing it often. I wish I lived closer because I would probably go once a week to get this,” she said.
“The hum of the bees is so relaxing and therapeutic. I just felt very, very relaxed and soothed when I left. It was excellent…. While I was lying there, I wasn't thinking about my stressors, or my clients or my deadlines.”
Bourassa said the experience was not claustrophobic and assured it’s safe, as people can also wear a protective jacket.
The cost for each 60-minute session, according to Graham's website, is $85 for one person, $120 for two people, and $300 for a group of four to six people.
Bee bed buzz started in Ireland
Known as “the queen bee” to her friends, Graham inspects the hives, pulls frames with honey and checks in on the bees weekly to ensure they have space.
To set up the bee beds, Graham turned to Paul O'Neill in Ireland for guidance.
O'Neill and his partner, Anton Tovarnitskyi, a Ukrainian beekeeper and refugee, built Ireland’s first commercial bee bed houses on Valentia Island, drawing inspiration from bee beds in Ukraine.
“It's very new and unique around the world,” O’Neill told CBC’s Windsor Morning. “It's an old form of therapy and relaxation whereby you sit or lie on top of an active beehive.”
O’Neill said bee beds have become popular across Europe, and they have been approached by many people globally — including in the United States, Germany and Canada — to teach them how to build and manage their bee cabins. His facilities are frequented by tourists from around the world.
Amid more awareness and concern about the significance of bees, O’Neill said, the concept has been gaining traction.
“The concept of the bee beds relies around energy, microvibration, the sound of the bees and the air from the hive. It's about this kind of connection with bees that is the key concept of why we do it.”
While Graham and O’Neill shared experiences of people feeling relaxed using the bee beds, there’s still little scientific evidence that this form of therapy helps with mental health issues.
Health Canada was contacted for comment on bee bed therapy, but the federal department declined to comment.
CBC Windsor also reached out to the Ontario Ministry of Health to ask questions including if bee bed therapy is a recognized therapy in the province, if certification is needed to practise it and if there's any provincial health coverage.
An emailed response from a spokesperson for Health Minister Sylvia Jones said all insured services under the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP) are spelled out in the Health Insurance Act (HIA) and regulations, and bee bed therapy isn't an insured service under OHIP.
Bee sound helps reduce anxiety levels: researcher
In Turkey, Yanki Tandircioglu, whose research is published in Apis, a scientific journal on honey bee-related sciences, has been looking into the effects of bee bed therapy on anxiety levels.
When she started digging into the topic, Tandircioglu said, “there was no scientific study” around bee bed therapy. While doing her master’s degree, she and her research partners designed an experiment to understand the impact of bee beds on anxiety levels.
She said two groups of participants, totalling 60 people, were chosen. One group was made to experience the bee beds, while the other group was just asked to listen to bee buzzing sounds. They filled out an anxiety questionnaire before and after the exposure, and their brain electrical activity was recorded with a portable electroencephalogram (EEG) device.
“So, we got significant results from both groups that we can say the buzzing sound affected people's anxiety levels and it reduced it,” Tandircioglu said, referring to what was reported on the questionnaires.
But she also noted they could not “observe any significant change” in the brain activity based on EEG readings.
In her paper, she writes this study is “a first investigation” into the effects of bee beds on anxiety levels, laying the groundwork for further exploration in this area.
Since it’s still a relatively new field of research and there is no amassed scholarship around it, Tandircioglu said, she understands why bee bed therapy is still not mainstream.
The sound of the colony is different from a single bee buzzing, and the microvibrations and smell of the beehives, Tandircioglu said, add to the overall relaxing experience. She said the bee sound was found to be closer to pink noise, like waterfalls and rain, rather than white noise.
“Nature always heals, and so do the bees.”

Zhu Rongji, the former Chinese premier and principal architect of the country’s economic reforms, died this week at the age of 97.
He will be remembered as the man who masterminded China’s entry into the World Trade Organization (WTO). Zhu was a singular figure in Chinese politics — smart, acerbic and misunderstood. While many saw him as a reformer, they also failed to recognize he was a dedicated member of the Chinese Communist Party who was committed to its continuing rule — despite the many injustices he suffered at its hands.
Born in 1928 to a family of landowners and intellectuals, Zhu joined the CCP in 1949, the year it seized power, and graduated two years later from Tsinghua University, one of China’s leading schools. While working on economic policy in Beijing, he was among the many who took supreme leader Mao Zedong at his word when he invited criticism of the leadership during his “Hundred Flowers Campaign” in the late 1950s; the ever-mercurial and vindictive Mao then attacked his critics, expelling Zhu (among others) from the party.

The debate over whether a social media ban for under 13- or 16-year-olds should be implemented or not, and amid the Union government’s standoff with Meta, an interesting intervention appeared in the Lok Sabha last week, with a private members’ Bill listed in that House by Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MP Baijayant Panda, throwing a little light on what such a move could look like in its legislative form.
The ‘Safeguarding Healthy Internet Environments for Little Digital-Natives (Shield) Bill, 2025’ was listed on Friday (August 7, 2026) but could not be tabled as both Houses of Parliament adjourned early.
It is “now well established by multiple studies that many social media algorithms are not only designed to foster addiction but also to embellish and reinforce narrow and extreme viewpoints, rather than shed light on all angles of any issue,” Mr. Panda told The Hindu.
It was “particularly harmful for young teenagers and children”, Mr. Panda said. Many social media platforms had acknowledged these conclusions, and consequently, several countries had started imposing restrictions on social media access to minors, especially those under the ages of 16 or 13, with the Centre also seized of the issue. “I had drafted a private member’s Bill for this purpose a year ago, after wide consultations with all stakeholders,” he said.
“Opposition parties need to reflect and rethink their blanket disruption of Parliament even on issues such as this, where there is no dispute with the Treasury Benches,” the BJP legislator said.
The Bill specifically states that no child under 13 years of age shall create an account on any social media or online gaming platform without verified parental consent, and that every intermediary shall provide parental control dashboards enabling guardians to monitor activity, manage privacy settings, and restrict screen time.
Any harmful content reported by an individual, guardian or parent shall, subject to verification by the intermediary, be removed or disabled within 36 hours of receipt, or 24 hours if it involves child sexual material. Every application shall have a reporting button titled ‘Report Child Harm’ accessible to all users.
Any intermediary who fails to comply with the Act shall be liable to a penalty of up to ₹10 crore, and wilful or repeated violations will lead to suspension of the intermediary's services or blocking under the provisions of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Officers designated by intermediaries who fail to observe due diligence in matters, specifically child safety or content removal obligations, either because of connivance or neglect, will be personally liable and could face imprisonment for up to 3 years, a fine of ₹10 lakh, or both.
An annual child safety and risk assessment process, identifying exposure risks related to content algorithms and interactions on a service, has to be carried out and submitted to the government. Information collected about users via the verification requirement cannot be used for behavioural profiling, the Bill says.
As more and more countries appear to be bringing legislation that restricts social media usage by children, the Bill listed by Mr. Panda appears to be a timely signal of similar efforts in India.

President Donald Trump has recently made another run at birthright citizenship. He may be entitled to dislike the Supreme Court’s answer but he is really not entitled to keep fidgeting with it as though a constitutional Supreme Court judgment were merely a negotiating position.
The Supreme Court Ruling
On June 30, in Trump v. Barbara, the Supreme Court held that children born in the United States to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are “subject to the jurisdiction” of the United States and therefore citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment. The judgment was 6-3. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for five justices on the constitutional question, while Justice Brett Kavanaugh supplied the sixth vote for the judgment on statutory grounds. While that distinction may be important, it does not change the bottom line. Trump’s 2025 executive order failed. Birthright citizenship survived.
The Court’s language was emphatic. Roberts recalled that Reconstruction-era lawmakers sought to settle the question of citizenship “once and forever [to] rest.” Near the conclusion, he described citizenship as “the right to have rights” and declared: “We keep that promise today.”
Trump’s Response: Two New Executive Orders
Five weeks later, Trump signed two new executive orders.
One, Ending Birth Tourism, directs the Departments of State and Homeland Security to take stronger measures against people using temporary visas to enter the United States principally to give birth. The second, Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship, identifies additional categories of children whom the administration says should not receive citizenship at birth. They include some children of alleged “alien enemies,” foreign government employees and parents involved in commercial arrangements intended to obtain birthright citizenship.
The first order principally raises an immigration-enforcement question. The second ventures directly back into the constitutional ground the Supreme Court addressed only weeks ago.
Enforcing Visa Laws - No Problem
There is nothing inherently improper about enforcing the visa laws. Existing regulations already provide that obtaining a visitor visa primarily to give birth in the United States to secure citizenship for a child is not legitimate B-visa tourism. They also create a presumption against applicants believed to be travelling primarily for that purpose.
Enforce those rules. Investigate fraud. Deny visas where applicants do not qualify. Prosecute criminal schemes where the evidence warrants it. But that is a different question from citizenship. The government can regulate who may enter the country. It can punish fraud by parents or businesses. What it cannot do is transform misconduct by a parent into a constitutional disability for a newborn child.
That is the line the administration continues to blur.
The 14th Amendment
The 14th Amendment does not say citizenship belongs only to children of lawful permanent residents, or only to children whose parents behaved properly, told the truth on visa applications or entered with motives the government approves. It grants citizenship to persons born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction, period. Congress incorporated essentially the same formula in 8 U.S.C. §1401(a), declaring a person born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction a citizen at birth. That statutory protection mattered especially to Justice Kavanaugh. He disagreed with the majority’s constitutional interpretation but concluded that Trump’s earlier executive order could not stand because it conflicted with §1401(a). Congress, he wrote in substance, had not enacted the additional exceptions the administration wanted.
Changing Labels
Even by that narrower route, the President cannot simply invent a new citizenship code. That is why the administration’s latest manoeuver is troubling. A president who loses a constitutional case should not treat the judgment as an invitation to change a few labels and start again. Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project and lead counsel in the litigation, put it plainly: “President Trump may not like the fact that birthright citizenship is a constitutional right,” but that is “beside the point.” Amia Trigg, deputy director of litigation at the Legal Defense Fund, was equally direct. She accused the President of trying to “double down” after the Supreme Court rejected the attempt to redefine American citizenship through executive action.
Exceptions To The Amendment
The organizations that prevailed in Trump v. Barbara returned to federal court in New Hampshire on August 11, 2026 asking the court to clarify that children covered by the class action remain protected despite the new order. Their motion argues that the administration is attempting to expand the historically narrow exceptions recognized in United States v. Wong Kim Ark. Those exceptions matter. Birthright citizenship has never been literally without qualification. Children of foreign diplomats traditionally fall outside the general rule because diplomats enjoy a special jurisdictional status. The Supreme Court has also recognized the historic exception for children born to enemy forces during hostile occupation.
But those are narrow exceptions grounded in jurisdiction. They are not a blank check allowing presidents to create new categories whenever immigration policy becomes politically inconvenient. Aarti Kohli, executive director of the Asian Law Caucus, captured the essential point: “It’s the Constitution, not the president, who determines who is American.”
That should not be a partisan proposition. It describes the American constitutional system. The Constitution was designed precisely so that no president would be sovereign. Congress legislates. Courts interpret the law. The Constitution stands above both. Presidents have enormous authority, particularly in immigration and foreign affairs, but they do not possess a royal prerogative to rewrite the Constitution by proclamation.
Citizenship Is The Starting Point Of America
Citizenship is the legal starting point of belonging. It should not depend upon whether a future administration approves of a parent’s immigration status, occupation, nationality, politics or conduct. Once citizenship at birth begins turning on categories devised by executive officials, the certainty the 14th Amendment was intended to establish starts to disappear.
What Trump Can Do, And What He Can’t
Trump has lawful tools available. If he wants tougher screening of temporary visitors, he should use them. If he wants different immigration laws, he should ask Congress to enact them. If he believes the Constitution itself should establish a different rule for citizenship, he can advocate a constitutional amendment. Those routes are difficult by design but available to him. What Trump should not do is keep testing variations of executive orders against a Supreme Court ruling that has already answered the central question. Courts cannot function as a coequal branch if their constitutional judgments are treated as temporary obstacles for the executive branch to manoeuver around.
Presidents lose cases. Every administration does. Accepting those losses is part of governing under the rule of law. Trump can criticize Trump v. Barbara. He can contend that the Court misread history. He can campaign for a different constitutional rule. But the Supreme Court has spoken, and the executive branch is bound by its judgment unless the governing law is changed through lawful constitutional means. Birthright citizenship survived Trump’s first effort to rewrite it. The wiser course now is not another round of constitutional improvisation. It is to accept the judgment, enforce the immigration laws that exist—and move on.

I’m already growing hoarse in Golden Gate Park as Charli XCX takes the stage at a San Francisco music festival. The crowd starts jumping as a guitar hook hits, and I reluctantly comply, bouncing around on these aging knees as my chunky Puff necklace almost flies off the chain.
During a lull in the set, someone next to me compliments the necklace, which has stainless steel swirls and a bulbous orange center. Their eyes grow wide as I flip the cap off and explain that it’s a hidden USB flash drive—I plugged the Puff into my phone to show off the animations.
When Harry Isaac and Sebastian Bidegain, working together under the Noware moniker, posted an early prototype of their retro-futuristic necklace on social media in 2025, it quickly racked up over a million views with thousands of waitlist sign-ups to buy one. The duo has spent the last year attempting to turn the online attention on their prototype into a mass-produced reality. Now, Noware is finally ready to ship units this October.
The pair arrived at the WIRED office wearing Puff necklaces, naturally, that match with their trendy gorpcore outfits. They seem nervous, albeit excited, to show off their creation. Neither has had a wide release for their products before, though both are well-versed in whimsical designs. Isaac previously went viral for making an electric scooter that shoots out bubbles. Bidegain was already sculpturally approaching electronics, with prototypes like a vape camera and lo-fi sampler built into a rock.
The design ethos of the Puff is just as much about aesthetics as it is about usefulness. Noware’s marketing materials show a cool girl with a Puff clipped onto her purse, where a Labubu might have sat last year, as well as styled on her neck with a pile of other silver chains. Bidegain says the “squishy, doughy” textures of food partially inspired Puff’s design, as well as cellular biology and tactile devices, like old phones and radios.
“On one end, I want anyone to be able to wear it, just if they think it's pretty,” he says. “Though, I also want people who actually find utility in flash drives as part of their workflow: photographers, DJs, IT people.”
The small screen in the middle of the necklace is my favorite aspect. When it’s plugged into my phone or laptop, Puff’s center lights up with a customizable design. The Noware duo showed me goopy animations that reacted to the direction I held the phone as well as an aquarium mode. They even put the WIRED logo on it through custom software anyone can use to craft their own designs. The Puff doesn’t have an internal battery, so the USB drive can live as a piece of jewelry far longer than the expiration date of most electronics.
The necklace’s biggest drawback is its price: a whopping $179 for only 128 GB of storage. A basic flash drive with similar storage costs around $30. The duo doesn’t want the Puff to remain that expensive and hopes to reach a more accessible price. “We want it to get cheaper over time, but we're just trying to make it exist first,” says Isaac. They blame it partially on the inflated cost of memory right now, thanks to the AI boom. Depending on how Puff’s initial release goes, future iterations may include more budget-friendly options, like a nonmetal version.
This experimental device from two New York City-based makers was the perfect accessory for a weekend-long festival, with its retro-futuristic vibe and sharp colors.
“We're very interested in making electronics that are more opinionated, playful, and personal,” Isaac says. It was a lighthearted conversation piece as I made small talk with vendors, and at least one friend assumed I was hiding drugs in it. (Nope, just a bunch of nudes.)

How Does WIRED Test Cooling Mattresses?
Mattresses are tested for at least a week, but in many cases for longer. I slept on the majority of these mattresses for half a month or more to really get a feel for the product. I tested them at different times of the season and with different types of sheets and bedding. I sat on the edges to test for edge support, jumped, and performed some other methods to test the bounce and motion transfer of the mattress. Perhaps most important for this guide, I was my normal, perpetually warm (and sweaty) self, and gauged more abstract things like my overall comfort at night, and how well I thought air flowed through the mattress, or how much heat was trapped in.
What Should You Look for in a Cooling Mattress?
When shopping for a cooling mattress, here are a few things to consider:
- Composition: Opt for mattress materials designed to promote airflow, which will help prevent heat buildup. Many mattresses are infused with gel or copper, which are designed to dissipate heat and keep you cool. A hybrid mattress combines the best of both worlds by using a coil support system under a foam, latex, or polyfoam comfort top. Hybrid mattresses tend to retain less heat than all-foam mattresses because they have a layer or two of springs to help dissipate heat.
- Cover fabric: Consider mattresses with covers made from moisture-wicking fabrics and phase-change fibers to draw sweat away from the body. Breathable fabrics include bamboo, Tencel lyocell, and synthetic fabrics, which are engineered to help regulate body temperature. Perforated cooling covers further amplify airflow between your body and the fabric. We find quilted tops help too, since they have ridges and valleys that allow air to escape.
- Airflow: With proper airflow, the heat you generate overnight is properly conducted through the mattress. Hybrid mattresses with individual coils help with this, but many mattresses marketed for their cooling benefits have other tricks.
- Firmness: While the debate of soft versus firm mattresses is a personal preference, your choice can play a crucial role in the way your body traps heat. Softer mattresses tend to envelop your body, leading to increased heat retention as your body sinks into the surface. Conversely, firmer mattresses provide better support and allow for more air circulation around your body.
How Did WIRED Select Models to Be Reviewed?
We have tested over 100 mattresses across all of our guides, like Best Organic Mattresses, Best Mattresses for Back Pain, and Best Mattresses You Can Buy Online, as well as for individual review. We talk with each other, discussing which mattress brands in general we're fans of, and which we aren't. Some mattresses are provided as review samples by the manufacturers, with the understanding that we don't guarantee coverage or type of coverage—we aren't paid for glowing reviews on products we think are just mid. We purchase and expense models we aren't able to get a sample of.
We try to test a range of mattress types, firmness, and brands to ensure we know what's out on the market, so we can best give you our honest, unbiased opinion on which mattresses you should spend your money (and one-third of your life sleeping) on.
What Does WIRED Do With Mattresses After Testing?
We keep top picks for longer-term durability testing in our own homes and the homes of other staffers, friends, and family members, while other models are donated locally.

Tropical storm Lala closes in, hitting Hawaii's Big Island with rain, wind
'This is an enormous storm,' Gov. Josh Green said of potentially destructive system
Tropical storm Lala was already whipping and soaking Hawaii's Big Island early Saturday, with forecasts saying it could strengthen into a hurricane or, at the least, bring hurricane-force winds as it approaches land.
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) issued a rare hurricane warning for the island, which hasn’t experienced a direct hurricane landfall in 155 years.
Forecasters said higher elevations could get as much as 635 millimetres of rain. That could cause life-threatening mudslides in a mountainous area where people live off the grid in improvised housing, and authorities urged them to find safe shelters quickly.
"This is an enormous storm," Gov. Josh Green said. Tropical storm force winds extended outward for as much as 350 kilometres and were expected to hit the islands of Oahu and Kauai by Sunday morning.
Destructive flooding and even wildfires kicked up by the strong winds were possible in the islands.
A hurricane warning was issued for the Big Island, and a tropical storm warning was in effect for Maui County, which includes the islands of Maui, Molokai, Lanai and Kahoolawe. A tropical storm warming was also in effect for Oahu and Kauai County, including Kauai and Niihau islands.
Even if the storm remains just shy of a hurricane as it approaches land, the NHC said wind speeds atop mountains and on the windward and leeward slopes "are often up to 30 per cent stronger than the near-surface winds" indicated in its advisory, suggesting nearly hurricane-force winds in Hawaii's higher-altitude communities.
According to a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist’s research of newspaper accounts, a Category 3 hurricane hit the northeast corner of the island in 1871. The latest forecast has Lala striking "very close to the southern tip of the Big Island," said Vanessa Almanza, a weather service meteorologist in Honolulu.
Officials and residents braced for Lala regardless of whether Hawaii takes a direct hit. Shelters were scheduled to open, and various events were canceled.
"It doesn’t take landfall to create destruction," Almanza said, noting that a lot of the impacts are felt outside the hurricane's centre.
The NHC predicted 203 to 305 millimetres of rainfall totals across Maui and lower elevations of the Big Island, and 102 to 152 millimetres across the island chain.
It also warned that the storm could cause "life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," along with a dangerous storm surge and ocean swells "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."
As of 5 a.m. local time in Hawaii, tropical storm Lala was located about 175 kilometres southeast of South Point, Hawaii, with maximum sustained winds of 100 km/h and was moving toward the west-northwest at 20 km/h, the hurricane centre said.
Officials urge taking the storm seriously
State Rep. Jeanné Kapela travelled from Honolulu to be closer to her constituents on the Big Island and urged people to remain alert.
The southern end of the island is remote and rural, with agriculture including coffee and cattle, but it's growing in population because of its affordability. Kapela said she was especially worried about people who live off the grid in unpermitted structures.
"If you feel now that your house doesn’t have a great roof or might not be able to withstand hurricane force winds, then first things first: you go to a family or friend’s house and you kind of hunker down there," she texted to The Associated Press as her flight took off Friday. "We're hopeful the storm moves through quickly, but we're preparing for whatever comes."
Many parts of Hawaii are still dealing with the aftermath of devastating flooding in March, Kapela said. "We know how quickly heavy rain and flooding can impact our rural communities."
Growers still recovering from the spring floods, including on Oahu's North Shore, were worried about suffering more damage, according to Brian Miyamoto, executive director of the Hawaii Farm Bureau.
Coffee farmer Bruce Corker said it was "sunny and beautiful" Friday in Holualoa, on the west side of the Big Island, and the island's only Costco seemed normal a day earlier, but the prospect of "streams overflowing and high winds" was worrisome.
Wildfire risks increase during windy weather
As winds ramped up across the islands, Almanza said dry and breezy conditions outside the storm would elevate fire concerns.
In 2023 the Maui town of Lahaina burned during extreme winds as a hurricane passed far to the south.
"Since the fire, everybody is way more aware of weather in general and our environment and things that are happening," said Archie Kalepa of Lahaina, who is well known in the area for his surfing, paddling and other ocean skills and has been watching the storm closely.
Kauai, which is several islands northwest up the archipelago from the Big Island, saw Hurricane Iniki make landfall as a Category 4 hurricane in 1992. That, like this year, was an El Nino year, when a warming of the Pacific near the equator increases Pacific hurricane activity and affects weather patterns across the globe.

It felt like the absolute worst time to take a trip. Our son was home from college for the summer, our oldest daughter had just gotten married, and our youngest daughter had graduated from high school and was preparing to leave for college in late August.
Everything in me wanted to soak up every minute I could with my kids.
But a realization has been settling in: My kids are really leaving, and my husband and I will become empty nesters. We need to make our lives a bit more about us again. After more than 20 years of building our lives around our children, shifting our focus back to ourselves feels difficult.
The opportunity to travel came unexpectedly, and even after I made arrangements, I nearly talked myself out of it. But I knew we had to take the trip.
For the first time in decades, I agreed to a trip that wasn't about our children
We planned a trip to a wellness resort in the heart of the Berkshires.
We would be away for four nights/five days —longer than we'd ever been away without the kids. Whether it was schedules, work, or money, something always came up. This time, we didn't let things get in the way. I made sure the kids and the dog were taken care of, and we set out to enjoy ourselves.
This trip wouldn't be a family celebration or on someone else's schedule. This time, it was just about my husband and me.
Driving away felt exciting and scary
I couldn't help but wonder if the kids would be OK. I found myself checking Life360 to make sure people made it where they were supposed to be.
Did they feel bad that we were leaving? Would they make good choices? The questions rolled through my mind like a news ticker as we drove through the mountains.
Once we arrived, we headed straight for dinner and made plans for the next few days. We both wanted time to relax and try new things together. A couples massage, a cooking class, and a pickleball lesson all made the list. The rest would unfold one day at a time. It felt good to have a few things planned and a lot of time to figure out the rest together.
Having nearly a week away helped us relax. With meals taken care of, we could simply enjoy ourselves. We took time to think and see how we felt. If we were hungry, we ate. If we wanted fresh air, we went out exploring.
We filled our days with things we rarely make time for at home. My husband tried fly fishing and archery, while I took a workout class and tried a sound bath. Together, we explored the area and lingered over coffee without worrying about anyone else's schedule.
As we navigated our days, a familiar feeling rose to the surface
There were some times that felt awkward. When you're used to a rambunctious table full of kids at every meal, a table for two felt quiet. We sat across from each other and realized we'd forgotten how to have long conversations that weren't about the kids.
Still, there were quiet moments that felt comfortable. The time together forced us to navigate how to talk about new things, something we will need to do come fall.
We didn't have to worry about where someone needed to be or when a kid's sports game started. For the first time in a long time, it was just about us.
It wasn't the us we used to be; time and 20 years of parenting have changed us. Instead, it was a safe way to test the waters and see how we would handle living our days — just the two of us.
Our time together wasn't all easy, but we walked through it together
Life will be different when our kids head off to school, but it won't only be about work and responsibilities. This trip allowed us to reconnect and get excited for the next season.
As we drove away, I began to think about what our lives will look like in the fall. Parenting doesn't end when the kids leave the nest, but it does change. For a long time, I've been scared of that change.
Yes, I will miss my kids and the life we've built around them. But for the first time, I wasn't only grieving what was ending. I was beginning to look forward to what comes next for my husband and me.
