Differential: Ben White (£5.5m, defender)
Pras: The England right-back offers attacking threat and a realistic path to regular minutes while Jurrien Timber remains out.
White might not be a season-keeper but is a strong pick to start off with.
Player to avoid: Christos Tzolis (£6.5m, midfielder)
Pras: The new signing has talent and has been involved in quite a few pre-season goals, but manager Mikel Arteta's rotation among the wide left attackers makes consistent starts far from guaranteed for the Greece international. Plus, they seem to be in the market for another left winger.
Aston Villa
Talisman: Ollie Watkins (£8m, forward)
Holly: Watkins has seen a £1m price drop going into this campaign and will likely be Aston Villa's main man following the departure of Morgan Rogers to Chelsea in the transfer window.
He remains incredibly consistent, scoring on average 16 goals in his past four seasons at the club and he's also potentially a penalty taker now Youri Tielemans has gone to Manchester United.
Differential: Matty Cash (£4.5m, defender)
Holly: Villa's defence remains a consistent one for investment, with nine clean sheets last campaign. Cash sits in around 8% of sides, and is first choice as right-back.
He produced six goal involvements last season, three goals and three assists. He had 30 shots on goal and made 30 key passes, highlighting his routes to points.
Player to avoid: Alejandro Garnacho (£6m, midfielder)
Holly: Former Manchester United man Alejandro Garnacho may be well fancied after arriving at Villa on loan from Chelsea this summer, but Emi Buendia may be hard to displace in midfield.
Garnacho comes in kindly priced, but played just 1,261 minutes last season, providing one goal and four assists. There are more consistent options at this price point.
Bournemouth
Talisman: Marcus Tavernier (£6m, midfielder)
Gianni: Since Antoine Semenyo left Bournemouth, you could argue they have no clear standout individual, and some would say that's a strength of the team – the ability of the collective is all important.
But Tavernier is their chief creator and responsible for a lot of their set-pieces.
With 11 attacking returns last season he's likely to be their talisman once again. Justin Kluivert (£6m) is set to be Bournemouth's penalty taker but, when the Dutchman is not on the pitch, expect Tavernier to step up.
Differential: Adrien Truffert (£5.5m, defender)
Gianni: At only 5% owned, left-back Truffert, who scored the second-most FPL points for the Cherries last season (165), may also be their best differential.
The Frenchman ghosts into dangerous advanced positions and carries open-play goal and assist threat as well as being good for defensive contributions and bonus points.
He is an all action hero.
Player to avoid: Evanilson (£6m, forward)
Gianni: There are a plethora of £6m forwards in FPL this year and Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Igor Jesus and Brian Brobbey are just three that standout as better picks than Evanilson, who only scored six goals in his 32 league games last season.
- What has changed in FPL for 2026-27 season? 
  - Published1 day ago
Brentford
Talisman: Igor Thiago (£8m, forward)
Heisenberg: Thiago is the clear talisman for Brentford after a sensational goal-scoring season, netting 22 league goals. The Brazilian finished the campaign with 181 FPL points, and his £8m starting price reflects just how much Brentford will rely on him again this season.
The concern is whether he can justify such a significant price rise, but the upside is obvious.
Thiago has the profile of a forward who can deliver in bursts, particularly against weaker opposition, and Brentford are likely to continue looking for him regularly inside the penalty area.
Differential: Dango Ouattara (£6.5m, midfielder)
Heisenberg: Ouattara is my favourite Brentford differential. He showed plenty of attacking promise last season, averaging more than five FPL points per start and producing four double-figure hauls.
The big appeal is the combination of price and attacking potential. At £6.5m, he does not need to become a premium-level scorer to represent excellent value, and his low ownership means you'll get a nice rank boost if he hits the ground running.
Player to avoid: Callum Wilson (£5.5m, forward)
Heisenberg: Wilson is a former FPL favourite of mine, but I cannot see him getting many minutes for Brentford with Igor Thiago leading the line.
Even if Thiago gets injured at some point, then Brentford could use the likes of Outtara or Kevin Schade instead, meaning Wilson's minutes would still be patchy.
Brighton
Talisman: Pascal Gross (£5.5m, midfielder)
Pras: The veteran German midfielder is the safest Brighton option.
Gross is involved in all set-pieces, including penalties, and provides steady midfield returns.
And his price point makes him a great enabler too, allowing you to spend more cash elsewhere in midfield.
Differential: Luka Vuskovic (£5m, defender)
Pras: The new centre-back signing from Spurs should start regularly and offers the prospect of defensive contribution points (defcon) plus clean-sheet potential at low ownership.
Brighton managed 10 clean sheets last season, bettered by only six teams.
Player to avoid: Georginio Rutter (£5.5m, forward)
Pras: The Frenchman has been reclassified as a forward and is facing competition for minutes alongside Greek youngster Charalampos Kostoulas.
Rutter's potential for consistent starts looks less secure and he will now earn fewer points when he scores.
Chelsea
Talisman: Joao Pedro (£7.5m, forward)
Holly: Cole Palmer might be Chelsea's most expensive FPL asset, but it is striker Joao Pedro who is the most popular pick, sitting in over half of teams going into Gameweek 1.
He produced 15 goals and nine assists last season and has had the summer off. He has made that count, with a hat-trick among his stash of pre-season goals.
Differential: Levi Colwill (£5m, defender)
Holly: Colwill seems kindly priced in the heart of Chelsea's defence, coming in a whole £1m cheaper than summer signing Maxence Lacroix.
He missed much of last season through injury but should be well suited to picking up defensive contribution points. A home game against promoted Hull in gameweek four shows potential.
Player to avoid: Enzo Fernandez (£7m, midfielder)
Holly: Fernandez's World Cup run came to an ignominious end with a red card in the final, having had an impressive tournament, scoring two goals.
There are strong rumours he may leave Chelsea in the summer transfer window which provides uncertainty and he may be late to return anyway before gameweek one.
Coventry
Talisman: Haji Wright (£5.5m, forward)
Gianni: The USA forward is Coventry's main man up top and scored 17 league goals in the Championship last season.
Those on a stategy to bench boost in gamweek two will surely be interested in Wright who plays against Hull City at home. A word of warning though, he is often substituted around the 70-80 minute mark.
Talisman: Carl Rushworth (£4.5m, goalkeeper)
Gianni: At 1% owned Rushworth is worth a look if you're going with two cheap rotating goalkeepers. He rotates really well with Bart Verbruggen (£4.5m) of Brighton.
Player to avoid: Milan van Ewijk (£4m, defender)
Gianni: The Dutch right-back is 15% owned and did catch the eye in the Championship last season with eight assists.
But there are lower-owned cheap defensive alternatives who will pick up defcon points regularly, such as club-mate Bobby Thomas (£4m).
Crystal Palace
Talisman: Ismaila Sarr (£6.5m, midfielder)
Heisenberg: Sarr was a hugely important part of Palace's attacking game last season and he ranked highly for shots and big chances. He also has some penalty potential when Jean-Philippe Mateta is off the pitch.
At £6.5m, Sarr is potentially slightly underpriced and, if he continues to receive a large share of Palace's shots and attacking transitions, he has the potential to be one of the standout mid-priced midfielders in FPL.
Differential: Daniel Munoz (£5.5m, defender)
Heisenberg: Munoz is arguably the most exciting Crystal Palace FPL asset because of the sheer number of routes to points. He can earn through clean sheets, defensive contributions, assists and goals, while his attacking positioning makes him much more than a conventional full-back.
Under previous manager Oliver Glasner, he was one of the most attacking defenders in the league (from open play). It'll be interesting to see if this continues under Pierre Sage, so he's one to monitor if you're interested in starting the season with him in your FPL team.
Munoz has been subject of transfer rumours, but even if he switches teams in the Premier League he will remain an excellent option.
Player to avoid: Jorgen Strand Larsen (£6m, forward)
Heisenberg: Strand Larsen is a decent centre forward, but, if we assume Mateta is first choice then the Norwegian will find gametime hard to come by.
For FPL, certainty of minutes is key. If you are spending £6m on a forward, you could get the likes of Calvert-Lewin who is close to being guaranteed to play 90 minutes most weeks and on penalties.
Until the preferred number nine becomes clearer, I would rather avoid Strand Larsen and monitor the situation.
Everton
Talisman: James Tarkowski (£6m, defender)
Pras: The centre-back should continue to accumulate strong defcon numbers that netted 170 points last year as the fifth-highest scoring defender.
To a large extent Tarkowski is fixture agnostic as an FPL pick - he will accumulate points no matter the opposition so set him and forget.
Differential: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall (£6.5m, midfielder)
Pras: On the back of eight goals and seven assists last season, Dewsbury-Hall could play an essential role again in the Everton team.
The midfielder is on some set-pieces, which only adds to his appeal as an FPL pick.
Player to avoid: Beto (£5.5m, forward)
Pras: The striker's minutes are shared with Thierno Barry and Everton's attack is unlikely to deliver enough consistent returns.
He only started 17 games lasts season, scoring nine goals, so just spend the extra £0.5m on a striker.
Fulham
Talisman: Rodrigo Muniz (£5.5m, forward)
Holly: Losing Harry Wilson and Raul Jimenez in this transfer window leaves slim pickings in terms of a talisman at Fulham, with remaining striker Rodrigo Muniz among their most expensive assets.
New recruit Gonzalo Garcia comes in £0.5m more expensive to provide competition in the Fulham frontline, with Muniz producing one goal and one assist from 10 starts last season.
Differential: Antonee Robinson (£4.5m, defender)
Holly: Fulham's Robinson is an intriguing pick and seemingly good value at this price point. He had a quieter 2025-26 campaign, after registering 10 assists the previous season.
He certainly has the routes to points, with Fulham keeping nine clean sheets last season. There is also an outside shout of him being on penalties, following the departures from Craven Cottage in this window.
Player to avoid: Sander Berge (£5m, midfielder)
Holly: Berge started 34 games for Fulham last season, picking up three assists and defcon points on five occasions to finish the campaign on 91 fantasy points.
He has been repeatedly linked with a move away from Craven Cottage in this transfer window and so there is a reluctance to include him in gameweek one drafts.
Hull City
Talisman: Oli McBurnie (£5.5m, forward)
Heisenberg: McBurnie is one of the most interesting £5.5m forwards in the game. His stoppage-time goal in the Championship play-off final secured Hull's promotion, and he finished the Championship campaign with 17 goals and eight assists.
McBurnie comes in £0.5m cheaper than some popular forwards like Calvert-Lewin and Brobbey. However, I would rather spend a little more on one of those two rather than McBurnie as I will be avoiding all Hull's assets to start the season.
Differential: Ryan Giles (£4m, defender)
Heisenberg: Giles recorded eight assists during Hull's promotion campaign and remains capable of getting forward from left-back, however, he will potentially be competing with Matty Targett for regular starts in the team.
Another issue is Hull's clean-sheet potential. It is slim pickings when assessing Hull's assets, so it's likely best to look at players from other clubs for your FPL teams at this point.
Player to avoid: Liam Millar (£5m, midfielder)
Heisenberg: I could have picked pretty much any Hull player as one to avoid, because in all honesty we should be avoiding most of their squad.
Hull are likely to face plenty of matches where their attacking opportunities are limited and they are unlikely to get many clean sheets.
If I was to choose a cheap Hull midfielder, then may as well save the £0.5m and suggest Regan Slater for £4.5m instead.
Ipswich Town
Talisman: Emersonn (£5.5m, forward)
Gianni: The Brazilian forward signed for a then-club record fee this summer from Toulouse. He will likely lead the line and could go on to become manager Gary O'Neil's star man.
Differential: Daizen Maeda (£5.5m, midfielder)
Gianni: There have been lots of personnel changes to the Ipswich attack and wide forward Maeda, categorised as a midfielder, is a 0.4% differential to monitor after his summer signing from Celtic.
He scored 50 goals in 149 games in the Scottish Premiership and had an excellent World Cup for Japan.
Player to avoid: Chuba Akpom (£5m, forward)
Gianni: Akpom is likely to be an impact substitute.
The Arsenal graduate is a familiar name that some managers might be drawn to, having done well at Middlesborough in 2022-23, but he will struggle for minutes.
Leeds United
Talisman: Dominic Calvert-Lewin (£6m, forward)
Holly: Calvert-Lewin comes in at a tempting price point following his 14 goals and two assists last season and he is being backed by around a quarter of fantasy managers.
He managed to stay consistently fit last campaign, making 35 appearances in his debut season with the club. With penalties too, it is clear to see why he is dominating the budget forward category.
Differential: Harry Wilson (£6.5m, midfielder)
Holly: Wilson sits among some high-profile signings for the club over the summer, with the former Fulham man producing 19 goal involvements last season, 10 goals and nine assists.
If he becomes a regular in the Leeds United attack then he could be a key man for them and potentially dominating set-pieces too. His price tag, at £0.5m more than Calvert-Lewin, may be a sticking point.
Player to avoid: Jaka Bijol (£5m, defender)
Holly: Leeds kept eight clean sheets last season, which is a figure they will aim to improve on with the arrival of former Manchester City goalkeeper James Trafford this summer.
There are cheaper routes into the Leeds United defence than Bijol at £5m, with Joe Rodon's minutes looking secure for just £4.5m. He produced 20 defensive contribution points last campaign.
Liverpool
Talisman: Dominik Szoboszlai (£7m, midfielder)
Pras: The Hungary international is the strongest Liverpool option.
He offers consistent minutes, set-piece involvement and solid all-round output which explains why nearly half of managers already own him.
Differential: Florian Wirtz (£7.5m, midfielder)
Pras: Wirtz's creative quality gives him a high points ceiling if the system clicks under new manager Andoni Iraola, where he will be a lot closer to the goal.
FPL managers should expect him to easily better last season's return of five goals and four assists.
Player to avoid: Jeremy Jacquet (£5m, defender)
Pras: Returning from a long-standing injury, limited pre-season games and the recent loan signing of Ronald Araujo all point to a slow integration into the Premier League for the France Under-21 defender.
Manchester City
Talisman: Erling Haaland (£15.5m, striker)
Gianni: The Norwegian has a record-breaking starting price and will again be the highest-owned player in the game.
Playing 90 minutes versus Bournemouth on the opening weekend is far from guaranteed given his lack of pre-season but with Crystal Palace and Coventry fixtures following that, you are a brave manager going without the best talisman in the game.
Differential: Phil Foden (£7m, midfielder)
Gianni: Foden has had a full pre-season and looks set to start against Bournemouth but if he has a bad game the risk of being dropped is fairly high given City's squad depth. At 7% owned he's a fun differential that has a high ceiling.
Player to avoid: Marc Guehi (£6m, defender)
Gianni: Guehi is the fourth most popular defender in the game but not guaranteed a starting spot under Enzo Maresca who has been complimentary about Ruben Dias (£5.5m) and Josko Gvardiol (£5.5m), both also centre-backs.
Manchester United
Talisman: Bruno Fernandes (£12m, midfielder)
Heisenberg: Fernandes produced 235 FPL points last season, including 24 assists, and has now been given a deserved price increase to £12m. His set-piece involvement, penalties and creative responsibility give him multiple routes to huge hauls (and he's excellent on the bonus points system too).
The opening fixtures make him particularly attractive as United face Hull and Ipswich in weeks one and two.
The price is a major drawback, but his combination of reliability, captaincy potential and fixture quality makes him an excellent pick.
Differential: Matheus Cunha (£8m, midfielder)
Heisenberg: Cunha is arguably the best differential at United. He's currently in just 12.7% of FPL teams compared to Bryan Mbeumo's 23.9% ownership. He finished last season strongly, scoring four goals and providing an assist in his final seven matches of the season.
Cunha has the ability to play across the frontline which makes him particularly dangerous (although there's a chance he could share minutes with other attacking options).
Player to avoid: Benjamin Sesko (£7m, forward)
Heisenberg: Sesko is probably the hardest United player to assess.
The Slovenian has enormous potential and finished his first Premier League season with a respectable 11 goals.
However, my big concern last season was security of minutes and that remains the case, especially as United will have more fixtures this season given Champions League involvement.
The temptation is obvious given United's opening fixtures and Sesko's undeniable potential, but Cunha and Fernandes currently offer more established routes into the attack - at least to start the season.
Newcastle United
Talisman: Nick Woltemade (£6m, forward)
Holly: It has been a dismal summer for Newcastle United with key player departures and a managerial change, leaving Nick Woltemade as the main target for fantasy potential.
The striker produced eight goals and four assists from 24 starts last season, and will look to stay ahead of Yoane Wissa for minutes coming into this campaign.
Differential: Malick Thiaw (£5m, defender)
Holly: Historically, the Magpies have been a sound defensive outfit. However, seven clean sheets last season was a little wide of the mark, with Thiaw their highest scoring defender.
He scored four goals in 33 appearances, while also racking up defensive contribution points on 12 occasions. He will justify his price tag if he can repeat that in this campaign.
Player to avoid: Lewis Hall (£5m, defender)
Holly: Full-back Lewis Hall produced 47 fantasy points fewer than Thiaw last season, despite creating three goal involvements from a similar number of appearances as his team-mate.
His output was less suited to the scoring matrix and he's also been linked with a move away from St James' Park in this window, making him an early season avoid.
Nottingham Forest
Talisman: Morgan Gibbs-White (£8m, midfielder)
Pras: Gibbs-White was Forest's key creator and goalscorer last season and should thrive under new manager Oliver Glasner in the left-sided number 10 role.
Can he replicate the 15 goals and four assists that made him the third-highest-scoring FPL midfielder in 25-26?
Differential: Neco Williams (£5m, defender)
Pras: Williams is likely to get some attacking returns from wing-back in Glasner's formation, plus he does well for defcon and takes some set-pieces.
That all makes him excellent value in the five-at-the-back system his new manager likes to play - remember how well Daniel Munoz did under Glasner last season?
Player to avoid: Chris Wood (£6m, striker)
Pras: The New Zealand striker faces increased competition up front, especially from Brazil forward Igor Jesus (£6m) who has been on form in pre-season.
That reduces his minutes security, especially given he is 34 years old and spent a large part of last season injured.
Sunderland
Talisman: Enzo le Fee (£6m, midfielder)
Heisenberg: Le Fee enjoyed a decent first Premier League season, returning five goals and six assists, while also picking up points through defensive contributions.
At £6m, Le Fee offers a very appealing combination of price, minutes and multiple routes to FPL points (including penalties potentially).
Sunderland have several exciting attacking players, but Le Fee looks like the player most capable of consistently contributing across the season.
Differential: Granit Xhaka (£5.5m, midfielder)
Heisenberg: Xhaka will not score you many goals, but he is one of Sunderland's most reliable FPL assets. He produced one goal, six assists and 26 defensive contribution points from 32 starts last season, giving him several routes to points.
The other major attraction is Sunderland's opening run. They visit Ipswich in gameweek one before hosting Fulham, giving Xhaka an excellent opportunity to produce immediately.
Player to avoid: Wilson Isidor (£5.5m, forward)
Heisenberg: Isidor is a classic FPL trap at the moment. His price is appealing and he has shown that he can score goals, but Sunderland have competition for the central striker position, most notably Brian Brobbey.
Unless Isidor can force his way above Brobbey in the pecking order, he is an avoid for me. Also, there are plenty of other cheap forwards to choose from before resorting to Isidor.
Tottenham
Talisman: Pedro Porro (£5.5m, defender)
Gianni: The right-back is the closest player Spurs have to a clear talisman. He is their highest-owned asset and was their standout player last season.
Off the back of an excellent World Cup for Spain, he is going to be very popular heading in to gameweek one.
Both striker Dominic Solanke (£6m) and James Maddison (£6.5m) could end up offering excellent value at times this season but with their injury struggles they are a wait and see to start the season.
Differential: Mathys Tel (£6m, midfielder)
Gianni: The Frenchman is under 0.5% owned and seems to be a favourite of manager Roberto de Zerbi.
He ended last season in great form high and wide on the left and looked sharp pre-season scoring a 30-yard direct free kick against Sydney FC.
Player to avoid: Marcos Senesi (£6m, defender)
GIanni: The Argentine was one of the FPL performers of the season last time out, for Bournemouth but he is an easy avoid for the time being.
There is uncertainty over how De Zerbi will line up, and Senesi is at risk of being benched given Tottenham's depth at centre-back.

These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved in
- Published
From a distance, Malaysia's Forest City looks 3D-printed: a bristle of identical white blocks clustered on an otherwise unremarkable coastline.
When it was unveiled by Chinese developers in 2016, the $100bn mega-project was pitched as "a dream paradise for all mankind": a special financial zone that could house some 700,000 residents. But a decade later, this 14-sq-km (3,400-acre) artificial island on Singapore's doorstep is thought to be inhabited by less than 1% of that.
Rows of eerily vacant skyscrapers loom over quiet streets. Inside empty apartments, benchtops and windows are filmed with dust.
"In 2016 they described it here like the golden city; very, very beautiful," says Jason Deng, a 56-year-old investor who was among the first to buy in Forest City, paying "a lot of money" for five properties.
"If I had known it was not so good I would not have bought so many apartments," he says now. "I thought it would be much, much better."
As it turns out, this is only a golden city for some people – and they're not the ones developers had hoped to attract.
In mid-July, Malaysian police raided two alleged scam operations spread across 32 premises in Forest City, arresting 335 people and seizing assets worth about one million ringgit (£181,810; $245,000), including 313 computers, 1,557 mobile phones, 17 laptops and 10 modems.
From these two call centre hubs – one occupying 27 apartments across five storeys of a residential tower, the other spread between five bungalows – cryptocurrency syndicates ran investment and love scams targeting victims abroad, according to police.
Those arrested include 309 Chinese nationals, 19 Indonesians, three Malaysians and four Myanmar nationals. Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said authorities were working with Interpol to track down the mastermind behind the operations.
The BBC reached out to Forest City and Johor police for comment, but did not receive a response.
Experts and locals tell the BBC this is likely to be the tip of the iceberg – and a symptom of a global scam industry that is spreading, evolving, and professionalising.
"The reality is that many of these organisations now resemble multinational corporations more than a traditional organised crime network or gang," says John Wojcik, an analyst at TRM Labs, which investigates crypto-facilitated crime. "They have dedicated recruitment teams, IT departments, money-laundering specialists and infrastructure."
Authorities and experts agree that the Forest City operations were probably staffed by criminals who had been driven out of Cambodia, a global nerve centre for transnational scams.
Over the past five years, this criminal sector has ballooned into a multi-billion-dollar industry, built on the forced labour of brutalised trafficking victims who work under threat of torture and abuse.
Since late last year, the Cambodian government has stepped up efforts to stamp out these operations. Authorities recently estimated that 300,000 people had left the country within a few months as raids on industrial-scale compounds intensified.
But these Malaysian offshoots do not appear to have been scam "compounds" in the traditional sense.
Compared to more infamous walled complexes in places like Sihanoukville or the Myanmar borderlands, the alleged scam hubs in Forest City appear almost white collar, reportedly staffed by local residents and sitting wall-to-wall with the homes of unsuspecting neighbours.
Kevin, a tenant who also works in property sales for Forest City, believes scammers are still operating in "condominiums or serviced apartments" in the complex. He asked for his name to be changed for fear of repercussions.
"We know what they're doing," he says. "This is actually a very common issue in Johor city and Kuala Lumpur, but especially in Forest City. Forest City is very special."
Part of what makes Forest City "special", according to Kevin, Wojcik and others, is the very thing that has gained it so much notoriety: its reputation as a semi-abandoned "ghost city".
"When we speak to clients or customers, the company teaches us to say 'we already have 23,000 residents living in this area'," says Kevin – but the reality, he quietly adds, is there are "less than 5,000".
"That's the reason" scammers have chosen Forest City to set up shop, he suggests.
"They have their own privacy... Nobody comes here."
There are several factors which precipitated what many see as the downfall of Forest City.
Spearheaded by Country Garden, one of China's largest property developers, and Danga 88, a private company controlled by Malaysian Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, the project was initially dreamed up as an eco-friendly metropolis for well-heeled Chinese clients - featuring a high-end hotel, golf course and water park. The resort-style city's seafront offices and apartments were expected to be in high demand.
But the combined weight of the Covid pandemic, China's spiralling property slump and constricted borrowing limits for its citizens have sunk those sky-high ambitions, and all but ground the project to a standstill.
The lights are still on, but almost no-one is home.
And that appears to have made the complex a honeypot for scammers.
"Forest City reflects the conditions organised crime have been targeting for years - a flagship location marketed as a prestigious, luxury, master-planned smart city that never came close to fulfilling that vision," Wojcik says.
"Developments like this offer precisely what these syndicates look for: modern infrastructure, large numbers of vacant properties, and international connectivity all wrapped around the veneer of legitimate economic activity to ensure that the criminal nature of what goes on inside remains unnoticed."
With this in mind, the glittering facade of Forest City echoes a more infamous metropolis 1,800 kilometres (1,120 miles) to the north: Shwe Kokko, the so-called resort city on Myanmar's Thai border, which is one of the world's most notorious scam hubs.
Built by the private Chinese conglomerate Yatai, Shwe Kokko markets itself as a safe holiday destination for Chinese tourists and a haven for the super-rich. But behind its tree-lined streets and luxury villas is a nexus of fraud, money-laundering and human trafficking.
For all its headwinds, and despite the fact that only 15 to 20% of the originally proposed project has been completed, Forest City similarly still markets itself as an up-and-coming hotbed for property investment, tech innovation and tax-free business ventures.
Such entrepreneurial packaging serves as a Trojan horse for scammers wanting to set up shop without drawing unwanted attention – and allows them to perpetrate their fraud more effectively.
Wojcik explains that "when scam syndicates can embed themselves behind seemingly legitimate businesses in ordinary commercial developments, they not only become more difficult to detect and disrupt, they become capable of exerting serious amounts of power and influence through the massive profits they generate".
This power and influence in turn allows scammers to professionalise in other ways.
Though human trafficking still largely fuels much of the scam industry's labour force, there is now a noticeable trend of syndicate operators recruiting and retaining experienced scammers with higher pay and better working conditions.
Meanwhile, in the same Telegram groups where scam jobs are being advertised, career scammers are also now posting detailed resumes, outlining their experience in fraudulent activities and emphasising their eagerness to work.
"It's a sign the industry is maturing into a more professionalised criminal enterprise," Wojcik explains, "while coercion and exploitation still remain widespread".
The Forest City raids highlight a transnational scam industry that is shifting in size and shape. But this is far from the first time such operations have been detected in Malaysia.
Throughout 2022, before the industry gained widespread global attention, Malaysian authorities raided several scam centres operating out of bungalows and condominiums in the southern state of Johor, the northern state of Penang and the capital city of Kuala Lumpur.
Yet while these and other major crackdowns sent a message of zero tolerance to fraud syndicates, Wojcik notes that Malaysia has remained home to influential criminal networks - and that "any signs of large-scale re-emergence deserve close attention".
In Forest City, such signs may already be emerging.
Kevin says it's long been an "open secret" that scams are happening here, and that "the only shocking thing is that the police were effective".
He's certain there are more, too – but is unperturbed at the idea that his neighbours might be defrauding people out of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
"For me, I don't care," he says. "It's not my business... I work here just for the salary."
Other residents feel the same way.
Phillip, whose name we have also changed, moved to Forest City from Singapore last year, attracted by the relatively cheap property market and the idea that he could get more value for his money. He works in tech, and says he is "very focused" on the topic of cyber protection.
"Yes they [the scammers] might be on my doorstep, they might be my neighbours... [they] could be one of the ones that's running one of these syndicates. At the end of the day, it doesn't matter where you go – this is going to happen."
He says he was "not surprised" to hear about the reports of scam centres in his complex. What has surprised him is the fact that "more and more people are moving" to Forest City.
One of the reasons he chose the development where he lives is because of the peace and quiet, he says – but he's pleased to see that it is evolving from a "ghost town" into a place where people seem to want to be.
"So many people have lost money on these developments," he points out. "But the last three months, you see the lights on in the condos. You've gone from one in 20 to maybe one in five."

No cases of Ebola have been detected among passengers on a river boat that was placed in quarantine near Kinshasa, health authorities have said.
The confirmation announced on Saturday (August 8, 2026) eased concerns that the rare Bundibugyo virus might spread to the Congolese capital.
More than 200 boat passengers were placed in quarantine on Thursday (August 6) in the port of Maluku, 65 kilometres (40 miles) from Kinshasa, after one traveller who was previously aboard the boat died with symptoms matching the Ebola virus.
Specialist teams from the Ministry of Health were deployed to Maluku to examine all of those on board. Those exhibiting suspicious symptoms had samples taken and sent to a laboratory for analysis, the Ministry said on Saturday (August 8), adding that the vessel was also decontaminated.
The National Institute of Biomedical Research, which is responsible for testing, said that all suspected cases tested negative for Bundibugyo. It urged the population of Kinshasa to remain calm.
Congo has been battling an Ebola outbreak that has been deemed the fastest in history in terms of transmission, with confirmed cases since it started in May reaching 4,200, including over 1,900 deaths.
The riverboat passenger had become sick and disembarked nearly three weeks ago in Pimu, in the province of Mongala, more than 1,000 kilometres from Kinshasa along the Congo River, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya said on Thursday (August 6). The capital has no confirmed Ebola case, he added.
News of the passenger's death caused panic in Kinshasa, which is far from the eastern region hit by the outbreak, the second-largest outbreak on record, behind the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak that recorded more than 28,000 cases, including over 11,000 deaths.
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing.
Health authorities say between 60% and 70% of new cases in the current outbreak are recorded outside of contacts being monitored, and that the outbreak is spreading at an “alarming” rate faster than efforts to track it.
The medical charity Doctors Without Borders said this week that the outbreak is still “spreading at an alarming and unprecedented rate” and that the response, which has been expanding, “is still not reaching communities quickly enough to break transmission chains.”

Ride-hailing majors Uber and Rapido reportedly held talks in May to combine their India operations, but the discussions broke down over structure of the proposed deal. According to an ET report, the talks took place during Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi’s India visit, with the US-based ride-hailing major proposing to bring the two businesses together under Rapido’s management. During the visit, Khosrowshahi met government officials, business partners, and Uber employees. He also met Rapido cofounder and CEO Aravind Sanka and other senior executives as the two companies explored a potential transaction. Rapido subsequently made a counterproposal to acquire Uber’s India operations through a cash-and-stock transaction, with Uber retaining a minority stake in the Bengaluru-based startup, according to the report. However, the proposal was not acceptable to Uber, which was unwilling to exit India or cede control of its operations. “Uber was looking at a combination, but Rapido’s proposal was closer to an acquisition of Uber’s India business,” ET quoted a source as saying. The talks eventually collapsed without an agreement. Rapido denied the report in response to Inc42’s queries, saying, “There is no truth to the speculation. Rapido has no such plans and remains focused on independently building and scaling its mobility business in India.” Uber, meanwhile, declined to comment, saying, “We do not comment on market speculation or private conversations with industry participants.” The development comes amid Uber’s efforts to expand its share of India’s two-wheeler mobility market, which Rapido currently dominates. Earlier this week, Uber announced the expansion of Uber Bike to 100 more cities, taking its overall footprint in India to more than 220 cities. The new markets span 18 states and one Union territory and include Jammu, Tirunelveli, Silchar, and Jamnagar. The expansion is expected to take Uber deeper into smaller cities and intensify its competition with Rapido, particularly in the bike-taxi segment. Rapido accounts for nearly half of India’s ride-hailing volumes, according to industry estimates. Its share of the two-wheeler segment is estimated at 60%-75%, while it commands an estimated 20%-30% share of the four-wheeler cab segment. The startup also strengthened its war chest in May by raising $240 Mn in primary capital in a funding round led by existing investor Prosus. WestBridge Capital, Accel, and other investors also participated in the round. The funding was part of a broader $730 Mn primary-and-secondary transaction that valued Rapido at $3 Bn on a post-money basis. Rapido plans to use the fresh capital to enter new markets, deepen its presence in existing ones, expand its driver network, and invest in technology and hiring. India’s Crowded Ride-Hailing Market The reported talks came as competition in India’s ride-hailing market intensifies, with established platforms and a growing number of new entrants competing for a share of a rapidly expanding market. India’s ride-hailing services market is estimated at $2.9 Bn in 2026 and is projected to reach $11 Bn by 2033, growing at a CAGR of 20.7%. The opportunity is attracting companies beyond traditional ride-hailing platforms. Automakers are increasingly moving into mobility services, with VinFast-backed Green SM entering India earlier this year with an all-electric ride-hailing service. Bharat Taxi and newer platforms such as Trevel and Plush Miles are also seeking to establish a foothold. Many of these entrants are attempting to differentiate themselves through EV fleets, lower commissions, and driver-focused business models, increasing pressure on incumbents such as Uber, Ola, and Rapido. As competition intensifies, the battle for market share is increasingly centred on driver retention, fleet availability, fares, and unit economics. Against this backdrop, a combination of Uber and Rapido’s India operations could have significantly altered the competitive dynamics of the country’s ride-hailing market.

Apple Watches are smart little gadgets, but they don't always fit the vibe. There were plenty of nights when I left mine at home because, as much as I wanted to check my notifications discreetly, the watch just didn't match my outfit. I've also had my fair share of faux pas and just let the neon orange sport band clash with my neutral ensemble.
Fortunately, Apple Watch bands are a simple and relatively affordable way to zhuzh up the look of your wearable. Beyond aesthetics, different styles also impact performance and functionality. For example, I don't want a heavy stainless steel or high-quality leather band weighing me down during a sweaty workout, just as I wouldn't wear a flimsy silicone band to a dinner party.
At WIRED, we've been testing bands since the very first Apple Watch launched in 2015. After years of wearing and swapping, I've rounded up the best bands for every occasion. Be sure to check out our related product guides, including the Best Apple Watch Accessories, Best Apple Watch, and Best Smartwatches for more recommendations.

How I Test Apple Watch Bands
I research Apple Watch bands across major retailers, including Apple, Amazon, and Nike. I also consulted former WIRED editor Adrienne So, who had covered fitness trackers and Apple Watch bands for a decade. I look for bestsellers, affordable dupes, and niche finds.
I test Apple Watch bands all day, every day, across workouts, commutes, and overnight. Each band is worn for at least two weeks and subjected to sweat, water, and everyday friction. That's typically enough time to evaluate comfort, quality, and durability. If it's severely uncomfortable or triggers skin irritation on the first day of testing, it is ruled out. My top picks remain in my rotation for months so I can compare them against newer models and assess how they hold up over time.
- Comfort: Apple Watch bands shouldn't pinch, trap moisture, or feel insecure. I also pay attention to breathability and potential irritation, especially with silicone and metal bands, and factor in how different skin types might react over time.
- Quality: Closures are fastened, unfastened, and adjusted repeatedly to see how they hold up. A good band should lock in place, adjust easily with one hand, and resist loosening over time. I also examine materials for flexibility, finish, and overall craftsmanship.
- Durability: To test claims of water resistance, I wear each band while I wash my hands, trek through the Chicago rain, and shower (if the brand says it's safe). Whenever relevant, I revisit bands after extended wear. I track discoloration, odor retention, and hardware fatigue.
- Ease of setup and use: I swap bands across multiple Apple Watch case sizes to ensure the lugs slide in easily and lock securely. I also judge how easy they are to install and remove.
- Adjustability and sizing: I test fit across a range of wrist sizes—with help from former WIRED editors Adrienne So and Martin Cizmar—and note whether the brands offer inclusive sizing.
- Versatility: I wear each band in casual, work, and dressier settings to see how well it adapts to different environments. I also note whether it complements different finishes and case colors.
Most of the Apple Watch bands remain in storage so I can continue long-term testing and compare newer releases against older models. Any discontinued models are donated once testing is complete.
What Am I Testing Next?
I'm testing the Nomad Sport Band. I'm also reevaluating the Nomad Tempo Band, the Apple Trail Loop, and the Apple Milanese Titanium Band.
Best Band for Everyday Wear
The Nike Sport Loop has been my everyday band since 2020. I bought another in 2023 because I wanted to swap colors, and I figured after three years, I should buy a brand-new one, but it has held up remarkably well. Made from a blend of recycled polyester, spandex, and nylon, it's breathable and lightweight. The double-layered nylon weave is designed with dense loops that help prevent moisture from getting trapped against your skin. As long as you regularly hand-wash it to rid it of sweat buildup and dirt, it stays odor-free.
The hook-and-loop fastener and pull tab make it easy to adjust with one hand. It is Velcro, so beware—it can snag on softer fabrics. Still, for a band designed with sports in mind, it's understated enough to wear almost anywhere. I wouldn't wear it to a formal event, but for the office or casual social events, it's perfect.

Nomad originally designed the Stratos Band for the Apple Watch Ultra, but it fits just as well with the SE and Series 1 through 11. It's easy to adjust, refined enough for the office, and backed by Grade 4 titanium hardware with a scratch-resistant DLC coating. It's technically suited for workouts and outdoor use, but it is a hefty band that I personally prefer for casual everyday wear.
The hardware comes in natural or black finishes, which is nice if you're particular about matching your setup. Best Silicone Apple Watch Band
Moft's Snap Duo Watch Band is made from nontoxic, food-grade silicone, but you wouldn't know it at a glance. The pebbled finish mimics leather, giving it a more elevated look, without the stiffness or upkeep. Also, unlike leather, it's noticeably soft, waterproof, and resistant to direct, which makes it just as suitable for workouts and water sports as it is for the office.
The design is particularly interesting. Each band features two colors, and thanks to a bidirectional connector, you can flip and swap sides to create four different looks. Switching it up is easy, and the magnetic link is even easier to snap on. Keep in mind, there's no manual release mechanism, so it may not feel sturdy on its own. Moft includes a removable buckle as an extra precaution, and while it takes a bit of fiddling to attach, it's worth using for a more secure fit.

Honorable Mentions
Apple Sport Band for $49: The Sport Band is decent—I’m wearing it right now—and its sweat-resistant fluoroelastomer makes it a solid choice for workouts and anyone who wants a low-maintenance band they can easily wipe clean. The pin-and-tuck closure doesn’t offer as much adjustability as I’d like. My usual setting feels a little too loose for workouts when I want accurate tracking, but tightening it one notch is uncomfortable. Also, if you’re trying to avoid fluoroelastomer, I’d skip this one for now. Apple has said it’s working to phase out PFAs from its products, but that transition will take time.
Apple Milanese Titanium Band for $199: The Apple Watch Ultra 2 came in a black finish, which was matched by this special black titanium Milanese loop. The standout feature is the parachute-style buckle, which Apple claims was historically used for diving and other underwater activities. (I seem to remember that most water activities use ratchet tie downs and threaded cam buckles for straps, but I will let this slide.) The titanium doesn't irritate my skin, and the band and buckle smooth and easy to adjust. It's carbon-neutral, and it turns your sporty watch into a much dressier watch. —Adrienne So
Apple Trail Loop for $99: Apple has several band varieties for different activities: the Alpine Loop ($99) for outdoor adventures, the Ocean Band ($99) for water sports, and the Trail Loop for endurance runs and hikes.
Nomad Tempo Band for $59: If you must have a fluoroelastomer band, the Tempo bands are PFAS-free. It's slightly too big for my 150-mm wrist, and Nomad hedges its bets with sizing by making each band backward-compatible with two sizes; for example, the smallest size is compatible with both 41- and 42-mm watch sizes. This doesn't quite work if you have the older, smaller-size watch, but it fits my 46-mm Series 10 well. —Adrienne So
Wrangler Ranch Rider Calf Hair Band for $35: This collaboration between Wrangler and accessory company WithIt includes seven bands of all different materials, from a turquoise-and-silver bracelet band to a denim band. I was unexpectedly charmed by the Rodeo Ready, which is made from calf hair that has been bleached and dyed. It can be sized to fit all Apple Watch models, from the older 38-mm versions to the Apple Watch Ultra 3. It is comfortable and tacky—in a good way—especially if you're wearing a bunch of silver bangles and beads and patting a horse. —Adrienne So
Zzdzz Silicone Magnetic Strap for $20: My Instagram feed is bombarded with ads for easy-to-put-on adjustable silicone straps, so I bought this cheap one off Amazon. The colors are vibrant, and it is, indeed, very comfortable and easy to adjust. However, the flip side of that is that it falls off very easily, and I can't vouch for its durability. Also, the little loop that holds the strap down isn't attached to the band at any point, so I lose it constantly. Whatever—it's less than $20. —Adrienne So
Avoid These Apple Watch Bands
Apple Solo Loop for $49: Apple really hawks its precisely sized Solo Loops, which form a single loop around your wrist. But they're expensive, and as an active person, I can't size them correctly. They're always too tight when I'm working out and too loose when I'm not. I prefer an adjustable band. —Adrienne So
Hopo Resin Band for $13: My mom has this gorgeous Machete Apple Watch tortoiseshell resin bracelet band ($80), so I figured I'd do her one better and order the cheap one off Amazon. It's a no-go—the included pin remover is too short, so I can't take links out to make the band smaller. I will just get the Machete band next time. —Adrienne So

On video: Vande Mataram kickstarts Red Fort Independence Day celebrations in a historic first
PM Modi highlighted the significance of Vande Mataram being rendered at the Red Fort and described it as a historic moment.
In a historic first, Vande Mataram, the national song of India, was played at the Red Fort on Saturday morning as India celebrated its 80th Independence Day. Vande Mataram was followed by the recitation of the national anthem at the grand event where Prime Minister Narendra Modi hoisted the tricolour. Track live updates on Independence Day celebrations
This comes after the Parliament passed the Vande Mataram Bill during the recently concluded monsoon session. This was followed by President Droupadi Murmu giving assent to the Bill, granting the National Song the same legal protection as the national anthem.
The grand function marks 150 years of the national song,'Vande Mataram', as floral decoration on the ramparts depicted the national flag at the centre flanked by 'Vande Mataram' in Hindi.
Also read: Armed Naxalism dealt with, now time to isolate ‘dimaagi Naxals’: PM Modi in I-Day speech
Deep Dive
An Army band played the tune of 'Vande Mataram' while the guests present at Red Fort sung the national song. The guests included Union home minister Amit Shah, defence minister Rajnath Singh, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman, external affairs minister S Jaishankar, among others.
Watch ‘Vande Mataram’ rendition at Red Fort
Vande Mataram recitation was followed by the prime minister hoisting the national flag. The national anthem was sung later.
The Vande Mataram Bill received the President's assent on Tuesday, making it a law and bringing the national song under the ambit of Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act which earlier prohibited intentionally preventing the singing of the national anthem (Jana Gana Mana) or causing disturbance to any assembly engaged in such singing.
Also read: PM Modi announces free online coaching for competitive exams in Independence Day speech
In his speech, Modi on Saturday also highlighted the significance of Vande Mataram being rendered at the Red Fort and said, “For everyone present at this ceremony today, this is also a historic moment. For the first time since Independence, Vande Mataram is echoing from the Red Fort on August 15.”
Written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 1875, Vande Mataram became a rallying cry during India's struggle for freedom from the British colonial rule. 'Vande Mataram' as a political slogan was first used on August 7, 1905, according to a note '150 Years of Vande Mataram: A Melody That Became a Movement', shared by the government on November 6 last year.
It was subsequently adopted as India's national song by the Constituent Assembly in 1950, three years after India attained independence.
The government last November launched a year-long celebration to mark 150 years of 'Vande Mataram'.
Highlights from PM Modi's Independence Day speech
Reiterating the government's resolve, PM Modi on Friday said India will become ‘Viksit Bharat’ by 2047.
“In the last 12 years, every Indian has tried to take the country to new heights. That is why 25 crore Indians have broken free of poverty in such a short time,” Modi said, as he said that said that India cannot be dependent on other nations.
The prime minister added that in the past 12 years, defence production increased by four times, electronic manufacturing by seven times, high-tech railway coach production by 21 times, and mobile phone manufacturing by 33 times.
He highlighted that the country saw numerous achievements in the digital and innovation sector as well.
"Internet consumers increased by four times. Grant of patents went up by four times. Digital transactions increased by 100 per cent," Modi added.

Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan has publicly backed Andrew Bragg and urged colleagues to “follow his lead” after a public speech that has split colleagues and triggered a rebuke from opposition leader, Angus Taylor.
At the National Press Club on Wednesday, Bragg announced a policy to slash the national construction code and suggested net overseas migration should be dropped from the current level of about 300,000 to below 180,000 a year to keep pace with new housing builds.
Senior colleagues, including Taylor, were quick to dismiss the migration figure this week, saying they were Bragg’s “personal views” and that the party’s policy was yet to be finalised. The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson had said: “I don’t think you should bank that at all” in response to the number.
Privately, Taylor counselled his frontbencher.
Moderates, including McLachlan and Queensland senator Paul Scarr, called Bragg’s speech “terrific” while others privately said the reaction by the media and some internally was “overblown”.
McLachlan, an outspoken South Australian senator who has publicly criticised his party’s positions on migration and the climate crisis, said Bragg “delivered a masterclass in thought leadership”.
“His address was an important step in the development of a policy suite that seeks advance the nation,” McLachlan told Guardian Australia.
“His aspiration for Australia is admirable. Every member of the Coalition should follow his lead and discuss policy pathways openly.”
Scarr, who has also defied his party and crossed the Senate floor in March to censure Pauline Hanson after she wore a burqa in the Upper House, said he “thought it was a terrific speech. High-level and reinforcing our core Liberal values”.
Other Liberals have been frustrated at the intervention by Bragg, with one MP saying privately colleagues were angry at the lack of discipline and this could be “his last chance”.
Even after critical commentary from his colleagues in recent days, Bragg has maintained it was important to talk about big ideas.
The NSW senator said while many of his ideas, such as a specific net overseas migration target, hadn’t been green-ticked by the shadow cabinet, it was important to “move the debate on”.
Bragg said voters needed “ambitious policy for tomorrow, not micro-announcements for today that aim to please and appease”.
“I’m confident that we will be rewarded for putting more detail on the table,” he told Guardian Australia.
On Friday, he also corrected comments made in an interview on RN Breakfast where he responded “yes, definitely”, when asked whether Australians should accept substandard homes under his changes to the construction code, which would make energy efficiency standards voluntary.
In a social media post, Bragg said he had misheard the question, adding “houses built to this standard would be strong, safe and sound homes with all the basic amenity, such as insulation, plumbing, sewerage etc”.
“I did not intend to agree that houses complying with the Basic Australian Standard would be ‘substandard’. They wouldn’t be.”
One Liberal MP, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said there had been overreaction to the speech internally which likely came from “not reading what was actually in the speech”.
“Like any disruption, you might be a bit uncomfortable first. I think maybe just a little bit of surprise for some. I think he did a good job and he was brave.”
They welcomed the fresh take from Bragg and said the Sydney senator consistently showed he wasn’t a “benchwarmer”, but wanted to engage in substantial policy.
“Clearly what we’ve been doing over the last five or six years in particular has not worked. So maybe taking a different approach or approaching the problem in a different way is a sensible thing to do.”
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, was quick to shoot down any cuts to working holiday visas as Bragg suggested in his speech, but praised his “big ideas”.
“I love Andrew Bragg. He’s he’s full of ideas … we need people like him because he’s full of energy and enthusiasm,” he told ABC’s Radio National on Friday.

Japanese companies have stepped up their efforts to prevent their employees from suffering heatstroke as temperatures exceeded 40 degrees Celsius in some parts of Japan this summer.
General contractor Obayashi had its employees work at construction sites from 7 a.m. to 1 p.m. in July and August, earlier than their usual work hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
The company, in introducing the summer shift, looked to “further reduce the risk of heatstroke,” an official said. If a construction schedule is affected by the shift, work hours are extended when temperatures are low.
Since May, West Japan Railway has provided workers in charge of on-site maintenance and inspections with an app developed by the company to allow such workers to obtain information on heatstroke prevention.
At the company, examples of measures and products used to deal with heat are being shared. In September, short-sleeved polo shirt uniforms will be introduced on a trial basis to about 15,000 station staff and crew members. The uniforms will offer improved breathability and sweat absorption.
Seibu Railway is providing staff working in mountainous regions with recreational vehicles equipped with air conditioners, refrigerators and other amenities to serve as rest areas and to improve work efficiency. Previously, a round trip to a rest area took about 40 minutes in total.
Heatstroke measures are also being undertaken at busy commercial facilities.
At a beer garden on the rooftop of Matsuya department store in the upscale Ginza district in Tokyo, employees put stickers on their arms to get a visual representation of changes in their body temperature under a demonstration program with cosmetics and health food company Fancl, which supplies the stickers.
“The kitchen is especially hot,” Mizuki Shimomura, a 23-year-old employee, said. “As the color (of my sticker) changes, I’ve become more conscious about drinking water.”
Last year, the ordinance on industrial safety and health was revised to oblige business operators to implement measures against heatstroke.
According to a survey conducted by research company Teikoku Databank in July, 50.0% of companies said their operations had been disrupted by intense heat.

The DCU is on unsteady ground, but it is hoping that one new offering in particular will deliver it from blackest night. That would be Lanterns, the True Detective inspired Green Lantern series airing on HBO Max this Sunday. Reviews are in, and everyone from Warner Bros. to fans should be able to breathe easy.
As it stands, Lanterns has a verified fresh 90% Rotten Tomatoes review score from 40 critics, a sizable sampling, and almost everyone has something good to say. That puts it as one of the top-scoring DCU projects so far, but not quite touching the hem of Matt Reeves’ The Penguin at a 95%. Still, if it’s even close, that’s quite an achievement. Here are the other official DCU projects it’s competing against:
- Creature Commandos – 95% critic score, 79% audience score
- Peacemaker – 93% critic score, 83% audience score
- Superman – 83% critic score, 90% audience score
- Supergirl – 52% critic score, 73% audience score.
Lanterns is a test on two fronts. First, this needs to be good because of how badly Supergirl just made the DCU look. It’s not just a lackluster movie, it is one of the biggest superhero financial flops of all time.
Second, this is only the second DCU project that is entirely free of James Gunn's writing or directing. He delegated Supergirl, and that did poorly. He delegated this, and well, it seems to be going great. Here, Gunn has gotten Damon Lindelof involved, who previously worked on Watchmen and The Leftovers, both great television series, with the former a (different kind of) DC superhero property. It’s a contrast to Supergirl, which had both a new writer and a new director in the genre.
Lanterns has had a bit of a rocky road to release here, at least in terms of fan perception, outside of all the DCU drama. Namely, it seemed to be very much downplaying the actual…Green Lantern stuff, and it was mostly just two guys walking around in dusty jackets. But in time, they showed the suits, they showed the powers, and the end result seems to be a good balance of realism and cosmic superheroism.
Kyle Chandler plays Hal Jordan, who fans have calculated has been the canon Green Lantern for Earth for almost a decade before Superman arrived. Aaron Pierre is his protégé, John Stewart, an actor who was effectively fan-cast as soon as he showed up in the Netflix hit Rebel Ridge. A month after that movie was released, he had the job.
The plot is a murder mystery with broader implications for the DC universe, and it may, in fact, be a great way to introduce a core Justice League member at a moment when the DCU needs it. We will all find out this Sunday.

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Last year, I asked The Atlantic’s writers and editors to name a perfect episode of TV, but a perfect finale is especially hard to pull off—and nothing invokes the wrath of fans quite like a bad ending. Here are eight shows that make the most out of their last minutes.
The following contains spoilers for the shows mentioned.
Fleabag (streaming on Prime Video)
Almost nobody is left happy by the final moments of Fleabag—not the heartbroken but resolute “Hot Priest”; not the protagonist Fleabag, watching a fox trail behind the man who has just left her for God; and certainly not the viewer, who has no choice but to let Fleabag look into the camera, shake her head, and leave us behind.
But the best ending is a cathartic one. Fleabag, played by the show’s creator, Phoebe Waller-Bridge, is a dry-humored, unabashed, fourth-wall-breaking character who encounters God and new meaning in the second season, which is also the last. She attends a Quaker meeting and is moved by the Holy Spirit to say one of my favorite lines of the series: “I sometimes worry I wouldn’t be such a feminist if I had bigger tits.” She and her sister, Claire, repair their relationship and each kneel, exasperated, before different men to ask for deliverance—Claire from her obnoxious husband, and Fleabag from her suffering. And in the last moments of the finale, after a backyard wedding and the implosion of Claire’s marriage, Fleabag tells the Hot Priest that she loves him, and he tells her, “It’ll pass.” To anybody still reeling from the conclusion of this perfectly short-lived show, that’s also a message to us: This is the end, and one day it will feel like enough.
— Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor
Twin Peaks (streaming on Pluto TV and Paramount+)
Twin Peaks had multiple conclusions over its strange life as a TV show, first ending on a shocking second season cliff-hanger in 1991, then failing to resolve that with a follow-up film a year later, leaving fans feeling frustrated by what could have been. But in 2017, the co-creators David Lynch and Mark Frost delivered a magnificent and challenging third season with an even more mind-bending last episode. In the true finale of Twin Peaks, titled “Part 18” or “What Is Your Name?,” the heroic Special Agent Dale Cooper (played by Kyle MacLachlan) finally frees himself from the demonic possession that he’s been under for the entire season and travels back in time to the start of the show to try to undo Laura Palmer’s murder. Whatever he does, however, creates an entirely new world that seems even more confusing, and the screen cuts to black as some new version of Laura lets out a chilling scream. It’s another dramatic cliff-hanger, but this time a more intentional one, underlining the hubris in Cooper’s straight-arrow heroism: Try as he might to fix the world’s wrongs, its fundamental evil and suffering are impossible to scrub away.
— David Sims, staff writer
Nathan for You (streaming on HBO Max)
The overarching story of Nathan for You, the brilliant docu-comedy hosted by Nathan Fielder, is easy to miss. Fielder’s show ran for four seasons on an episodic premise: He uses his very minimal business acumen to help local entrepreneurs and store owners boost their foot traffic through absurd means that are clearly destined to fail. Fielder performs the role of a stoic, socially awkward, sometimes-cruel game master with aplomb, but amid all the tomfoolery is a very human through line: Fielder, the show implies, really just wants to connect.
That context explains why the series finale is a moving, feature-length meditation on love, remorse, and loneliness. “Finding Frances” focuses on a man named Bill Heath, who previously appeared on the show as the world’s least convincing Bill Gates impersonator. Fielder endeavors to reunite him with a long-lost old girlfriend, and the episode makes clear that he is afraid that he may eventually become Bill, who, in his 70s, is alone and full of regret, having funneled all of his energy into his career. The quest to locate the titular Frances is full of the usual contrivances, but it’s also sentimental and shockingly earnest. The very last scene—in which Fielder has to choose between his heart and his humor—ends the show with a reveal that rings poignant, even a little sad.
— Allegra Frank, senior editor
Cowboy Bebop (streaming on Crunchyroll)
This 1998 anime about bounty hunters adventuring through galaxies aboard a spaceship is nothing like its more famous Cartoon Network contemporaries Sailor Moon and Dragon Ball Z. Cowboy Bebop isn’t kid friendly (though I did first discover it at age 12): There is bloodshed, sex, and criminal activity, but most of all, there is the profoundly adult theme of running away from one’s past. Among the hunters is Spike, who split from a crime syndicate under circumstances I won’t spoil; Faye, a wanted amnesiac; Jet, the hulking captain, who lost a love; Ed, the quirky teenage hacker left by her father; and Ein, a corgi rescued from a lab.
For me, a perfect finale needs to feel both inevitable and surprising, and it needs to actually round out the story. Cowboy Bebop takes care to draw out every character’s past, and gives them arcs that befit their endings. This does mean that the found family you’ve grown attached to over the course of 26 episodes may not stay together in perpetuity. But I wouldn’t want to see the show finish any other way.
— Shan Wang, programming director
Insecure (streaming on HBO Max)
Issa Rae’s namesake character on Insecure routinely looks at herself in the mirror and talks to her alter ego. Her reflection is a little more outgoing and blunt than she is in real life, and in the series finale, that alter ego is once again laughing at her for a situation she put herself in: “You’re down bad. I don’t know where you go from here.” In real life, Issa replies that she just wants “to fast-forward to the part where everything is okay.”
But life is not lived in a series of highs. “One could collect the highest peaks of the whole world but put together they would not be a continent,” Zora Neale Hurston once wrote. “Just a collection of bristling peaks. No nuances of valleys and plains.” Insecure, as a show, follows the relationships and friendships of two Black women in Los Angeles, giving us a look into the minutiae of their daily lives and how big everything can seem. The finale, in contrast, is a series of vignettes showing each central character’s birthday at some point in the future—the moments when they think they have it all figured out, and the moments amid those highs when they remain insecure.
— Adam Harris, Radio Atlantic host
The O.C. (streaming on Hulu, Disney+, and HBO Max)
The last season of this popular early-2000s teen drama is somewhat controversial among fans. There are plenty of cringeworthy plotlines (Chris Pratt plays an animal-rights activist named Ché; a main character’s absent father suddenly reappears), but the finale manages to save the show from the mess it’s made. The episode follows Seth Cohen and Ryan Atwood, who was taken in by Seth’s family at the series’ start, as they all prepare to move out of the titular O.C.
The storyline provides closure while leaving just enough open-ended. A flash-forward in the final minutes allows viewers to catch a glimpse of the futures they have yearned to see for these characters: Seth and Summer get married; Ryan goes to college and later offers to help a young boy the way the Cohens once helped him. Set to Patrick Park’s “Life Is a Song,” the montage provides one last moving musical moment on a show known for them. It also delivers what I think all finales should: emotional payoff and an ending that feels earned.
— Kate Guarino, senior editor
The Jinx (streaming on HBO Max)
There has never been a finale like the Season 1 finale of The Jinx. The 2015 HBO documentary series investigated the 1982 disappearance of Kathie Durst, the wife of the real-estate heir Robert Durst, as well as the murders of two of his acquaintances. It sounds like your typical true-crime doc. It isn’t.
If, in the 11 years since it came out, you have by some miracle not been spoiled on what happens, do not read the rest of this blurb. I’m serious. To those in the know or stubborn enough to stay for the spoilers, I will say this: I have never been as shocked by anything on television as when Durst seemingly confesses on mic: “Killed them all, of course.”
I know I am bending the rules a bit here—technically, the Season 1 finale of The Jinx isn’t a series finale, but at the time, it was supposed to be. And the evidence revealed in that season directly contributed to Durst’s arrest and eventual murder conviction, which the show covered when it aired a second season nearly a decade later.
The Jinx ruined all other true-crime documentaries for me. If you aren’t going to actually catch the killer, why would I even watch?
— Julie Beck, staff writer
St. Elsewhere (available to rent on Prime Video and Apple TV+)
During its run in the 1980s, the NBC medical drama St. Elsewhere engaged in plenty of creative experiments. But the 1988 finale is a masterpiece, a loving homage to time-honored shows such as The Fugitive and M*A*S*H (an autopsy is performed on “patient 4077 … Blake, Henry”). Why so many inside jokes about old TV shows?
Because, as we find out in the show’s last few minutes, the entire series is merely the dream of an autistic boy named Tommy Westphall. The two top doctors at St. Elsewhere are actually, in Tommy’s real life, his grandfather and his construction-worker father, who wonder what Tommy thinks about all day while sitting in front of the TV and staring into a snow globe with a model of the hospital in it.
This amazing moment lives on: It has spawned years of internet theories about the “Tommy Westphall Universe.” If St. Elsewhere is a dream, what about all of the crossovers from other shows? The doctors of St. Elsewhere visit the bar from Cheers, which is also set in Boston; is that show part of Tommy’s fantasies?
It is a fine ending to a quirky series, and almost 40 years later, I still wonder whether so many shows I loved were just dreams in a snow globe.
— Tom Nichols, staff writer
