The Best Pixel 10 Cases and Accessories for Accidental Phone-Droppers
Featured in this article
Google may spend years testing the durability of its own hardware, but because accidents happen, you’d still be wise to get a good case for your Pixel 10 phone. Most devices in the Pixel 10 line—the Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, and Pixel 10 Pro Fold—use Corning's Gorilla Glass Victus 2. (The Pixel 10a uses Gorilla Glass 7i.) It's tough glass, but it's not indestructible, nor is it as strong as what you'd find on other flagship phones, like Samsung's Galaxy S26 Ultra or Apple's iPhone 17 Pro, which embeds ceramic nanocrystals into the glass for extra strength.
No matter which Google Pixel 10 you have, you'll want to protect your device with a case at the very minimum (a screen protector is also a smart buy). This will decrease the odds of an accidental drop ruining your smartphone and preserve the phone’s appearance so it looks great over time. It’s an especially important detail if you plan on trading in the phone for a newer device in the future.
I've tested several Pixel 10 cases to find the best. I’ve included other accessories in this guide, as well, including some magnetic Qi2 gadgets. To get the most out of your Pixel 10, be sure to check out our guide to Key Pixel Settings to Change.
Updated August 2026: I’ve added new screen protectors from Mous and OtterBox, removed some discontinued picks, and confirmed accuracy and prices throughout.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Will Pixel 9 Cases Fit on the Pixel 10 Series?
Sometimes the stars align, and an updated phone model has the identical dimensions, shape, and design as the previous model, allowing you to use an older case. That is, unfortunately, not the case with the Pixel 10 series. Google updated the speakers on this line, so while you may be able to fit some soft Pixel 9 cases over the Pixel 10 phones, you'll run into other issues, namely blocking the speaker port. Pixel 9 cases without magnets will interrupt the Qi2 functionality on the Pixel 10 series. For the best experience, I recommend avoiding a Pixel 9 case altogether, whether it's for the Pixel 10 or Pixel 10 Pro.
Will Pixel 10 Cases Fit on the Pixel 10 Pro?
Most Pixel 10 cases will fit the Pixel 10 Pro, and vice versa. Several retailers market their cases (even Google) for both phones. I’ve tested several Pixel 10 Pro cases on the Pixel 10 and have had no issues. The cutouts are all accurate, the button placements are perfect, and the fit is snug. However, Pixel 10 and 10 Pro cases are not compatible with the Pixel 10 Pro XL.
Will Pixel 10 Cases Fit on the Pixel 10a?
Nope. The Pixel 10a is slightly taller, thicker, and wider than the Pixel 10, and the camera bumps are different, too. These cases are not interchangeable.
What Does ‘Qi2’ Mean for Pixel 10 Cases?
The Pixel 10 phones are the first Android flagships with native Qi2 wireless charging. That means magnets are built into the backs of the phones, just like Apple's iPhones and MagSafe, allowing you to access faster, more efficient wireless charging. Magnets also align the coils perfectly, eliminating any worries about your phone not charging because you didn't place it just right on a charging pad.
Not every Pixel 10 case has magnets baked in, though most of them do. (Almost all of the cases in this guide feature magnets.) However, I have asked nearly every case maker whether its cases are Qi2-certified by the Wireless Power Consortium (which manages the Qi2 standard), and the answer is almost universally no, which may point to less reliable and efficient charging. For the best experience, make sure to check the product listing to see if it mentions “Qi2,” “Made for Google,” or “Pixelsnap compatible,” which is Google's name for its magnetic accessory system. The latter two certifications at least ensure that the case was subject to a rigorous testing standard.
One neat feature to note: When you place your Pixel 10 on a Qi2 wireless charger, you should see an option to add a screensaver. This isn't a traditional screensaver, though you can totally just set a clock or photo and call it a day. There's also a Home Controls option, which lets you place your Google Home smart devices—like smart lights and smart shades—on the lock screen while the phone is charging for quick access. Head to Settings > Display & touch > Screen saver to set it up.
Will My Old Wireless Charger Work for the Pixel 10?
While Qi2 is backward compatible with Qi wireless charging, I have extensive evidence that not all Qi wireless chargers are fully compatible with Qi2 phones. The reason may come down to the placement of the wireless charging array on newer devices. By all means, try charging your new Pixel 10 with your preferred case on a wireless charger you already own. If it works, great! It won't be as fast or efficient, but at least it'll work. However, if it doesn't work, look for a Qi2 charger. You can check out several picks here (and below).
How I Test Cases
I install every case I receive over the Pixel 10 series and take a look at the fit, whether or not ports or speakers are blocked, and ensure the buttons are clicky and responsive. I also monitor how much the case sticks out from the display—the taller the better, as it'll keep your display off the ground. To test Qi2 accessories, I gauge the strength of the magnetic connection. I also install every screen protector to test the ease of the application process.
I don't do drop tests because I have a limited number of Pixel phones. In my experience, though, a case isn’t a guarantee your phone won’t crack when dropped, regardless of “drop test” claims from a manufacturer. Even so, a case improves your chances of protection, especially if you add a screen protector.
Enter the MagSafe Accessory World
WIRED has been testing MagSafe accessories for years; you should totally take advantage of the vast ecosystem with your Pixel 10. Whether you want a magnetic wallet or phone tripod, there’s a corresponding WIRED guide with plenty of tried-and-true recommendations. Most of our picks should work with the Pixel 10 series. Here they are:
Other Screen Protectors to Consider
Zagg Glass Elite, Glass Elite Privacy, and XTR4 for $50–$60: Zagg has a streamlined and intuitive installation process; my application was perfect. The Glass Elite ($50) uses aluminosilicate glass that’s neither too thick nor terribly thin, and the edges are rounded, so they don't feel sharp. (They don't quite extend all the way past the bezels.) I don't love the notch for the selfie camera because it stands out quite a bit. The Glass Elite Privacy ($55) is a two-way privacy screen protector, meaning folks on either side of you can't see what you're looking at (though someone standing above you can). Text can look a bit fuzzy if you look closely with this protector, and you take a small hit to overall screen brightness, but it's an otherwise solid option. Finally, the XTR4 ($60) covers more of the display, uses a stronger tempered glass, and strips away blue light (though whether that's really helpful remains up for debate). Sadly, for all of these options, you only get one protector in the box.
Spigen GlasTR EZ Fit Tempered Glass Screen Protector (2-pack) for $20: This is the best bang for your buck for screen protection. Spigen gives you two tempered glass protectors in the box, and its application tool makes installation mistakes nearly impossible. There's even a squeegee tool to push out air bubbles. All that for $20.
UAG Glass Shield Screen Protector for $40: UAG includes the usual wet wipe, dust-removal sticker, and microfiber cloth. There's also a plastic shell you place atop your Pixel to use as a guide when applying the tempered glass screen protector. It's not the easiest method I've tried, as there's room for some error (and potential to get grime or a smudge on the underside as you apply), but it was a fairly quick and painless installation nonetheless, and the air bubbles disappeared quickly.
Mous Tempered Glass Screen Protector (2-pack) for $30: This is another pretty standard and average screen-protector experience. You get two in the box, plus a caselike installation guide, a microfiber cloth, an air-bubble squeegee, and some dust stickers. Mous' packaging means it's hard to store the spare protector in the included box, but otherwise, I liked this protector.
OtterBox Glass Screen Protector for $40: Installation here is super straightforward: Put the frame on your phone, slide out the backing, and press down on the screen protector with your finger. Wait a few seconds, and the whole thing is perfectly applied. For the price, I wish this came with two protectors, but I like it fine otherwise.
Other Cases We Like
Bellroy Pixelsnap Leather Pixel Folio for $75: This case spruces up your Pixel 10 Pro Fold with leather in various colors. A slot on the flap’s interior can hold a credit card or two; the flap stays shut by magnetically sticking to the front edges of the Fold. It's an elegant look, but the bend when you flip open the Folio is a bit too thick and makes holding the phone feel unstable. Using it with the phone fully open isn't too bad, but the whole thing doesn't feel incredibly protective.
Casetify Impact Magnetic Case for $52: Casetify leaves a bad taste in my mouth after it was caught stealing artwork from Dbrand and JerryRigsEverything. Its cases are still solid, with a thick and grippy bumper and clicky buttons. It is one of the few places that offer many design options for Pixel phones.
Casetify Pixel 10 Pro Fold Impact Magnetic Case for $60: This case is more protective than the Bellroy above, but the lip around the screen is a little too thick for my taste. The design makes swiping in from the edges of the screen difficult. If that doesn’t bother you, you'll appreciate that Casetify doesn't use adhesives all over the case, but only in one spot (it provides extra stickers in the box if it comes off). It's one of the only folding case options with dozens of fun designs to choose from. The $60 price is lower than many of its peers, and there's a magnet for Pixelsnap wireless charging. It's a shame the clear version Casetify sent me attracts so much dust and lint.
Zagg Crystal Palace Lite for $30 and Crystal Palace Snap for $50: A super-simple, no-frills clear case, this Zagg option will do the job. There are two versions of the case. If you don't care about the Qi2 magnetic function of your Pixel, go for the Lite that doesn't have magnets baked in. (No Qi2 magnetic accessories will stick to it, and I'm not sure why you'd want to kill that functionality, especially since you can get magnetic cases for less than $20.) Alternatively, you can buy the Crystal Palace Snap, which adds the classic magnetic ring on the back. It also has textured edges for better grip. Either way, the buttons are responsive, the edges are nicely raised over the screen, and the clear back shows off your Pixel's color. I still think Dbrand's Ghost Case 2.0 is the better clear case, because the Snap seems to pick up scuffs easily.
Zagg Rainier Snap Magnetic Case for $70: Also available for the Pixel 10 Pro XL for $70, this rugged case has two pieces. Plop your Pixel into the thick back piece, and snap the front polycarbonate frame over top. It feels very rugged and protective without adding too much bulk, but the design leaves a lot to be desired. (It’s just a bit too tactical for me.) There's a sizable lip over the screen for great glass protection, even if it means swiping in from the edges is a bit trickier. The buttons are responsive but require a tiny bit more force to press. At least there are built-in magnets so you can take advantage of Qi2.
Mous Clarity Pixelsnap Case for $70: This is my second-favorite clear case after Dbrand's Ghost 2.0. There's a thick bumper around the phone to absorb impacts, a solid magnetic connection, and a nice lip around the screen to keep it off the ground. The buttons are clicky, too.
OtterBox Symmetry Clear Pixelsnap Case for $60: This is a nice, clear case that's also Pixelsnap-certified. The cutouts are accurate, the edges are slightly raised over the screen, and it offers a decent grip. If you prefer a completely clear case without a separate bumper, this will satisfy.
Spigen Parallax for $19, Nano Pop for $19, Tough for $20, and Liquid Air Pixelsnap Cases for $18: I've tried several Spigen cases, and the Rugged Armor is my top pick. These other options have different designs, but they're solid cases for the cost. I found the Parallax slippery, and the sides also felt a bit cheap. The Nano Pop had a decently grippy texture on the edges, but the Liquid Air is one of my favorite Spigen designs. The buttons are just a little stiffer than I'd like. The Tough has a built-in kickstand that's nice, although it can be difficult to pop out if you have short nails. These are minor gripes, though. They're great cases for $20 or less, especially considering they're all Made for Google–certified.
UAG Pathfinder Pixelsnap Case for $60: Someone probably likes how this case looks. That person is not me, but clearly, there's a market for this styling. If you fall in that camp, there's not much about the Pathfinder to complain about, except I found the buttons slightly stiffer than usual. It checks off all the other boxes, with a raised lip over the screen, but I just don't find it that attractive.
Burga Tough Case for $55: This is one of the few nonmagnetic cases I've tested for the Pixel 10 series. If you absolutely don't care for Qi2 and magnets in these phones, this is a perfectly fine case, and Burga has tons of designs you can choose from. The exterior is a hard plastic shell, but the phone is wrapped in a soft rubbery shell that absorbs impacts. The buttons are fairly clicky—but not the most responsive—and there's a solid lip around the screen.
Poetic Guardian for $27, Spartan for $26, and Revolution Case for $25: One point to note is that Poetic includes a screen protector that embeds itself into the case, like old-school cases that offered full protection. You can opt not to use it, as the case will work with or without the protector. The Revolution doesn't have any magnets but has a built-in kickstand and a cover that can completely protect your cameras; I find this a little extreme, so I don't care for it. It also, in my humble opinion, looks hideous. The Guardian looks much better, with a thick bumper, raised edges, and a covered port. The buttons are a little stiff, but at least it has built-in magnets for Qi2 (not certified). Finally, the Spartan (for Pixel 10a) has a built-in MagSafe ring stand that lets you use MagSafe accessories, grip your phone securely, and prop it up in kickstand mode. The buttons could be more responsive, but it's an option worth considering if you want a multitool sort of phone case.
Avoid These Cases
Peak Design Gnar Case: I like many of Peak Design's cases, but not the Gnar case for the iPhone 17 range or the Pixel 10. The edges of the phone feel way too slippery, and they also push in a little too much into the front screen, which disrupts my screen protector and creates a small air bubble. The lip around the display is also lackluster, and I find it a little too hard to pull out the flap that protects the USB-C charging port. I don't love the two-tone material choice on the back; it feels cheap and dull. The SlimLink square adds an extra layer of security for the Pixelsnap magnetic attachment, but you'll have to pair it with relevant SlimLink docks and mounts to get the most out of it. I think you should just stick with the Everyday Case if you want to make use of Peak Design's mounts.

Dutch officials have warned that a high-severity macOS vulnerability that allows attackers to execute malicious code is under active exploitation.
“The NCSC has received a notification indicating that active abuse of this vulnerability has been observed on multiple systems on which port 5900 was accessible from the Internet,” the Netherlands National Cyber Security Centrum warned earlier this week. “In all these cases, root had been accessed on the affected system and a Monero crypto miner had been placed.”
Do you know if your screen sharing is on?
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-65400, received a patch from Apple last week for macOS Tahoe, Sequoia, and Sonoma. The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 7.1 out of 10, stems from a bug in the macOS screen sharing capability, which allows a remote party to view the screen and control the keyboard and mouse while a machine is turned on. A flaw in the “state management,” which keeps track of preceding events, user interactions, variables, and other system states, is the underlying cause.
A video of the exploit in action can be found here. Details of CVE-2026-65400 became public at last week’s Black Hat security conference. Apple said last week that CVE-2026-65400 “may” allow an attacker without credentials to gain access to a Mac. It’s unclear why Apple hedged, but softening language is common among most tech developers when disclosing vulnerabilities.

Israeli air strikes on Lebanon kill 11 people in another test to truce
The attacks are the deadliest since the ceasefire that went into effect in June
Israeli air strikes on southern Lebanon killed at least 11 people on Saturday, in the deadliest attacks since a truce between Israel and Hezbollah went into effect on June 20.
Lebanon’s health ministry and state news agency said an air strike that targeted a home on the edge of Ansar village killed seven people, including three children, and wounded two. The second, on the village of Deir al-Zahrani, killed four and wounded 17.
Israel and the Lebanese government announced a “framework agreement” on June 26, laying out a plan for Israeli forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon in exchange for the disarmament of the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group.
It envisions steps towards an eventual peace agreement between the countries, which remain technically at war nearly 80 years after Israel’s establishment.
Hezbollah has refused direct talks and was not party to the deal.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam criticised Israel’s air strikes on southern Lebanon, saying they intimidate “residents in their homes” and undermine efforts to stabilise the situation in the south.

You’re reading Part 4 of Paying for AI, a series examining how new clinical artificial intelligence tools influence the affordability of health care and patients’ long-term health. Here’s Part 1, Part 2, and Part 3.
For hospitals, the promise of artificial intelligence is financial as much as clinical. A hospital might deploy an AI device because it promises to throw up an alert that could save a patient’s life — but the technology is far more likely to stick if it proves it can drive down costs.
Convincing hospitals and health systems that a new technology will provide that return on investment is tricky, though. So some AI startups have benefited from a temporary sweetener that helps customers get on board: Certain new technologies can apply to get add-on payments from Medicare for two or three years after they come to market. The tax-dollar-funded payments are meant as an incentive to help get new, expensive medical technologies to patients.

Top state Democrat found guilty by jury on federal charges in corruption trial
In March 2024, a grand jury indicted the 69-year-old Williams Stapleton on more than three dozen counts, including mail fraud, bribery, money laundering, and conspiracy to defraud the federal government
A prominent former Democratic lawmaker in New Mexico has been found guilty on dozens of federal counts after carrying out an extended kickback scheme that siphoned public education funds into a business owned by her friend.
The guilty verdict was returned by a jury on Friday, concluding a trial that featured testimony from investigators, tax specialists, and former associates of Sheryl Williams Stapleton.
Williams Stapleton chose not to take the stand and now faces up to 20 years in federal prison when she is sentenced.
Defense counsel indicated that all options were under consideration, including an appeal.
"We're obviously very disappointed with respect to the verdict rendered by the jury," defense attorney Ahmad Assed told The Associated Press via a text message. "Based on the evidence we put forward, we were hopeful for a different outcome."
In March 2024, a grand jury indicted the 69-year-old Williams Stapleton on more than three dozen counts, including mail fraud, bribery, money laundering, and conspiracy to defraud the federal government.
Those federal convictions follow separate charges brought in 2021 by state prosecutors, including money laundering and racketeering, with a state trial scheduled for October.
Williams Stapleton served as a state House majority leader and held an administrative role within Albuquerque Public Schools, the state's largest school district, after first winning election in 1994.
She stepped down from the state House two days after law enforcement officers executed search warrants at her home in mid-2021, and she was subsequently fired by Albuquerque Public Schools.
According to prosecutors, the school district funneled upwards of $3 million to Robotics Management Learning Systems LLC, a Washington, D.C.-based firm central to both the state and federal proceedings. The majority of that funding derived from federal grants intended for vocational education programs.
In her role as the school district's director of career and technical education, Williams Stapleton ensured that funding designated for those programs was directed to Robotics, which was owned by her friend and co-defendant, Joseph Johnson.
Prosecutors demonstrated that Williams Stapleton steered the firm's invoices through the procurement process. Meanwhile, Johnson supplied blank checks to Williams Stapleton, who wrote roughly 230 checks totaling $1,152,506 "for her own benefit," according to the indictment.
During testimony on Tuesday, Johnson maintained that he was unaware Williams Stapleton had withdrawn over $1 million from his company's bank account between 2013 and 2020. He explained that he lost focus on his business after his son was killed in a car crash in 2016.
Johnson told the jury that he relied on an office manager, claiming she was the person who mailed the blank checks to Williams Stapleton. Johnson was ultimately convicted on parallel charges to Williams Stapleton, including bribery and money laundering.
Williams Stapleton’s attorney, Ryan Villa, argued to jurors that while his client stole money directly from Johnson's enterprise, she did not steal money from state or federal taxpayers as alleged by federal prosecutors.
Evidence introduced by the government also revealed that neither Williams Stapleton nor Johnson reported thousands of dollars in payments from Robotics on their federal income tax returns.
At the start of the trial, Assistant U.S. Attorney Fred Federici highlighted that roughly 73% of the more than $3 million received by the company from the school district and federal vocational funds constituted profit. He stated that the co-defendants split those funds for their personal use.
Inquiries revealed that the bulk of the funds in the Robotics checking account originated from federal education money awarded through contracts with the school district. Prosecutors also displayed video from a surveillance stakeout of the company's post office box in Albuquerque, which caught Williams Stapleton checking mail for the firm.

The U.S. wants to know how loyal each NATO ally is to Donald Trump’s policies before cutting military assets defending the alliance.
In a document recently sent to NATO members and seen by reporters, the U.S. asks a series of questions that gauge support for the president’s approach. Has the country “been publicly supportive” of U.S. foreign policy? What “restrictions” has the country placed on the U.S. military using its bases?
The document also tries to assess whether countries are spending money with U.S. defense contractors. And it asks whether they have “publicly opposed regulations” that “inhibit” contracts with U.S. firms. Overall, it queries: “Has the country shown alignment with the U.S. approach to ‘strong, clear, and quiet’?” — referencing a line from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

With two convictions and nearly $1 billion in damages already stacked up, Meta will face another trial starting this week about alleged harms to children in a case brought by four U.S. states.
Also read | Meta faces Tennessee trial over allegations Instagram was designed to be addictive
The federal trial, one of the most consequential among a myriad of legal proceedings targeting social networks in the United States, will begin Wednesday (August 12, 2026) with jury selection at a federal court in Oakland, near San Francisco.
Opening statements are expected to start next week on August 18, with the trial lasting for roughly six weeks, followed by a verdict in early October.
The attorneys general of California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey allege the largest social media network in the world deliberately made Instagram and Facebook addictive for children.
And they are demanding a long list of restrictions on how Instagram and Facebook operate for minors, as well as up to $1.4 trillion in penalties — nearly Meta's entire market cap which exceeded $1.5 trillion on Friday (August 7).
CEO and founder Mark Zuckerberg is among the star witnesses the prosecution plans to call to the stand; he also testified six months ago in a separate case that took place in a Los Angeles court.
While Mr. Zuckerberg has been known to spend an increasing amount of time living at his home in Hawaii, the company's headquarters in Menlo Park is about an hour's drive from the courthouse.
‘Facebook Files’
The Oakland trial is the culmination of a standoff that began in late 2021, when a former employee, Frances Haugen, leaked thousands of pages of internal research, dubbed the "Facebook Files," which showed that Meta had internally measured the potential harm Instagram was causing to some teenage girls, while publicly downplaying the impact.
The revelations triggered a joint investigation by dozens of states, which two years later resulted in a complaint filed by around 30 state attorneys general.
Four states will now attempt to prove their case together in Oakland.
TikTok, Snapchat and Google-owned YouTube have also been sued by thousands of families, school districts and prosecutors across the country in various local, state and federal lawsuits.
In a landmark trial that concluded in March, Meta and YouTube were convicted by a Los Angeles jury, which found both companies were responsible for a teenager's social media addiction.
That jury awarded the teenager $6 million.
On Thursday (August 6, 2026), a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to implement product changes and pay more than half a billion dollars in damages to the state to fund the treatment and prevention of harms caused by Facebook and Instagram.
A jury in New Mexico previously ordered Meta to pay $375 million after it found the company liable for endangering children by making them vulnerable to predators on its platforms, among other harms.
Meta has appealed, or intends to appeal, all of these decisions.
Meta is "confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts," Meta told AFP in a statement Thursday (August 6).
The company intends to argue that mental health is an industry-wide issue, and that some of the states' claims are protected by free speech laws.
In May, Snap, TikTok, YouTube and Meta settled with a school district in Kentucky for $27 million to avoid another trial that was expected to set a precedent for around 1,200 similar lawsuits.
Immunity over content
The four states in the Oakland trial accuse Meta of violating their consumer protection laws, in addition to a federal law that protects children's data, known as COPPA.
They allege that multiple features were designed to keep minors hooked, particularly infinite scrolling, excessive notifications and "like" counts.
It's a strategy that focuses on how apps are designed, not what is posted on them, essentially sidestepping the broad immunity internet sites enjoy in the U.S. regarding content created by their users.
The staggering $1.4 trillion in alleged damages comes from estimating the number of affected users in the four states.
However, the jury will have only an advisory role and Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers — who oversaw major trials between Apple and Epic Games, and Elon Musk and OpenAI — will decide on penalties, if Meta loses the case.
Parents of teenagers allegedly harmed by social networks might watch from inside the courtroom, as they did in Los Angeles, while the rest of the country can follow the proceedings from an audio-only livestream on YouTube.

Looking for the right unit for your top build in Anime Origins can be hard. That is because the game gives plenty of low- and mid-tier options. But as veterans of anime TD games, we have recognised the meta early and think we may have found the best units for all game modes. Here is our official Anime Origins tier list that will help you pick the best units fast.
Full Anime Origins Tier List
Before you check the tier list and start summoning, make sure you collect enough gems by using the Anime Origins codes. Our tier list stretches from SS to D tier, which gives us enough room to tell you which ones deserve your gem spending. After the Anime Origins tier list overview, we will share a detailed breakdown, so you know why we ranked the units in specific tiers.
| Tier | Units | 
|---|---|
| SS | Madaro (Edo Tensei), Cursed Lover (Pure Love), Valcrad (Unleashed) | 
| S+ | Bon (Purgatory), Starku (Primordial), Igritto (Commander Starku), Goju (Honored One), Tango (Star of Festivals) | 
| S | Noroto (Linked), Tojei (Sorcerer Killer), Vegita (Super), Aneko (Queen), Shinaru (Butterfly Dance), Yoto (Calamity) | 
| A | Itsugo (Dangai), Zeldo (Piety), Konpatchi (Unleashed), Gyutari (Upper Moon), Goki (Super 3), Bluma (Data Analyst) | 
| B | Melio (Assault), Oxi (Mage), Mykie (Toman), Itsoda, Leorio | 
| C | Sosuke (Eternal) | 
| D | All rest of the low-rarity units | 
Anime Origins Tier List for Best Units Breakdown
Now that you know where your favorites rank in our Anime Origins tier list, here is a full breakdown to justify their rankings:
SS Tier
SS tier in our Anime Origins tier list is the units you should prioritize above everything else because they combine exceptional damage, strong abilities, or huge overall utility. Their kits give them enough value to remain useful across different situations rather than relying on one narrow strength.
- Madaro (Edo Tensei): Madaro is an incredible meta DPS with huge AoE damage, a 500% Damage Heaven Splitter attack, and extra attacks against enemies outside his Range. His Crowd Control resistance and additional Stun effects also make him extremely reliable against difficult enemies.
- Cursed Lover (Pure Love): Cursed Lover can copy and store up to four Active Abilities, giving him ridiculous flexibility alongside his own powerful attacks. His Love Beam deals 300% total Damage, making him one of the strongest meta DPS units for both damage and versatility.
- Valcrad (Unleashed): Valcrad gets Crit Chance, Range scaling, bonus Damage against bleeding enemies, summons, and stronger Restriction levels as he progresses. His Coffin Trap can also stun a boss for seven seconds, giving him excellent damage and control.
S+ Tier
These units in our tier list sit just below the absolute best picks and can still form the backbone of a strong team in Anime Origins. Their value comes from either excellent damage or support that can improve the performance of several other units.
- Bon (Purgatory): Bon is one of the best meta support units because his food can provide Damage, Cooldown, Range, and other useful buffs. He also increases the money earned from defeated enemies, giving him value in both combat and economy.
- Starku (Primordial): Starku has strong Damage for a Mythic and stands out because he has a powerful nuke that many other Mythics lack. His burst damage makes him a reliable meta DPS for dealing with tougher enemies.
- Igritto (Commander Starku): Igritto gets consistent combat buffs through Oppressing and can gain additional Damage and Cooldown bonuses through his ability. His steady output makes him a strong meta DPS instead of a unit that relies on one big attack.
- Goju (Honored One): Goju can nullify attacks against himself, slow enemies, and use Time Stop to control dangerous enemies. His strong crowd control makes him one of the best meta support units to have on a team.
- Tango (Star of Festivals): Tango is a strong Ground option and fits well into teams that need reliable Ground coverage. He sits below the very best Ground units because the available information does not show the same standout mechanics as the top picks.
S Tier
In our Anime Origins tier list, S-tier units are excellent and can perform extremely well when used in the right role. Some have slightly more specific strengths than the units above, but they remain strong choices for serious teams.
- Noroto (Linked): Noroto gains Damage, Cooldown, and Range during his Nine Tails’ Cloak transformation, while every third attack adds an AoE burst. The transformation gives him a major power spike and makes him particularly useful in longer battles.
- Tojei (Sorcerer Killer): Tojei has strong boss damage and Neutral typing, allowing him to deal reliable damage against different enemy types. His inability to receive buffs holds him back from the highest tiers and limits his potential as a meta DPS.
- Vegita (Super): Vegita is a strong Hill unit with good combat performance and useful multi placement potential. He becomes even stronger with Goku nearby, although relying on another unit for part of his passive keeps him below the top tier.
- Aneko (Queen): Aneko has full AoE and deals more Damage as enemies lose health, making her excellent against groups. Her AoE coverage makes her a strong contender for the best Hill unit in the right situation.
- Shinaru (Butterfly Dance): Shinaru is a strong meta support option that can provide useful team utility. She is slightly lower than the strongest supports because her overall impact does not appear as broad as Bon or Goju.
- Yoto (Calamity): Yoto provides solid overall combat value and can remain useful through longer stages. He does not have the same standout damage or utility as the SS and S+ units, which keeps him in S Tier.
A Tier
A Tier units in our Anime Origins tier list are dependable picks that can carry their weight in the right setup. They may lack the overwhelming combination of power and utility found in the higher tiers, but they are still worth investing in.
- Itsugo (Dangai): Itsugo has strong base Damage and gains more Damage as enemies move farther along the path. This makes him especially useful on longer maps where enemies spend more time progressing toward the end.
- Zeldo (Piety): Zeldo can increase his own Damage and works well alongside Meliodas. His straightforward kit is useful, but he does not offer enough extra utility to compete with the stronger meta DPS units.
- Konpatchi (Unleashed): Konpatchi has good Damage and becomes more useful against weakened enemies. His ability to deal extra damage and help finish enemies makes him a solid offensive pick.
- Gyutari (Upper Moon): Gyutari has full AoE, Poison, and Blood Cut attacks that can explode for additional damage around enemies. He is particularly useful when dealing with large groups, although his overall power falls short of the strongest meta DPS.
- Goki (Super 3): Goki is an excellent boss killer and can build Fighting Spirit stacks for additional Damage and Crit Chance. He can become very strong after building his stacks, making him a good choice for boss focused stages.
- Bluma (Data Analyst): Bluma is one of the best farming units because her Training Data can eventually provide a 30% Income boost. She is especially useful in infinite mode, where her economy scaling becomes more valuable over time.
B Tier
These units are useful and can perform well during progression, especially when you do not have stronger alternatives from our Anime Origins tier list. Their main weakness is that their value is more limited compared with the higher tier units.
- Melio (Assault): Melio can Petrify, Burn, Slow, buff Damage, and provide several other effects through his Commandments. The downside is that he cycles between them, so he cannot reliably provide the specific effect you need at any given moment.
- Oxi (Mage): Oxi provides useful support and can fill a support slot when you lack stronger options. He does not have the same level of impact as the game’s best meta support units, which keeps him lower.
- Mykie (Toman): Mykie can eventually provide a 10% Damage buff when placed as the leader, giving him some useful team support. The buff takes time to build and has strict placement conditions, making him less reliable than stronger supports.
- Itsoda: Itsoda is a useful Hill unit that can help cover enemies from elevated positions. He is a good option early on, but the stronger Hill units provide more overall value.
- Leorio: Leorio is useful for building an economy because he can refund part of an upgrade cost when upgrades are made within his Range. His lack of meaningful combat power makes him a farming specialist rather than a unit for your main meta DPS lineup.
C Tier
C Tier units are usable when your roster is still developing, but there are clear reasons to replace them once stronger options become available. They can still fill a role when your team lacks alternatives from the best Anime Origins units tier list.
- Sosuke (Eternal): Sosuke can serve as a Ground unit while you are still working toward stronger options. His overall performance is weaker than the better Ground units in Anime Origins, so he is unlikely to remain on your team once you obtain stronger picks.
D Tier
Any unit of lower rarity than the ones in our tier list is D tier. If you don’t pull anything from the C tier, save gems and keep trying.
That ends our ultimate Anime Origins tier list for the best units. Which ones are you pairing with the Anime Origins traits? Let us know in the comments.

Bluma (Data Analyst) is one of the best choices for Infinite Mode because her Income scaling becomes more valuable as the waves continue.

As if you needed more reason to love Carly Rae Jepsen’s “Call Me Maybe” beyond its pop perfection, it is also, according to lore, the genesis for Switched on Pop, one of the best music podcasts out there. Cohosts Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding obsessively dissect pop songs, from the theory behind their musical choices to their production techniques. If you’re a student of pop music, then this is a must-listen podcast.
Switched on Pop’s Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding love fresh vegetables and guitar pedals
The duo recently brought their deep dives on the art of pop music to Netflix.
Switched on Pop’s Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding love fresh vegetables and guitar pedals
The duo recently brought their deep dives on the art of pop music to Netflix.
Sloan is a composer and professor of musicology at USC Thornton School of Music, where he researches pop, but also jazz and even Tin Pan Alley. Harding is a songwriter, music journalist, and a professor as well. Their combined knowledge is near encyclopedic. Whether they’re talking about text painting in Justin Timberlake’s “Can’t Stop the Feeling!” or Taryn Southern’s AI experiments, the two reveal the rich tapestry of even the most simple-seeming songs.
Now, after 12 years and nearly 500 episodes, the show recently made the leap to video on Netflix, featuring guests like Aaron Dessner (The National), Trevor Horn (The Buggles, Yes), and Cypress Hill. Sloan and Harding told us about the importance of the metronome, fresh vegetables, and what seems to be a slightly problematic relationship with guitar pedals.
Switched on Pop is a production of New York Magazine’s Vulture and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
What is your most indispensable tool?
Charlie Harding: The Martin D-28 is the platonic idea of both what a guitar sounds like and, I’m ashamed to admit how much this matters to me, how a guitar looks. You’ve heard it on “Blackbird,” “Wish You Were Here,” and “Big Yellow Taxi.” I found one from 1970 sitting in an antique shop in Maine. But I’m still waiting for it to produce a timeless classic for me.
Nate Sloan: Sibelius music notation software. Whenever I’m analyzing a song, I don’t truly understand it until I transcribe its melody, harmony, and rhythm.
Which is the most underappreciated?
CH: Keyboard shortcuts and the app Rectangle save me hours of my life every year by doing the mundane task of repositioning windows on my computer. And they also make me feel like I’m mission control on some kind of spaceship.
NS: The metronome.
What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?
NS: AudioHijack for grabbing audio.
What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?
CH: This is very nitpicky, but it drives me mad. I extensively use focus modes on iOS to help keep away distractions. But I also need people in my family to be able to reach me, so they get exceptions to the focus modes. However, that means any group messaging chain with just one family member blows up my notifications when I’m presenting to a lecture hall full of songwriting students. This means I’m urgently notified every time my recently retired father catches a fish. I am happy for my dad, but I’d be more happy to find out after 5 pm when I’m off “do not disturb.” If this makes me sound like a curmudgeon, I am.
NS: I wish I could strum it like a guitar.
What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?
NS: ProQuest Historical Newspapers.
How many tabs do you have open right now?
CH: 92… but they are nicely organized into groups that only I understand.
NS: Two. I used to have hundreds open, but it was killing my attention span, so I now make a point of constantly closing them.
Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)?
NS: Instagram, guiltily.
What is your happy place online?
CH: Browsing Sweetwater for variations of guitar pedals that I already own.
NS: Watching ukulele tutorials on YouTube.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
CH: The Dato DUO synthesizer and Dato DRUM drum machine. They are the easiest way to learn to program a synthesizer, and you can’t make a bad sound. My kids jam on them every night. It’s turned them into Brooklyn DJs, unfortunately.
NS: The iPod that I traveled around the world with in 2006.
Which was the most disappointing?
NS: The minidisc player.
What game do you have the fondest memories of?
NS: Pac-Man.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
CH: AI music slop, full stop.
NS: Wearable computing.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
CH: In 2007 I pitched my college friends on creating an app that would allow you to legally hitchhike in other people’s cars. We started a tea company instead, which was ultimately less of a liability.
NS: Autotune.
What creation are you most proud of?
CH: Switched On Pop. My wife read this and said I should add my children.
NS: Coining the term “pop drop” to describe the instrumental postchorus in a pop song.
Which are you least proud of?
CH: My wife read this and said I should say my guitar pedal collection.
NS: Getting dunked on by YouTuber Rick Beato after calling the Jonas Brothers “stupefyingly funky” in a New York Times article.
What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?
CH: You can never have too many guitar pedals.
NS: Have a short memory.
What is your current obsession?
NS: LeBron James signing with the 76ers.
What do you do when you need to focus?
CH: Drink some tea.
NS: Step away from the computer, take a walk, and start recording a voicenote about what I’m trying to accomplish.
What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?
CH: Drink some tea.
NS: Call Charlie Harding.
When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?
CH: During routine surgery.
NS: Whenever I go to the gym.
What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?
CH: The History of Sound by Ben Shattuck.
NS: Vinyl copy of the Jeff Parker IVTet.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
CH: My guitar pedals. And my beautiful wife.
NS: Fresh vegetables.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
CH: He is embarrassed there is a biopic about him.
NS: One man dared to overanalyze pop music, taking on BTS Army, Madonna stans, and the Little Monsters, and living to tell the tale.

For a movie about a superhero who can literally climb walls, Spider-Man: Brand New Day is seemingly interested in what happens when Peter Parker (Tom Holland) puts them up himself. Still reeling from the loss of the people closest to him, Peter has convinced himself that being alone is the price of being Spider-Man, and production designer Charles Wood had the task of making that isolation visible.
That meant giving Peter a new apartment that could feel like both a refuge and a prison, with a view of the New York life he can see but can’t quite join. Elsewhere in the concrete jungle, Wood and his team also had to build and stylize another part of New York through Yelena’s (Florence Pugh) elaborate bathhouse, built from scratch and based on spaces Wood discovered while scouting the city. And it meant creating Jean Grey’s (Sadie Sink) containment unit as a room that initially feels almost domestic before revealing itself to be something much more sinister.
Wood, whose production-design credits include several MCU projects such as Doctor Strange, Black Widow and both Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame, also had to account for Holland’s famously immersive approach to his performance by creating sets and props that didn’t just look real, but actually worked just as Peter Parker would hope.
Watch on Deadline
Below, Wood spoke to Deadline about the making of Brand New Day and the web-crawling details hidden within its narrative walls.
DEADLINE: What was the briefing from Destin Daniel Cretton about what this Spider-Man world should feel like?
CHARLES WOOD: I think he wanted it very street level. It’s a very grounded feel. Everywhere we went into this place we created, he wanted the audience to feel that Peter Parker could really be around the corner. So, in the creation of New York in the U.K., he wanted to make sure it felt natural. Given that this is based on fantastic comics, there’s a twist of that sort of graphic iconography applied to it.
DEADLINE: Let’s jump into a few locales now. First and foremost, this bodega that Peter constantly visits. Talk about creating that New York bodega, and did you have to import all those American snack goods?
WOOD: We might have flown some things in, but I’m not entirely sure. There are actually quite a lot of American products available in London because many Americans live there. But there’s also a bit of product placement here [laughs]. Honestly, we did an awful lot of research on that. I went to New York a lot, and the team photographed a lot of bodegas because places like this you really have to work hard to try and be as authentic as you can, because you can lose the audience if it doesn’t work. And we had an awful lot of Americans coming in and looking at these sets—a tough bunch [laughs].
DEADLINE: What was the flavor profile of creating Ned and MJ’s shared apartment?
WOOD: Destin and I went back and forth on whether or not it would be set in Astoria or Queens. We ultimately wanted to say that it was Queens above a shop, and we wanted it set in an old tenement building. So we gave the set a lot of history – like maybe this building was around a hundred years old. It’s supposed to be set in a well-trodden, fun neighborhood, but not in one that depicts huge wealth.
DEADLINE: I don’t think we ever get to see MJ’s room. Did you all have any discussions about what her room would look like?
WOOD: There is actually a little bedroom for her in there. When Tom first enters the apartment, I mean, to be really prescriptive here, on the left. I don’t even know if it made it into the movie, but there was a little bedroom for her. It just wasn’t a place where the story naturally played out. Even on the day we were changing things around, when Tom came in and wanted to work on it to make it work for them both. And then, quite frankly, the rest of the apartment was really more about the idea that it was just somewhere they could all come together – which was by the window.
MJ’s room, I believe, had something to do with stuff from her past and education, but I can’t quite remember [laughs].
DEADLINE: Was Yelena’s bathhouse a location or built set?
WOOD: That’s a built set. There’s a nice story there, because I went to New York with Destin, Brett Pawlak, the cinematographer, Jerome Chen, the visual effects supervisor, and David Kane, our producer. We happened to go to a place called Brighton Beach, and there was this building that we thought could have been an old bathhouse. Then when we thought we were going to film in Manchester, we found this old Victorian bathhouse that felt right. So, we took the ideas from that.
The guys built this really beautiful, hand-tiled set, and the pool was also all made.
DEADLINE: I don’t know how online you are, but –
WOOD: Not at all, they would eat me alive on there.
DEADLINE: I want to ask on the fans’ behalf—the water. There’s a running joke about the MCU having the most magical water that clouds everything.
WOOD: Ultimately, we needed to cloud the water.
DEADLINE: Right.
WOOD: Florence obviously wears a bodysuit, so there’s nothing there. But, I mean, we have to do these things because of the ratings.
DEADLINE: Of course. The question is less about that and more about the water’s composition. For example is it like 15% soap suds, 30% dye, 40% milk, etc?
WOOD: It’s a type of dye, I think. In the old days, when I first started in the business, you used milk because it worked very quickly to cloud something. But, interestingly enough, we ran all sorts of tests to figure out the right consistency. And ultimately that’s what we came up with. Also, it was all heated and very comfortable, with lots of benches underwater that Tom was floating around on, and it was funny. I love that sequence, a very good scene.
I should also mention that we spent a lot of time chipping tile and making sure the grout matched to bring that level of reality to it. These characters are big, so if you drop the ball, you don’t make these spaces feel truly real. And if you can do that, then I think that’s a good place to be in because it’s all about the performance. If you produce a set which feels like a set, you can pull the audience away from that. So it’s an important thing. We spend a lot of time, a lot of money, a lot of effort to bring authenticity to these places.
DEADLINE: What was the biggest challenge in designing this Spider-Man movie?
WOOD: Making New York, because it is a fabulously interesting city. It’s incredibly layered. It’s so interesting culturally. Its heritage is extraordinary. And as a non-New Yorker, but as someone who, for instance, lives in London and has spent a lot of time there, bringing all of that detail, cultural realism, and history to a place in London, in England, is really difficult. And we spend an awful lot of time photographing. I spent a lot of time photographing New York, getting a lot of advice from New Yorkers, and trying to make it feel natural. That was the biggest challenge in that movie.
DEADLINE: What is your favorite prop that you built for a set?
WOOD: The fabricator, I suppose. That’s a big prop because it’s the machine that built the inhibitor. Like Peter, we felt like we needed to apply a lot of mechanical detail too. We wanted to create something that could have come in 500 Amazon boxes, but that was also something you could build and a great mind could build. And we wanted it to be very tactile. It worked, it buzzed, it did all the things. It actually was this mad kind of almost sewing machine. We wanted everything to be tactile.
It helped because Tom is completely immersive. Once he gets into a space, he starts to understand what his world is, and he then wants to react with it. We try to do all of those things to make that interesting for him.
DEADLINE: Jean Grey’s containment cell was pretty massive, it seems. What went into making that room within a glass containment?
WOOD: The whole idea of it was that Jean’s sister was taken to this room by Damage Control. We looked at all these strange rooms from all sorts of places. We found this wooden space. And we wanted it to be odd enough to not sit well with you, but real enough to say, “This is clearly where she is and is it her bedroom, question mark, because all of her stuff’s near, but why are the walls glassy?” So, when you are first in there, if you look at the walls, they are actually glass. There’s glass in front of them. And then it became this idea where actually at some point during the sequence, we realize the room isn’t the room. It’s actually a glass cell that is housed within a larger room.
And then we decided to actually do this reveal because it was all in camera; that’s not visual effects. All the walls lifted to reveal this much larger space where she was housed.
DEADLINE: What was your favorite set to build?
WOOD: Probably the New York backlot. We built two or three city blocks of New York: 40 big buildings. I love building the rooftops. I like the Silver Cup rooftop because we built that big sign and the big rooftop. I always love doing those wells above New York. I think that’s a really interesting thing to do. But people don’t generally go. And being in New York and having access, it’s a lovely thing about my job to all of these brilliant buildings and actually getting up top, going out some fire escape somewhere many hundreds of feet up in the building was brilliant. And recreating those worlds to display the historical nature of them…lots of things are forgotten on New York rooftops, and I loved getting into all of that; the eccentricity was really interesting.
DEADLINE: What was an environment that looked ordinary on screen, but was incredibly complicated to build?
WOOD: Peter’s apartment was complicated, believe it or not. There were a lot of surfaces. There’s a lot in that place, and that was with all the skylights and all the different finishes and the history. We really wanted to come up with some crazy old pad. It was tricky because we had to think about New York, because everywhere’s valuable. Everywhere’s worth something and most places are worth an awful lot. And so it was odd coming up with a cinematically interesting place, but didn’t look as though it was worth a few million. So we had to sort of play with it quite a lot to make it feel really neglected. But not so neglected that it felt non-authentic or you couldn’t have a place like that. It was difficult to find the sweet spot.
And when he walks in, and it’s all full of that junk, and we’ve cleared the junk away, we wanted something to be there but not trying to grandstand anything. But you could feel its history and neglect, which, in a way, very much suited the scene we were trying to convey.
From a narrative viewpoint, we wanted to do something where Peter had these great big windows, but actually, if you were to look at the windows just beyond, we were actually on the other side of the East River. And in the distance, we did have these lights on these big backings where you could see New York and the Queensboro Bridge. The idea was all about being somewhere he had this view of the city he could never join. He could look at families across the way, but he could never be part of that. This place represented a barrier between him and, in a sense, the happiness, all the togetherness he missed.
Then the way it was designed with materials, you wanted the rain to hit the skylight above him, the clitter clatter and all the awnings which gave different lighting moods, and the coldness of the brick and the heat of the pipes. Then there was us having the clattery old washing machine that wasn’t quite working.

The Lesson Watergate Was Supposed to Teach
Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr. thought Nixon’s downfall would restrain presidents for generations. Instead, Watergate helped write the script for the scandals that followed.
This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.
Historians are generally better off interpreting the past than predicting the future. By training, we’re meant to read sources, not tea leaves. In the fall of 1973, during the middle acts of Watergate’s Shakespearean drama, Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr. tried to do a little bit of both. In the cover story of The Atlantic’s November issue that year, “The Runaway Presidency,” Schlesinger cast President Richard Nixon’s abuses as the result of long-standing historical trends that had empowered the chief executive, and in the process offered a hopeful prognosis for what was to come. “Watergate,” Schlesinger wrote, “is potentially the best thing to have happened to the presidency in a long time. If the trails are followed to their end, many, many years will pass before another White House staff dares take the liberties with the Constitution and the laws the Nixon White House has taken.”
Nixon resigned 52 years ago this month, marking an end to the scandal, but bringing no such catharsis to our national life and no stop to the runaway presidency. Underscoring just how poorly Schlesinger’s optimism aged, J. D. Vance mused in June that “if Watergate happened tomorrow, it would be like a 12-hour news story. The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy.” As my colleague David A. Graham noted at the time, the remark was a startling admission from a member of an administration that has taken liberties with the Constitution and the laws. It’s also entirely plausible: Scandals that would have previously brought the nation to a standstill barely register for more than a few days, in part because there are simply so many of them under Donald Trump. To understand how Schlesinger got it so wrong, first you have to understand what he got right.
In 1973, Schlesinger published a brick of a book titled The Imperial Presidency. He’d begun writing it as a pamphlet that March, but the project quickly swelled to 200,000 words as the spectacle of Watergate unfolded. The book tracked the aggregation of executive power from the founding onward, which accelerated during World War II and the Cold War. By the early ’70s, the office had grown so far beyond its constitutional bounds, Schlesinger wrote, that it posed “a revolutionary challenge to the separation of powers itself.”
Schlesinger’s Atlantic essay was preaching from his own text. In that account, Nixon’s abuses were symptoms that made visible a larger sickness. The expansion of the presidency, especially in the realm of war and foreign policy, was clear enough, but Nixon showed the dangers and “intoxications” that came with such power at home. Previous presidents may have possessed such authority but, Schlesinger argued, they had the character and restraint not to use it. Nixon was a different kind of case, demonstrating what would happen when a person “not open and modest,” but “from the start ambitious of power and contemptuous of law,” reached the nation’s highest office.
The president’s place at the center of the American political story exacerbated the problem. Congress should restrain the executive to reassert its place in the constitutional order, Schlesinger argued (he had advocated for Nixon’s impeachment as a starting point), but the American people also had a role to play: They must form “a new attitude” toward their presidents, becoming more skeptical and less reverent toward the office. Doing so would administer fewer “intoxications” to its occupant, Schlesinger wrote. But his prescriptions struck his critics as rich, to say the least. As he admitted in The Imperial Presidency, “historians and political scientists, this writer among them, contributed to the rise of the presidential mystique.” Contributed, indeed. Over the course of his career, Schlesinger had endowed Democratic presidents with just the stature he now feared. In 1965, he’d memorialized John F. Kennedy (to whom he served as special assistant) in a book so reverential that the writer Christopher Hitchens later called it “the founding breviary of the cult of JFK.”
Schlesinger may have only got religion because of the sins of the Republican Nixon administration, but he wasn’t exactly wrong. Many others in the moment hoped that Nixon’s transgressions would spark something of a democratic revival to check the dangerous tendencies that had made Watergate possible. And reforms did come: A slew of legislation from 1973 to 1978 attempted to address abuses exposed by Watergate and restrain presidential power on war, impoundment, elections, secrecy, and surveillance.
What Schlesinger failed to see was that although the dramas of Watergate may have pierced the mystique of the presidency, they also heightened the American fascination with it. Many people did lose their reverence for the office, but they didn’t turn their attention away. Perversely, it seemed that the spectacle of the presidency was enhanced rather than diminished by its subsequent scandals. Watergate supplied more than the inevitable suffix for all presidential crises to come—it also established the script. The crime and the cover-up; the drip of revelations; the question of what the president knew, and when he knew it; the obscure Washington characters thrust into the spotlight; the marathon hearings; the stern reports on the nightly news.
But presidential scandals, which once dominated the media cycle for weeks and months, now come and go at the speed of an attention economy that demands constant novelty. Meanwhile, the institutions that might have checked presidential power now enable it. Congress’s inaction and the Supreme Court’s expansive doctrine of executive authority have brought us closer to Nixon’s later assertion that “when the president does it, that means it is not illegal.” Watergate would be a 12-hour news story today, as Vance suggests, because there’s nothing to stop a new one from happening tomorrow. In an era of revelation without reckoning, we’re more transfixed than ever by the imperial presidency, whether we like it or not.
At the end of his 1973 Atlantic essay, Schlesinger suggested that corruption came to the White House in 50-year cycles, like monstrous cicadas. There is perhaps something to the idea. Start from the abuses of Nixon, in the early ’70s, and go back half a century to the abuses of Warren Harding, in the early 1920s. Do that again, and you would arrive at the scandals that plagued Ulysses S. Grant’s presidency, in the 1870s. Keep rewinding another 50 years—ignore John Quincy Adams’s reputation for probity and rectitude—and you’d land on the “Corrupt Bargain” that gave Adams the presidency in the election of 1824.
The cycle could be projected forward, too: Schlesinger closed with one more prediction, this one more right than wrong. “Around the year 2023,” he wrote, “the American people will be well advised to go on the alert and start nailing down everything in sight.” We can’t say we weren’t warned.

A common cause given for leg pain is muscle strain, and this may be attributed to standing for a long time, exercising incorrectly, or getting older. But sometimes, there may be something different going on. A pain that begins in the lower back and radiates down the buttock and to the leg, may indicate irritation or pressure on the sciatic nerve, and is referred to as sciatica.
The largest nerve in the body is the sciatic nerve. It extends from the lower back through buttocks and down each leg. If a nerve in the lower back is compressed or inflamed, it may result in pain that radiates down this nerve.
How do you know if you have sciatica pain?
Sciatica isn’t always typical leg pain. It can cause a sudden electric-like, burning or tearing sensation down the back of the thigh and sometimes into the calf or foot from the lower back or buttock.
Some people may also experience tingling, numbness or weakness in the affected leg. The pain can worsen after sitting for prolonged periods, or after coughing, sneezing or certain movements.
In some cases, the discomfort may be primarily experienced in the leg, and there may be very little discomfort in the back. This can be one explanation as to why people may confuse sciatica with leg muscle or joint pain.
What causes sciatica?
A common cause of sciatica is a slipped disc or a bulging disc in the lower portion of the spine. The discs between the bones of our spine work like cushions. If one of them bulges or tears, it can compress an adjacent nerve.
Other reasons include changes in the spine with age, constriction of the spinal canal, bone growth and, less frequently, injury or other spinal diseases.
Not all people suffering from sciatica require a surgery. With the right kind of rest, and the use of the remedies as prescribed by a physician, physiotherapy and a gradual return to normal activity, many people get better. Treatment depends on the cause and severity of the symptoms.
When to det a doctor’s advice
Some back or leg pain may get better over time, but certain symptoms shouldn’t be ignored. You should seek medical advice if the pain is severe, keeps returning, lasts for several weeks or is affecting your ability to walk, work or perform everyday activities.
Numbness or worsening weakness in the leg, trouble with urination or defecation or numbness around the inner thighs and genitals are emergencies.
Avoiding making every leg ache a diagnosis of sciatica is also important. Similar symptoms can occur due to problems involving the muscles, joints, blood vessels or other nerves, which is why it is important to consult a doctor. Your doctor can evaluate your symptoms, motion, muscle strength and reflexes and might suggest imaging if needed.
In addition to this, keeping a healthy weight, being physically active, strengthening core muscles and avoiding long periods of sitting can help keep your spine healthy.
The bottom line is: leg pain that radiates from the back or buttock is not necessarily from the leg and can be from the spine. Early identification of warning signs and proper diagnosis can prevent symptoms from becoming severe and can help to expedite a return to normal life.
(Dr. Kalidutta Das is chief and director of spine services, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital. Kaliduttadas@gmail.com)

Nigeria to miss Women's World Cup after South Africa and Ghana win play-offs
- Published
Nigeria have failed to qualify for the Fifa Women's World Cup for the first time after they were beaten 2-1 by South Africa in a play-off at the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon).
The continent's top-ranked team went into the tournament in Morocco as favourites to retain their title but were eliminated in the quarter-finals by Cameroon, having already lost to Malawi in the group stage.
With the four semi-finalists guaranteed a spot at next year's World Cup, Justin Madugu's side had one more chance to keep alive their hopes of reaching Brazil, with the winner of their one-off tie in Casablanca entering an inter-confederation qualifier.
But second-half goals from Thembi Kgatlana and Refiloe Jane were enough to give Banyana Banyana victory, despite unexpected late drama when Jane was sent off after picking up a second yellow card for handling the ball inside her own six-yard box.
Christy Ucheibe slotted home the penalty in the 93rd minute to set up a grandstand finish, and there was even time for goalkeeper Kaylin Swart, South Africa's hero, to save brilliantly with her feet to deny Michelle Alozie with almost the last kick of the game.
The 2022 Wafcon champions join Ghana in Fifa's inter-confederation qualifier after the Black Queens came from behind to beat Ivory Coast 2-1 earlier on Thursday.
End of the road for Oshoala?
Nigeria have appeared at all nine Women's World Cups since the first was held in China in 1991.
Missing out is unlikely to go down well in a country where football fans are used to their team dominating, with the Super Falcons having won Wafcon a record 10 times.
But seeing off Desiree Ellis' well-drilled Banyana team was never likely to be easy.
While the first half in Casablanca was a non-event, the second period was anything but, with chances aplenty.
Asisat Oshoala should have done better when she bundled her way through several challenges and poked goalwards from inside the six-yard box, failing to get the requisite power on her strike to trouble Swart.
The six-time African footballer of the year was subbed soon after and there will no doubt be questions about whether the 31-year-old might have appeared at her final Wafcon.
The breakthrough came on the counter in the 56th minute, with striker Ronnel Donnelly playing an exquisite through ball from midway inside her own half to set Hildah Magaia free.
Magaia's cross from the left was met by the onrushing Kgatlana, whose shot had enough power to sneak over the line despite keeper Chiamaka Nnadozie getting a strong hand to it.
Nnadozie did keep out another Kgatlana effort five minutes later, while Swart pulled off a stunning save from Uchenna Kanu's header, diving acrobatically to her left to palm the ball away one-handed.
Jane's goal came courtesy of a deflection off Ucheibe's outstretched foot in the 77th minute and Magaia should also have scored when clean through less than a minute after the restart.
It looked as if Nigeria would be unable to create a way back into the game until Jane's unnecessary handball was spotted by the video assistant referee (VAR).
The captain did not need to stretch out her arm, with Swart well placed to save on the goalline.
With the numerical advantage, Nigeria piled on the pressure and almost found salvation in the 97th minute when Alozie drilled the ball back across goal, only to see Swart's left boot shoot out to stop it flying into the bottom corner.
Swart and South Africa celebrated their victory with glee, but a place at the World Cup is far from certain.
They must first negotiate a six-team league alongside Ghana in November and December, with Asian sides Uzbekistan and Chinese Taipei, Papua New Guinea from Oceania and Ecuador from South America also involved.
The top two sides from that mini-league will advance to a final inter-continental qualifier in February, with three sides from that booking their spot in Brazil.
Black Queens through despite pay dispute
In the earlier game in Casablanca, Ivory Coast were awarded a penalty after just 44 seconds when Bernadette Kakounan was clipped by Princess Marfo.
After a VAR check, Ines Konan converted to give the Lady Elephants a fourth-minute lead despite Ghana keeper Cynthia Konlan getting a hand to the ball.
The Black Queens thought they had equalised early in the second half when Stella Nyamekye stabbed in, but South African referee Akhona Makalima adjudged that Evelyn Badu had kicked the ball out of the hands of Ivorian keeper Oceane Konan moments before.
Ghana did level in the 59th minute, with Marfo heading in from a corner to make amends for her earlier challenge, and the turnaround was complete when Josephine Bonsu scored from the penalty spot in the 72nd minute after VAR had again intervened.
Grace Asantewaa's fierce strike clearly hit the right arm of Ivory Coast defender Aboa Yapo just inside the area, but it took some deliberation and a trip to the pitch-side monitor before Makalima awarded the foul.
Ghana's victory came a day after the Black Queens squad had issued a statement claiming players and officials were awaiting several payments including Wafcon qualification bonuses, group-stage bonuses and per diem allowances.
Ghana's Ministry of Sports and Recreation challenged aspects of the allegations, with sports minister Kofi Adams insisting that per diem payments had already been settled.
A statement from a Ministry official added that the squad's win bonus from their group stage victory over Cape Verde was being processed, and said that the Black Queens qualifying for Wafcon "does not attract a separate bonus".

Kentucky governor says he has received no information on Mitch McConnell’s health as he rips into Congress
McConnell was discharged from a rehabilitation center earlier this month
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear sharply criticized Senator Mitch McConnell and the Senate at large over the Kentucky Republican’s prolonged absence from Congress due to health issues.
Beshear, a Democrat, said on Friday that he still had little information about the condition of McConnell, who was hospitalized in mid-June and released from a rehabilitation center earlier this month.
“I’ve received absolutely nothing, and that's the same that the people of Kentucky have received,” Beshear told MS Now. “This is why the Senate feels broken. These guys don’t think that they have a boss when the people of Kentucky are their boss. They don’t feel like they are accountable whatsoever.”
Beshear called on McConnell to make a video or call into a news show to update the public about his health.
“I want him to get better, but I just believe he has a responsibility to talk to the people of Kentucky, and I don’t think that’s asking a lot,” he added.
The governor also faulted Senate Majority Leader John Thune for not doing more to make a call on whether McConnell’s seat is officially vacant, which could prompt Beshear to call a special election to fill it.
Beshear has previously written to Senate leadership about McConnell and has called on him to “directly and verbally address the people of Kentucky and provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign.”
The Independent has contacted the offices of Thune and McConnell for comment.
McConnell was released from a rehab center last Thursday and is now getting care at home.
“Earlier today, I was discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home,” he said in a statement. “Elaine and I are grateful for the many well wishes and support from friends, colleagues, and Kentuckians, and for the attentive care I’ve received from excellent doctors, nurses, therapists, and hospital staff.”
“On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business,” he added.
Information has been scarce about McConnell’s condition.
Weeks after entering the hospital, McConnell disclosed he was admitted after a fall and had since developed a case of mild pneumonia.
“My doctors have confirmed that I didn’t break any bones or suffer a concussion,” McConnell said in a statement at the time. “I didn’t have a heart attack or a stroke. I don’t have any tumors or hemorrhages. But I was briefly unconscious and was taken to the hospital.”
McConnell’s lengthy absence from the Senate has been a subject of intense interest and debate in Washington and beyond, as the Trump administration looks to lock in any final legislative wins ahead of the November midterms, where Democrats could retake control of Congress.
Republican senators and conservative commentators insist they have spoken with McConnell and that he remains engaged and physically sound to carry on in office, though McConnell himself hasn’t appeared in any live video appearances that might assure doubters.
McConnell’s hospitalization came after a series of past medical scares, including falls and incidents where the senator froze mid-sentence.
His absence, as well as the recent death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, 71, reignited the long-running debate over whether members of Congress are too old to effectively serve.
About 58 percent of Americans think the share of elderly lawmakers in Congress, which is currently one of the oldest in U.S. history, is a major problem, according to a July CNN / SSRS poll.

Former U.S. president Joe Biden’s cancer has metastasised further, according to his son Hunter Biden, who shared the update in a recent interview with the BBC.
In May 2025, just four months after he left office as the oldest sitting President, the elder Biden revealed he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had spread to his bones.
He subsequently began treatment, including radiation and hormone therapy, which the 83-year-old described as going “really well” last month, during an announcement of his upcoming memoir.
In a wide-ranging interview published late Friday (August 7, 2026) with BBC Newsnight, Hunter Biden said his father’s disease has spread despite the treatment.
“The cancer has spread, is metastasized into his bones and further,” Mr. Joe Biden had said.
“It’s very painful, and it’s very debilitating in many respects, but he’s still out there. He’s still doing his thing... he so believes in this country.”
Mr. Hunter Biden appeared to get emotional at times during the interview while discussing his father’s health.
“It’s really, really hard, and it’s really sad to watch,” he added.
Despite persistent questions about his health as the oldest-ever U.S. President, Mr. Joe Biden, then aged 81, decided to run for a second term in 2024.
Following a disastrous debate performance against Donald Trump in June 2024 and a wave of pressure from Democrats, Mr. Joe Biden withdrew from the presidential race.
Mr. Trump went on to beat Mr. Joe Biden’s replacement candidate — then Vice President Kamala Harris.
