Vultures are disappearing in Nigeria - but the 'Vulture King' is fighting to reverse the trend
- Published
"People fear the environment where the shrine is. No evil will ever happen here. So, nobody fights vultures that perch here," a man they call the Vulture King tells the BBC.
Mostly associated with death and decay, perhaps it is not surprising that when vultures disappeared from the skies across many West African cities, they were not missed.
Yet across the continent, their disappearance is becoming impossible to ignore, as conservationists warn that hunting linked to traditional beliefs and spiritual practices continues to threaten several vulture species to the point of near extinction.
Without vultures, ecosystems would lose a natural defence against the spread of disease.
Thankfully in one part of south-eastern Nigeria, residents are bucking the trend.
Awka-Etiti is home to a sacred forest surrounding a shrine dedicated to a deity known as Nguma.
At first glance, the site is an unremarkable cluster of tall trees wrapped in thick greenery. But at its heart stands an ancient tree that locals say has watched over the community for hundreds of years, and remains the spiritual home of the shrine.
This is a largely Christian community but some residents continue to observe traditional practices, in which vultures play a key role.
Local resident Chukwuemeka Igwe, who has earned the nickname King of Vulture, thanks to his tireless volunteer work with Nigeria Conservation Foundation (NCF), says "the indigenous don't hunt vultures".
Instead, locals sometimes offer fresh animal sacrifices at the shrine which attract the birds, he explains.
"And there is an adage we use here that says: 'When you put down a sacrifice and you do not see vulture[s], know that something happened in the spirit world'."
It means that vultures are a good omen when a sacrifice has been made because their presence suggests that the deity has accepted the sacrifice and heard the residents' appeal to its power.
Now in his 50s, Igwe says the birds have been a feature of daily life in this town for as long as he can remember, walking around among humans and scavenging for food.
Yet for many who venture into the wild elsewhere on the continent, vultures are not the first birds to capture their attention. Rarely do we stop to admire vultures through binoculars or photograph in awe.
In the eyes of many people, vultures are downright ugly. But scientists say they provide one of nature's most important cleaning services.
Vultures consume dead animals within hours, helping prevent carcasses from becoming breeding grounds for dangerous bacteria and diseases.
Their disappearance can have serious consequences, says NCF conservation biologist Stella Egbe: "In places where the total collapse of vultures has happened, there has been impact of rising zoonotic diseases."
Vultures' powerful stomach acids allow them to safely consume infected animals, helping stop diseases such as anthrax and rabies from spreading.
Without vultures, experts warn ecosystems lose a natural defence system.
Rapid urban growth across Africa has also played its part, transforming landscapes, and destroying many of the tall trees that the birds nest in.
Habitat loss is far from the only factor.
Poisoning is the cause of death for an estimated 60% of vultures in Africa, according to BirdLife International, external.
These issues will be high on the agenda when researchers from across the region meet in Abuja later this year to review the West African Vulture Conservation Action Plan, which was drafted in 2022.
Experts say the use of vultures and their body parts in traditional medicine and Vodun (also known as Voodoo) has emerged as one of the most significant drivers of their decline, especially in West and southern Africa.
Dead adult vultures in Nigeria used to sell for around 25,000 to 30,000 naira ($18 to $22; £13 to £16) each - but can now fetch up to 200,000 naira ($145; £107) per bird, says Egbe.
Vulture eggs and nests are increasingly targeted too, which for such a slow-breeding species is a catastrophic and "shocking" development, says Egbe.
Adult vultures usually reach sexual maturity between the ages of five and seven, and produce only one chick every year or two. Plus many young vultures do not survive their first year.
"And so you imagine what will happen if a nest is removed and eggs are removed. That means a pair of vultures will not have a next generation for that year. So in addition to hunting, you're removing their habitat, you're removing their homes," she adds.
Seven species of vultures in Africa are now classified as globally Endangered or Critically Endangered by BirdLife International, the authority for birds on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.
A recent BirdLife report says African vulture populations have fallen by between 80% and 97% over a period of 50 years.
The group also says that in January 2020 more than 2,000 hooded vultures were found dead in Guinea-Bissau, many with their heads removed - a sign of belief-based practices rather than natural causes, researchers say.
As vulture populations continue to fall across the region, conservationists have been searching for communities where these birds are not hunted, feared or exploited.
They found one such example in Awka-Etiti.
Yet in recent years, Igwe says he and other residents became worried when they noticed outsiders arriving to hunt the birds and vulture numbers dwindled.
In his quest to save the birds he visits markets, buses and public spaces to spread the word: "I tell them that vulture is helpful to human life".
He says he "cannot run away" from his unusual nickname of Ezeudene, or the King of Vulture.
"I'm fighting to make nature exist the way it's supposed to be."
Working with the NCF for the past six years, Igwe has mobilised community leaders, local groups and security teams to protect the birds from outside hunters, with local bylaws now helping to formalise their protection.
Local volunteers monitoring the birds say they have now recorded more than 160 vultures, up from about 20 recorded in 2017.
We've heard shocking news that people are not just going for vultures anymore, they're going for the nests and even the eggs."
Nigeria has become a major hub for the illegal trade of vultures, conservationists say, partly because of its biodiversity and porous borders.
"We are doing everything possible to make sure that the smuggling of items, including vultures, including donkeys, and other species outside the country is suppressed to the barest minimum," insists Abdullahi Maiwada, a spokesman for the Nigerian Customs Service.
He says customs officials have carried out seizures of protected wildlife and supported prosecutions linked to illegal trafficking.
It is an example of how Nigeria is trying to live up its commitments as a member of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (Cites) - under which endangered species are not allowed to be traded across borders.
But Maiwada admits to the BBC that enforcement alone is not enough - education will be crucial too.
"We may not be able to do it without the cooperation or understanding of members of the community," he continues. "If people understand why these species should be preserved, then our enforcement will only be complementary to those who decide to be recalcitrant."
That message has been at the heart of conservation work in Awka-Etiti and across parts of Nigeria.
Although reliable population data remains limited, conservationists say there are encouraging signs in Awka-Etiti, with local engagement helping residents become vigilant against outside hunters.
"The missing vultures are almost back. If you go to the marketplace now, you see vultures. At one time they disappeared, but now they are coming back," Igwe confirms.
Egbe believes that this small, south-eastern town demonstrates what is possible when communities lead conservation efforts.
"What we've done in Awka-Etiti is one very good example of a success story where people have taken charge of what's going on in their environment. That makes us happy."
For Igwe, every returning bird represents hope.
But with populations still collapsing across Africa, he knows protecting them will require much more than one community.

Is there a summer COVID-19 surge this year? Yep, it's ramping up again
Hantavirus. Ebola. West Nile. Measles. And, of course, cyclospora — that stomach parasite making people miserable across the country. Americans have plenty to worry about this summer.
But remember COVID-19? It may not be surprising that many people may have almost forgotten about COVID. Unfortunately, COVID hasn't forgotten about us.
"We're now in the midst of a growing summer surge of COVID here in the United States," says Dr. John Brooks, an infectious disease doctor at Emory University in Atlanta, Ga., who used to work at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "I think most of us kind of feel like it's fading away and are certainly very grateful for that. But nationally we're seeing it ticking up pretty much everywhere."
The virus is spreading the most again in the South and West, but is also on the rise in the Northeast and Midwest. The good news is the virus is still at very low levels. And so far this summer's wave seems to be continuing the trend of getting milder each year, sending fewer people to the hospital and causing fewer deaths.
"What we're seeing is very likely evidence of growing herd immunity if you will," Brooks says. "More and more people have had one or more infections that give them some immunity against the virus and have had more than one vaccination, or maybe both. And all of that really has begun to offer us a lot of protection."
Now, that doesn't mean people don't have to worry about COVID at all anymore. The disease still makes lots of people feel awful for a week or two, foiling their summer vacations and forcing them to miss work and school.
And COVID can still cause serious disease for some people, sending them to emergency rooms, causing hospitalizations and even sometimes still causing death.
"COVID-19 is still dangerous, particularly for older adults, infants and people who are immunocompromised," says Caitlin Rivers, an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Md. And that is a lot of Americans. "In a typical office, if you have 20 colleagues, it's likely that one or two of them have some degree of immunocompromise. So it's very common that people have risk factors that make COVID-19 dangerous."
Unlike the flu, which only surges during the winter each year, COVID sees spikes twice a year – both in the summer and winter. The reason for that remains unclear.
"It's a big mystery as far as I'm concerned. It is the only seasonal respiratory virus that has a summer season," River says. "To my knowledge, we don't know what is causing this seasonality."
Rivers says she still masks up when she's in crowded places like busy airports, and recommends that people stay up to date on their vaccines. The next shots look like a good match for the dominant strain of COVID that's circulating and should start becoming available soon.
Unlike previous years, the CDC hasn't issued updated recommendations for the vaccines because of litigation over the Trump administration's efforts to overhaul immunizations in the U.S. The administration no longer recommends that everyone aged 6 months and older routinely get an annual shot.
But major medical groups still do recommend it. And insurers have indicated they will keep covering vaccines. The shots are likely to remain available for free through government programs like the Vaccines for Children program.
Public health experts worry that conflicting messages will cause confusion, discouraging people from getting another shot.
"The message is that COVID vaccine and flu vaccine will be available, they're covered by insurers, they're recommended by medical societies. People should get them and get them for their kids," says Clare Hannan, executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers, which advocates for immunization programs.
There's also even a new drug, called Xocava, that people can take right after they've been exposed to the virus to cut their chances of actually getting sick from COVID.
"It is something for people to just have in the back of their mind," Brooks says. It is expected to be a useful tool in hospitals and nursing homes when exposures happen to vulnerable people.

The Trump administration’s campaign to eradicate transgender health care for young people has run into a series of legal roadblocks: Judges have ruled against Justice Department subpoenas, a declaration from the health secretary, and parts of the president’s executive order halting all federal support for this care. But a new rule finalized this week by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services may prove more difficult to challenge.
The agency announced Tuesday it was barring the use of federal Medicaid and CHIP dollars to pay for pediatric gender-affirming medications and surgery. Then on Thursday, the Department of Health and Human Services released a report on diagnostic coding practices among gender-affirming care clinicians and referred hundreds of health care groups to the Justice Department for investigation into those practices. Despite many court losses, the administration has successfully pressured at least dozens of hospitals into closing or pausing gender-affirming care programs.
“What we see here is an ideological campaign to eradicate access to a kind of treatment because the president doesn’t like it,” said Elana Redfield, federal policy director at the Williams Institute, a UCLA School of Law think tank focused on LGBTQ+ issues. “But I would describe [the final CMS rule] as sort of a gray area,” Redfield said.
The agency received nearly 35,000 public comments after proposing the coverage rule, and as required, it responded to those concerns in the final document. By taking the rule through the typical regulatory process, the agency is “trying to position this rule to withstand the inevitable legal challenges,” according to Travis Jackson, a partner in health care law at McDermott Will & Schulte. “I think they’ve learned more about vulnerabilities that have thwarted their past efforts in this and other areas.”
Others agreed. “This rule feels less out there than some of the other proposals,” said Carmel Shachar, director of the Health Law and Policy Clinic at Harvard Law School.
Set to go into effect on Oct. 13, the rule bans the use of federal Medicaid funds for gender-affirming medication and surgery for anyone under 18; for the Children’s Health Insurance Program, the ban extends to anyone under 19. Mental health care still can be covered with federal funds, and states are not prohibited from using their own Medicaid dollars to pay for any gender-affirming care.
While legal experts expect the coverage restriction to endure in the short term, they don’t see it as impregnable. Lawsuits are expected — a press officer from Andrea Campbell’s office confirmed that the Massachusetts attorney general plans to challenge the rule in court.
Potential challenges to the rule
It’s not uncommon for certain health care offerings to be excluded from federal Medicaid coverage — the program doesn’t cover over-the-counter medications or abortion services, for example. CMS asserts in the final rule that the agency has “independent legal authority” to regulate which types of health care the federal government funds. But lawyers who spoke with STAT said the agency’s unilateral decision to revoke coverage without any directive from Congress is perhaps unprecedented.
“If they had a bunch of examples, they would cite them,” said Katie Keith, director of Georgetown University’s Center for Health Policy and the Law. The final rule’s most relevant example refers to the ban on federal coverage of abortion, which was dictated by Congress via the Hyde Amendment. The document also cites a 1976 regulation that prohibited federal financial participation in sterilization for people under age 21, issued in response to public outcry over the practice.
CMS also asserts that this rule is based on legal authority from other administration actions on gender-affirming care. “Superficially, they are correct,” Jackson said. Only one section of the president’s executive order on this care is currently enjoined. At the time, the court decided that a challenge to other sections, including directives on Medicaid funding, were not ready for litigation. Now that this rule has been finalized, that could change. Meaning, per Jackson, “they are correct, but they could also be wrong.”
Questions also linger about the validity of the scientific evidence cited in the rule, and whether the agency is attempting to regulate medical care, which would be under the states’ jurisdiction.
“There are parts of the rule where they make it clear they think this care should be tapering off,” Keith said, pointing to an explicit “tapering period” that was added to the final document, allowing federal funds to continue covering hormones for six months after the rule is in effect, until April 2027. Clinicians who provide gender-affirming care have emphasized that there is no safe way to wean transgender people off their medications.
“It gets a little bit muddled,” Keith said. “Is this just about federal funding or are you trying to take kids off their treatment?”
The final rule repeatedly references a gender dysphoria report released by HHS last year that questioned the standards of care for transgender youth, while criticizing the methodology of a report commissioned by the Utah State Legislature that came to different conclusions, and completely omitting a recent report out of the Netherlands that also contradicted the HHS review.
“I do think there are legitimate questions as to whether or not the record in front of HHS truly supports the actions that HHS is taking in the rule,” Jackson said.
Impact on patients and families
The health policy group KFF estimates that about 130,000 young transgender people covered by Medicaid or CHIP live in states where gender-affirming care is still legal. Clinicians, patients, and advocates say the final rule will effectively revoke potentially lifesaving care from those trans youth in low-income families.
While states are able to make up the lost federal funding, “this could be tough for states to do in a normal environment,” Keith said, but states are also dealing with other major coverage changes expected to push millions of people to lose Medicaid coverage.
Lawyers told STAT that the final CMS rule is seen as more legally viable than another rule that was proposed alongside it, which aims to restrict participation in Medicaid for hospitals that provide gender-affirming care to minors. CMS emphasized that these rules should not be lumped together. So while finalizing the rule that would end the use of federal dollars doesn’t exactly set the stage for the more sweeping one, its success could inform the administration’s next move.
“I see this rule coming out as a test as to the agency’s authority, and perhaps if it withstands that test — it’s not enjoined, etc. — then you may be more likely to see them take the more draconian action of the conditions of participation,” Jackson said.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have spent the past week reshaping their catching depth after making changes to a position group that have seen some setbacks this season. Now, the defending World Series champion has brought in a name familiar to their National League rival Atlanta Braves.
The move comes shortly after Atlanta parted ways with a veteran backstop who had spent years back and forth with the Braves, but if he’s able to stick with the Dodgers and help drive a third straight championship, his days in Atlanta might be officially over for good.
Atlanta Braves Veteran Moves On To Los Angeles Dodgers
Chadwick Tromp’s latest stint with the Braves came to an end earlier this season and now he’ll be looking to provide some needed depth for the Dodgers.
“(The) Dodgers have further bolstered their catching depth by signing Chadwick Tromp to a minor league deal, as he joins (the Triple-A affiliate Oklahoma City Comets) today,” Comets broadcaster Alex Freedman reported on Thursday. “(Tromp) has appeared in the majors with three teams over parts of seven seasons.”
Braves fans will recall that five of those seasons have included stints with the Braves, who have since settled on a catching duo of Drake Baldwin and Sean Murphy. He has also joined the Baltimore Orioles in two different stints between time with the Braves, though the Dodgers are a completely new organization for him.
“This is the first time in a while that Tromp signs with someone other than those two clubs,” Anthony Franco noted for MLB Trade Rumors. “He’d yo-yoed between Baltimore and Atlanta on a series of minor league deals going back to 2021. Tromp doesn’t hit much at the MLB or Triple-A level, but he’s a steady hand defensively who clearly made a strong clubhouse impression with both of his previous organizations.”
Los Angeles Dodgers Turn To Longtime Atlanta Braves Catcher
The Dodgers' decision to bring Tromp aboard has come as Los Angeles adjusts its own catching depth with some uncertainty ahead. Tromp appears to be a direct replacement for another veteran backstop who was released from Oklahoma City on Thursday.
“That explains why Los Angeles released Chuckie Robinson earlier,” Franco added. “Tromp can work with rookie Eliezer Alfonzo as depth behind the team’s big league catching duo of Hunter Feduccia and Ben Rortvedt.”
The Dodgers have been without star backstop Will Smith as he works through a neck injury and his primary backup, Dalton Rushing, has been sidelined with an elbow injury.

They fought for the U.S. in Afghanistan. Now they worry about losing their green cards
Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.
Hundreds of Afghans who fought alongside U.S. troops and supported the U.S. government in Afghanistan are now worried their green cards could be revoked.
In Afghanistan, their efforts ranged from custodial jobs at the U.S. embassy, to technology and engineering roles with U.S. contractors and companies. Some were on the frontlines of combat as interpreters.
In the years leading up to the U.S.'s chaotic 2021 withdrawal from Kabul, Congress and the Biden administration facilitated several programs for Afghans involved in military efforts to come to the U.S. with their families. Among them is the Special Immigrant Visa for Afghans, which was authorized in 2009. Since then, the State Department has issued 160,000 of those visas. More than half of them were granted since the U.S. closed its embassy in Kabul in 2021.
But now, five years after the U.S. left Afghanistan, hundreds of people who came on SIVs and now have green cards have received notices from the federal government warning them that the basis for their visas has been revoked or denied.
Families, many of whom were having children, learning English and enrolling in college, are now scrambling to find answers on the best way to respond to the government's letters.
"We are trying to work, study, raise our children and build a normal life in the U.S," said M., who asked NPR to refer to him by his first initial because he's concerned that speaking to the media could affect his green card. "But now we are also trying to find lawyers, contact congressional offices and understand what may happen to our green cards. It is very stressful because even immigration lawyers give different opinions."
The notices themselves are not necessarily new. The federal government began sending some out at the end of the Biden administration because they suspected some of the supporting documents for Afghans' SIV applications were not collected through the correct processes, potentially amounting to fraud.
But advocates, lawyers and Afghan nationals who spoke with NPR said the letters appear to be sent at a higher frequency and volume than what advocates expected, and are leaving some of these U.S. allies at risk of being deported. Over the last year, those helping allies settle into the U.S. noticed an uptick in the letters and a lack of pattern as to who was receiving them. The letters have added to the dwindling pathways for Afghans to become U.S. citizens and settle into their new lives.
"What we have seen specifically with the SIV program is people who are issued these visas and come to the U.S. have built lives here, gotten jobs, their kids are in school, they've integrated into their communities and are living their lives," said Jennifer Patota, deputy director of U.S. legal services at the International Refugee Assistance Project. "To get a withdrawal of approval letter years after the actual visa has been issued is something we haven't ever seen before."
The State Department and the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services branch of the Homeland Security Department, which are sending the letters, did not respond to requests for comment.
Fraud detection efforts combine with a mass deportation strategy
The first stage in the process of applying for the SIV is to get what is called a "Chief of Mission" approval. It involves providing an employer verification letter — letters of recommendation from a supervisor and proof that shows the employer was either the U.S. government or a contractor with the U.S. government, among other things.
Such verification became more difficult after the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan.
"Especially after the withdrawal of troops, many companies were shutting down, destroying all of their records, making it impossible in many cases to verify someone's employment," Patota said.
And then there was a concern of fraud — particularly that these immigrants, even unknowingly, had paid for letters of recommendation. In one case prosecuted by the Justice Department, a man was sentenced to 30 months in prison for a years-long bribery scheme where he accepted payments from Afghan nationals in exchange for drafting, submitting and verifying fraudulent letters of recommendation for Afghan nationals who applied for SIVs.
To combat the risk of fraud, the Biden administration created a plan to verify SIV information of individuals who could have connections to employers later suspected of such schemes. Shawn VanDiver, president of AfghanEvac, advocates for Afghans who worked alongside U.S. troops. He said his organization was notified by the previous administration that the notices would be going out.
"When this started, it had nothing to do with the Afghans. It was very much about the letter writers and companies," VanDiver said. "There were some companies and some letter writers that were up to no good – like selling letters and every single case associated with those companies or letter writers then got poisoned."
The expectation, he said, was that if the SIVs were fully revoked, individuals could still apply for, and would be likely to receive, asylum. But now, his organization and others are hearing from hundreds of people and believe the scope of the revocations is much larger.
Under this Trump administration, the letters and revocations come at a time when Afghan nationals feel particularly left out of the legal immigration system. The U.S. has paused other avenues for legal immigration available to Afghans, including the refugee resettlement program, which Trump halted on the first day of his second term, and the processing of other types of visas. Those already in the country on programs like Temporary Protected Status have also been stripped of that permission to stay.
"When the Department of State initiated a re-review of Chief of Mission applications in 2024, we understood the importance of that effort," said Jill Marie Bussey, director for legal affairs at Global Refuge. That group has been helping hundreds navigate this visa issue, as well as resettlement in the U.S. "The correspondence we saw at that time was generally tailored to the individual case and provided applicants with enough information to understand the decision and any available next steps."
But she says more recently, "there is a decline in the quality and clarity of some Department communications, including final appeal decisions that appear to raise questions about factual accuracy and provide little explanation for the outcome."
For now, it does not appear that Afghan nationals who received letters have had their green cards or citizenship revoked at scale. But advocates like VanDiver said the letters, alongside the crumbling of other programs like Temporary Protected Status and immigration application pauses, cause confusion and fear.
"These folks were on the frontlines of our war. They were interpreting. They were enabling our mission," VanDiver said. "Now it feels like it's all coming crashing down and they get no explanation of what to do."
Families fear for their futures
Across the country, Afghan nationals who helped the U.S. and their families are grappling with stress, confusion and potential financial instability after receiving the notices. Several asked that NPR use only their first names because they fear their immigration status could be affected by speaking to the press.
One of those people is Abdul who lives in Texas and was an engineer working with the U.S. Army in Afghanistan from 2017 to 2021. He was evacuated from Kabul to Qatar by the State Department and eventually got his SIV approved and came to the U.S. with his wife and two young kids.
"Most of my friends living in the U.S. three or four years, all of them receive a letter," he said. "All my friends are very depressed, most of them very worried about this issue. What will happen to us? What should we do?"
The letters are reaching people who had a long history of working alongside American efforts. Sasad, who lives in Washington state and is a former engineer, worked with the U.S. government in 2014 until the withdrawal. He began his visa process in 2019, before the fall of Kabul.
He lives with his wife, and they have U.S.-born children, including one with health issues that has required surgery and regular hospital visits. Sasad will soon be eligible to apply for citizenship, but after receiving his letter, he is afraid to begin the process.
"I've been here for more than four years, and then in the next year, I am eligible to apply for my citizenship. But when I go to the USCIS [United States Citizenship and Immigration Services], I'm stressed that they will detain me," he said, adding that his plans to go back to school and work are less certain now that he fears losing his legal permission to stay.
The Afghan nationals NPR spoke to described returning to Afghanistan as unimaginable, stressful and a death sentence. The country, which has been under the complete control of the Taliban, has also experienced deadly strikes from Pakistan, earthquakes and widespread hunger and malnutrition.
"When I came here, I thought that all my problems were solved, that now is the time to build my future right here," Sasad said, adding that he is concerned about his ability to stay in school, have a career or even travel outside the U.S. in an emergency. "What now? I cannot focus on my long-term goals. Now all of my thoughts are 'what if?' situations. A lot of 'what if?' situations [are] giving me anxiety and depression."

Israel’s defence minister wants to transfer law enforcement powers for Israelis in the occupied West Bank over to the police, a plan that Palestine’s vice-president described as a “flagrant violation of international law” and step towards full Israeli annexation.
Israel Katz announced that he had ordered the military to draw up plans for the handover of responsibility for policing Israeli settlers amid domestic and international criticism of the army’s failure to tackle militants besieging three Palestinian families.
The Palestinian vice-president, Hussein al-Sheikh, called for international intervention to enforce international law and stop a move that would “entrench the illegitimate annexation of Palestinian land”.
Katz unveiled his plan as a settler siege in the Palestinian village of Qusra entered its sixth day. The Israeli army has proved unable or unwilling to remove the group of militants trying to drive out Palestinian residents through a campaign of terror.
Michael Sfard, a leading Israeli human rights lawyer, said a transfer of law enforcement powers could constitute a major step towards formal annexation.
“The military can delegate enforcement but not responsibility [of the law],” Sfard said. “If they want to create a normative legal framework that absolves the army from responsibility and transfers it to police, that would be another brick, a very major one, of annexation.”
However, Israel could also legally expand police powers in the occupied West Bank under the current occupation framework, he added, and the lack of detail in Katz’s statement indicated it may have been driven more by politics than clear policy.
“This is a cowardly statement made by a minister of defence who is under scrutiny, because the army that reached Syria, Iran and Lebanon and annihilated Gaza cannot evacuate a few Jewish terrorists that invaded a Palestinian home in an area under occupation for six decades.”
There has been a surge in attacks on Palestinians and construction of new settlements across the occupied West Bank, as extremists backed by the most far-right government in Israel’s history intensify a campaign of ethnic cleansing ahead of national elections set for October.
On Thursday Katz celebrated the re-establishment of a settlement evacuated by Israel in 2005, under then-prime minister Ariel Sharon’s disengagement plan.
“Here, this is the land of Israel. Here, we are staying forever,” Katz said at the ceremony in Ganim, where two dozen prefabricated homes have already been installed, and the hillside is being levelled to make space for more.
On the road that leads to the settlement the army had levelled Palestinian property and used piles of rubble to block access roads for Palestinian communities.
On Friday the commander of Israeli forces for the occupied West Bank, Gen Avi Bluth, made a second visit to Qusra. Two days earlier he told Palestinians the army would remove the settlers, but soldiers retreated from confrontation with the group.
Instead they forced one of the Palestinian families out of their home, saying they needed it as a base for the unsuccessful military operation against the settlers.
One of the homes is owned by a US citizen, and US ambassador Mike Huckabee described the Israelis besieging it as terrorists, and said he had requested the Israeli police and army act to remove them.
Huckabee, who supports the settlement movement’s vision of establishing a “Greater Israel” on land seized from Palestinians and neighbouring countries, said the militants in Qusra represent a “very small minority” of the settler movement.
State and settler violence has driven a surge in displacement of Palestinian communities in the past three years.
Since October 2023, Israel has forcibly displaced 64 entire Palestinian communities and parts of 15 additional communities, affecting nearly 5,000 people, according to data from Israeli rights group B’tselem.
On Friday Israeli gunmen opened fire at a group of unarmed Israeli and Palestinian activists as they attempted to peacefully reclaim Palestinian land seized by settlers in Beit Sahour, just outside Jerusalem. A Catholic bishop and journalists covering the event were also targeted by the attackers.
Israeli settlers had put a large Star of David and Israeli flags on the roof an old, dilapidated house, owned by Palestinians, just 500 metres from a Palestinian family home.
Mia Biran, from the group Combatants for Peace, said: “They are all the time threatened by the settlers. We were about a hundred activists, our goal was to clean the area, plant some trees, to show presence and to stand with the residents who are very scared. We were on private Palestinian land.”
A few minutes after they started work, the group heard gunfire from the settler outpost and were forced to take cover. One gunman moved close to the group, opened fire in the air and aimed the gun at activists, in an attack videoed by the group.
He was later joined by three or four others. “We screamed in Hebrew ‘do not fire’ and then they understood there are Israelis among the crowd,” Biran said.
“I called the police to tell them we are threatened by settlers, the activists who were at the roof saw there was a military Jeep all the time in the area who did nothing.”
After they withdrew from the area, settlers visited the nearby Palestinian home and threatened to burn it down, she added. Settlers regularly launch arson attacks on Palestinian homes. One such attack in 2015 killed a baby and his parents, orphaning their only surviving son.
Quique Kierszenbaum and Sufian Taha contributed reporting

For a while, Japanese cultural exports seemed to specialize in making people feel better. Marie Kondo taught us to “spark joy” in our housekeeping. “Terrace House” offered a softer, slower version of reality TV where drama often hinged on a glance across a kitchen. And Nintendo’s Animal Crossing: New Horizons gave millions of gamers a quiet place to spend the pandemic.
Japanese popular literature was also, by and large, cozy and comforting. Toshikazu Kawaguchi’s “Before the Coffee Gets Cold” series, about a cafe where customers can briefly revisit the past, became an international bestseller by offering readers a chance to sit with regret, grief and the possibility of acceptance.
But lately, another side of Japanese culture has been attracting attention: stories designed to unsettle. While J-horror cinema and morbid manga have long had their adherents, this darker turn is now particularly prominent in the publishing industry.

There’s a lot of discussion about Jewish voters in politics this cycle.
What American Jews want from the midterms
Though a small electorate, Jewish voters are being pushed to the center of political debates this midterm cycle.
With Democrats embroiled in loud arguments over Israel and Gaza, Republicans have been hoping to capture more of the Jewish vote by linking criticism of Israel to antisemitism. “How a Jewish person can vote for a Democrat is beyond me,” President Donald Trump said last month. His administration has made cracking down on anti-Israel campus activists — a top early priority — and has called Democrats “Palestinian” or “jihadists.”
Meanwhile, Democrats have pointed to the rise of openly antisemitic influencers within the conservative movement, which has become a divisive topic on the right that also runs into debates over Israel, as a pressing threat to Jews.
But what do Jewish voters themselves actually want? That’s a nuanced question, and one that we have fresh polling and voting data on to help us dissect this cycle.
American Jews aren’t a large voting bloc — just over 2 percent of the population — but there are also significant communities in some key swing states and competitive districts. As a matter of partisan politics, Jews have historically voted Democratic by wide margins, but Republicans have long hoped to peel them off, often by emphasizing their support for Israel. Though it’s been a common refrain from pro-Israel and Republican activists for decades that a GOP realignment was just around the corner, it wasn’t until the 2024 presidential election that these voices got a firm boost. Nationally, and in local communities, Jewish support for the Democratic Party seemed to drop slightly.
Key takeaways
- Jewish voters remain strongly and consistently Democratic overall, despite a modest Republican shift in 2024.
- Domestic concerns — especially democracy, affordability, healthcare, and abortion rights — are key issues, while rising antisemitism and personal safety have become major unifying anxieties.
- Views on Israel are complex: Most Jewish Americans identify as pro-Israel while criticizing Netanyahu or Israeli policies, and many distinguish legitimate policy debate from antisemitism — even as they worry that anti-Israel rhetoric can cross that line.
Elections since then have been difficult to parse. In last year’s New York City mayoral election, for example, Zohran Mamdani won about 33 percent of Jewish voters, compared to the 63 percent that went for Andrew Cuomo in a race where divisions over Israel and antisemitism featured strongly. In the primary, many Cuomo voters also backed Mamdani ally Brad Lander, a Jewish progressive who was sharply critical of Israel — and who went on to easily defeat Rep. Dan Goldman in a congressional primary in a heavily Jewish district this year while running to his left on Israel issues. Meanwhile, in New Jersey, left-wing Democrat Analilia Mejia won a special election for a House seat while harshly criticizing Israel. But her candidacy led some Jewish strongholds to swing massively toward Republicans.
So, what happens to the Jewish vote in the 2026 midterms? This segment of voters is no monolith, experts say, and finding the “right” way to talk about Israel is no guarantor of electoral success. Polls show Jewish voters hold competing priorities in their minds: They’re increasingly concerned about antisemitism and their personal safety in America, and they hold complex and divergent views on Israel, which often is not a defining voting issue, even as it seems to be the dominant way strategists and pundits talk about this electorate.
Here’s what the latest data has to say about what Jewish voters want and how their politics are changing this cycle.
The remarkable consistency of the Jewish electorate
Aside from Black voters, there have traditionally been no more loyal Democratic voters than Jewish Americans. Since 2008, between 60 and 80 percent of these voters picked the Democratic candidate, while about 60 percent have consistently identified with the party over the last two decades.
That changed slightly after 2024, when exit polls suggested a six-point swing toward Donald Trump compared to 2020. Jewish communities in New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania, meanwhile, shifted more dramatically — which analysts for the election data site Split Ticket argued last year represented a 5 to 10 percentage-point swing against Democrats.
There are plenty of arguments over how and why this happened — pollsters and experts I spoke with told me that, despite the majority of Jewish American voters still siding with Democrats, the voting group mirrored other traditionally Democratic voting groups’ swing against the incumbent.
“Biden won the election, Harris lost the election,” Tali deGroot, the national political director of J Street, told Vox. “That means that every single community likely saw shifts with fewer people voting for the Democrat.”
Others argue it was a return to more of a baseline of voter behavior. 2020 was the aberration, with remarkably high support for Biden because of pandemic conditions.
But what still stands out beyond these trendlines is the steady support Democrats receive from these voters — whether because of the high level of college education among these constituents (a blue-coded trait in the Trump era), the geographic location of these voters (primarily in Democratic states like New York and California), or the socially liberal beliefs many of these voters hold (Jews historically support abortion rights, for example).
Even heading into 2026, Democrats still hold overwhelmingly strong support from these voters, Jim Gerstein, a founding partner of the polling firm GBAO, told me.
“What’s remarkable is actually how consistent Jewish voting behavior and political beliefs and values have been for years and still through today,” Gerstein said. “You have these massive developments in domestic, international, political events, actual things that happen in the real world, and the Jewish vote is just remarkably stable.”
Entering 2026, Gerstein argues, two dynamics remain at play that are preserving their Democratic lean. The long-held liberal ideological bent of Jewish Americans, along with the issues they prioritize, broadly align with the Democratic Party. And, on the other end, their antipathy to Trump and the Republican Party is “intense,” a force that pushes these voters away from the GOP, even if there were broader reasons to realign.
“Not only do they identify with the Democrats, they share positions on the major issues, shared values,” Gerstein said. “And they also have a strong opposition to the Republican Party and leading Republican figures.”
These dynamics also reveal themselves when looking at various denominations within the Jewish electorate. The largest segments — nondenominational, Reform, and Conservative Jews — lean heavily Democratic and have remained more or less steadily Democratic over the last few years. A smaller segment, Orthodox Jews — who make up about a tenth of the Jewish population but are growing — lean toward Republicans, are more strongly supportive of Trump and Israel, and have been shifting right over the last five years.
“The Orthodox population is in its own political world relative to the rest of the Jewish population,” Gerstein said. “To the extent there’s any shifting [broadly], there’s been some shifting among Orthodox to make them even more Republican. That is offset by the fact that the Reform population is much larger. They are extraordinarily Democratic, and if anything, are moving a little bit more Democratic.”
How Jewish American voters are feeling about 2026
Polls of Jewish voters this year suggests these dynamics are largely baked into the electorate at this point. A national AP-NORC survey of voters, with an oversampling of Jewish Americans, in June found that Jewish adults’ approval of how Trump is handling his job is nearly 10 points lower than among all American adults generally.
“We see that same pattern on most of the issues that we asked about, such as the economy, immigration, and Iran,” Emily Alvarez, a senior research scientist at NORC, told me. “But when it comes to his handling of Israel, they’re actually slightly more likely than the general public to approve. It’s a very small difference, but it is a difference, and it’s kind of a reversal of that trend that we saw with the other issues.”
NORC’s polling also suggests that domestic, kitchen table issues continue to be the dominant priorities of these voters generally. More than 80 percent of Jewish adults say the economy and healthcare are top priorities for them this year. About 56 and 66 percent say Israel or foreign policy are important concerns.
This June finding roughly matches the priorities that two other pollsters identified this year. The Mellman Group’s polling for the Jewish Electorate Institute from March found that Jewish voters largely say Democrats are better aligned with their views on abortion rights, healthcare, fair elections, and supporting the middle class.
And polling from GBAO on behalf of the Jewish Voters Resource Center in the spring found that the future of democracy (37 percent) and the cost of living/affordability (32 percent) are the top two issue priorities of Jewish voters, broadly speaking. Concerns over antisemitism round out the top three (25 percent).
Fear of discrimination and antisemitism is the biggest unifying concern for Jewish adults. When GBAO asked respondents about dealbreaker issues, 20 percent cited antisemitism as being their red line for supporting a candidate. And AP-NORC’s polling found that 62 percent of Jewish adults feel they are less safe than before October 7.
And while Jewish voters tend to be more aligned with Democrats on issues, the polling also found they remain wary of partisan politics — a common trait among many demographics in recent cycles.
“Jewish Americans really feel a sense of political dissatisfaction. They don’t feel particularly well supported by either political party. Very few say Democrats or Republicans support them well,” Alvarez said. “Republicans tend to feel a lot better supported by Republicans, and then they feel really supported by President Trump, but then far fewer Democrats feel the same way about their own party or about the president.”
The Israel factor
It’s hard to disentangle the effect of the Israel-Gaza war from the current political environment for Jewish voters.
Sam Markstein, the political director of the Republican Jewish Coalition, told me that October 7 was a defining moment for many Jewish voters who had preexisting misgivings about the Democratic Party. Changing political and public opinion on Israel and acts of violence against Jewish people and at places of worship, as well as shifts among Democrats and the left’s broader tension with AIPAC, suddenly made safety and antisemitism more pressing issues.
“After October 7, American Jews focused a lot more on their safety,” Markstein told me. “The main questions we heard, time and time, was who would best keep us safe, who would stand up for our students on the college campus quad, who would make us feel better about walking with our young kids to shul on Saturday morning, who would actually stand with the Jewish community and empower us to wear our Stars of David in public and not have to hide it.”
While concerns about antisemitism are widespread, views on Israel and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict itself are nuanced, particularly among Jewish Democrats, various pollsters told me.
AP-NORC’s polling, for example, found that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was broadly disliked by American Jews, with six-in-10 adults expressing unfavorable views. By contrast, Mamdani, the New York City mayor who recently explored arresting Netanyahu, was viewed favorably by 44 percent of Jews, with 39 percent expressing an unfavorable view. 30 percent of Jews said they believed Israel had committed genocide in its war in Gaza, while 49 percent said it had not.
One important wrinkle that’s often divided Israel critics is the context of that criticism. Many Jews are concerned about Israel’s security and direction and hope to see a new government with a stronger commitment to forging peace with Palestinians and neighboring states. Michael Bloomfield, a lead pollster and managing director for the Mellman Group, told me that “what often gets forgotten is that almost all American Jews, 86 percent, consider themselves pro-Israel,” including a similar share of Jewish Democrats.
But a rising segment of the left — including candidates like Abdul El-Sayed — often describe Israel’s founding vision of a homeland for Jews as inherently oppressive and sometimes calls for replacing the country with a secular and binational Arab-Jewish state. By contrast, New York’s Brad Lander, also on the left, describes himself as a “liberal Zionist” who wants a peaceful two-state solution that preserves Israel’s existence.
Polling this year, sponsored by the Jewish Electorate Institute, found that, while many Jewish Democrats are critical of Israeli government policies and the US partnership with Israel in the war in Iran, they are still strongly supportive of Israel as a state.
Overall, nearly nine in 10 American Jews describe themselves as pro-Israel, they found, but only about a quarter, 23 percent, consider themselves both pro-Israel and supportive of Israeli government policies. Six in 10 are pro-Israel and critical, half of whom are critical of “some” and another half who are critical of “many” policies. That broadly aligns with partisan identification. While 84 perfect of Jewish Democrats are “pro-Israel,” 73 percent of them are critical of Israeli policies. Republicans, a smaller share overall, are less likely to be critical.
There are also differences based on religious and cultural identity within the Jewish electorate, apparent in the NORC polling. Jews with a religious affiliation or strong attachment to Israel as part of their religious identity tend to be more supportive of Israel’s actions than secular Jews. About half of those with religious affiliation say the Gaza military campaign is justified, while a quarter believe Israel has committed genocide, compared to about two in 10 secular Jews who say the Gaza campaign is justified, and 4 in 10 who agree with the genocide charge. Three-quarters of that cohort say they are “not too” or “not at all” emotionally attached to Israel.
While concerns about antisemitism are rising, there’s room for nuance, Bloomfield told me.
“There is a policy debate about how much aid Israel should get, there’s a policy debate about where our relationship should be,” Bloomfield told me. “That is different than the worry when it gets to antisemitism and feeling uncomfortable in the Democratic Party.” The Mellman poll for JEI found that a majority of American Jews agree with the statement that “too many supporters of Israel claim any criticism of Israel is antisemitism as a way to avoid legitimate debate over Israeli policy.”
Nearly half of Jewish Republicans (47 percent) agree with that, along with 59 percent of Democrats. At the same time, 83 percent of Jewish Americans agree that “too many critics of Israel use tropes and generalizations about Jews to play into antisemitism, whether they mean to or not.”
Those nuanced views speak to the moment of uncertainty that many Jewish Democrats feel right now, he said. Israel, and the US relationship with it, does not dominate their vote choice or decision-making, but the way the party’s rising leaders, activist class, and press talk about it may become a bigger pressure point later this cycle. In the latest Mellman/JEI polling, few Jews say they’ve been following the discourse and debate over AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups’ spending in primary contests. Some 62 percent of all Jews say they have not heard much — including a majority of Jewish Democrats.
That number has likely gone up since then, given high-profile contests like Michigan’s Senate primary this month, which featured extensive arguments about pro-Israel spending and whether criticizing them shaded into antisemitism. And the salience of these debates may change in either direction depending on the news. Democrats could pursue a more aggressive policy to pressure Israel if they win the House, for example, or Israel might find room for a reset if Netanyahu loses his premiership later this year.
“There are cross currents and Jews can feel both ways at the same time,” Bloomfield said. “We ourselves can be concerned where people use antisemitism as cries as a way to get out of legitimate debate. On the other hand, there’s even more of us concerned that a lot of what is being debated by Israel often does veer too quickly into something that’s antisemitism. We can have both feelings at the same time.”

ICE detained a Venezuelan soccer pro. His case shows the immigration backlog crisis
Homero Calderón used to spend his days training at the gym and on the soccer pitch. The professional soccer player built a long career, playing for clubs in Venezuela, Portugal, Cyprus and, most recently, Italy.
But for the last five months, Calderón has spent his days inside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in Folkston, Ga.
He's a father of two U.S. citizens, ages 1 and 3. Stuck in detention, his family says he's growing despondent. He recently missed his daughter's first birthday.
"I've been 17 years with Homero," his wife Daniela Molina said in a video published on social media. "I had never heard him cry or ask for help like he has."
Calderón was driving to a car shop in Florida in late February when he was pulled over for speeding by the Marion County Sheriff's Office and arrested for driving without a valid Florida license, the Department of Homeland Security told NPR in a statement. Molina said her husband had a valid international driving permit.
Calderón was eventually transferred to ICE custody. He's been in detention ever since.
In a statement to NPR, DHS said Calderón had "permission to stay until September 5, 2025" but that "he overstayed his welcome in violation of our nation's laws."
But Calderón was in the middle of two pending immigration cases when he was detained: he had applied on Aug. 25, 2025 for an extension of his tourist visa, and had also applied for a visa for people with extraordinary abilities. Called EB-1A visa, it allows people with extraordinary ability or achievement in fields including athletics, science, arts, education, and business to stay in the U.S. with a green card.
Neither open case kept him from being swept up in President Trump's immigration crackdown. His case represents a broader pattern, said Shev Dalal-Dheini, the senior director of government relations at the American Immigration Lawyers Association.
"His case is symbolic of so many other individuals who are stuck in processing backlogs at USCIS (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services) — individuals doing the right thing by filing their applications timely," Dalal-Dheini said. "But it's taking many, many, many months, if not in certain instances years, to have a case processed."
She believes the slow pace is by design.
"It's an easy way for the government to meet their quota to detain and deport individuals when they know who individuals are because they've done the right thing and applied for something," Dalal-Dheini said.
The backlog of cases at USCIS now stands at a staggering 11.3 million pending cases. The backlog was already high before President Trump took office, but since 2025 it has increased by more than 1.6 million cases, according to an analysis by the American Immigration Council.
And even though USCIS has received fewer immigration petitions, it also processed about 41% fewer cases at the beginning of the 2025 fiscal year, the group found.
"As the government takes longer to process applications, that means people are vulnerable to being arrested by ICE because they don't have a set status approved by the federal government," said Adriel Orozco, a senior policy counsel with the American Immigration Council.
According to Homero Calderón's family, the man has never committed a crime in the U.S. or in any other part of the world. NPR found no evidence of any past or pending criminal cases.
In the past, people like Calderón with pending USCIS applications or immigration court cases weren't priorities for detention.
"The government would allow those individuals to continue to follow that process," Orozco said, adding that going after them is "a waste of resources because at the end of the day, those individuals could be potentially approved for those statuses."
But Orozco says under the Trump administration that has shifted. Now every immigrant — despite the status of their immigration case — could be detained.
Waiting for his release
Ramón Calderón told NPR his brother Homero is disciplined, a skill honed after years of playing soccer professionally.
"When he was 2-years-old I remember when I used to play, he was running around the field," Ramón Calderón said.
At 16, Homero Calderón signed his first professional contract with Sport Club Guaraní in Venezuela, his brother said. Most of his career he's played midfield.
He last played professional soccer last year for the Italian team A.S.D. Arboris Belli 1979.
Throughout his life, his brother said, Homero Calderón has always followed the rules and laws no matter in which country he was.
That's what he did when he came to the U.S., Ramón Calderón said.
"He followed every single step of the process legally to obtain the legal status," he said.
Ramón Calderón himself is a U.S. citizen. He said his brother and mother have been coming to the U.S. since they were little kids. They never overstayed their visas, he said.
"We've done everything under the legality of what the immigration laws are," Ramón Calderón said. "So it's very, very hard and very difficult for our family to see him go through this nightmare."
It's unclear for how long Homero Calderón will remain in detention.
In a statement, DHS said Calderón will remain in ICE custody "pending the outcome of his immigration proceedings."
His brother hopes a resolution comes soon.
"We thought his case was strong, that we will get him out on bail and then follow his process and everything was going to be good there, but it's been six months," Ramón Calderón said. "We just need his process to have an answer, a final answer on his visa and his residency case. Whatever that result is going to be, we will accept."

WhatsApp is on a roll lately, adding plenty of features to its platform. While some of the features are very useful, others are cluttering the core experience and blurring the line that separates it from other Meta apps.
WhatsApp is still the most used communication app around the world, with billions of users exchanging messages every single day. Most people only utilize the basic features of WhatsApp.
WhatsApp is also feature-packed like other applications, with plenty of useful features that can come in handy while using the app. Most of these useful features are buried inside settings, which most people are generally not aware of.
In this guide, I will walk you through a full collection of the best WhatsApp tips and tricks to help you get the absolute most out of the app. Most of these features are free to use, and Meta isn’t limiting these features to their paid WhatsApp subscription. Create and Share a WhatsApp Username Without Revealing Your Phone Number
WhatsApp finally rolls out usernames, where you can now create and share them with others to contact you without revealing your phone number. Up until now, if anybody wants to contact you through WhatsApp or you want to contact anyone, you need the user’s phone number.
Phone number sharing isn’t a feasible option since it can be used for other purposes, not just for contacting on WhatsApp. Additionally, more people are hesitant about sharing their phone number with strangers.

Usernames have already started rolling out on WhatsApp. If you haven’t reserved one, you can follow the guide below and do it as soon as possible. Please remember that you will still be required to link your phone number to WhatsApp to get a username.
Annotate PDFs Directly in WhatsApp Without Downloading Them
Annotating PDFs is the most stressful job that many of us go through frequently. Even to make basic edits, you need a separate application like Adobe Acrobat, or you have to depend on browsers’ built-in annotation tools, which sometimes also require you to go through multiple steps.
With the introduction of basic annotation tools on WhatsApp, the need for basic annotation tools is solved if you use WhatsApp on the web or desktop.
WhatsApp recently announced basic PDF annotation tools for WhatsApp Web and desktop, which are powered by Adobe Acrobat. It lets you annotate PDFs without downloading them if you received them on WhatsApp.You can also annotate PDFs outside WhatsApp by directly uploading the file by messaging yourself, and performing basic annotation tasks such as highlighting text, underlining, and drawing.
You can then download or share it with others. The only downside is that WhatsApp currently only offers the basic tools, which include drawing, highlighting, underlining, and a strikethrough tool. It would be nice if WhatsApp also added the ability to quickly add a signature.
To do that, open WhatsApp on the desktop and follow these steps:
Step 1: Tap on the message icon and tap on “Message yourself”.
Step 2: Upload the PDF and then tap on it.
Step 3: Tap on “Edit PDF” from the top menu.
From there, you can edit the document. Once you are done, you can directly share it on WhatsApp or click on the download option to download it locally.
Use Two WhatsApp Accounts on One Phone
WhatsApp now allows you to use multiple accounts (maximum of two) in a single app. Previously, the reliable solution was installing the WhatsApp Business app to use multiple accounts, but WhatsApp has made it easy. You can now switch between accounts and link another WhatsApp just by using a second phone number. Here is how to add a second WhatsApp account.
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and tap the horizontal menu in the top right corner.
Step 2: Tap on the settings option.
Step 3: Tap on the plus icon next to your profile name.
Step 4: Tap on Add New WhatsApp Account
Step 5: Agree to the privacy policies and enter your phone number. Enter your phone number, enter the OTP, and enter your secondary verification PIN if you have set it; that’s it. WhatsApp Privacy Checkup is designed to help you control these settings very easily. You get a single dashboard with a detailed, step-by-step guide that lets you manage those settings easily. Here is how you can use it:
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and tap on the three-dot menu, then tap on Settings
Step 2: Scroll down and tap on the Privacy option
Step 3: Scroll down and tap on the Privacy Checkup option, and from here you can go through each step to control all your WhatsApp privacy settings.
Read Voice Messages With Automatic Transcriptions
WhatsApp voice chats are great. You can simply record your voice and send a note, and also receive them.
There are times when you receive a personal voice message, or you are in a place where you cannot play your voice note. In those cases, you can simply transcribe the voice note and read it instead of listening. You can long-press and tap on Transcribe to generate a translated text of the voice note. If you don’t see this option, you should first enable it from the settings.
Step 1: You need to enable transcription first. To do that, open WhatsApp, tap on the three-dot menu in the top right corner, and tap on Settings.
Step 2: Scroll down and tap on Chats
Step 3: Now scroll down again and tap on the option that says Voice message transcripts.
Step 4: Once done transcribing chats, open a chat and long-press on any voice message, tap on the three-dot menu at the top, and tap on the Transcribe option.
Summarize Unread WhatsApp Messages Instantly
Hundreds of messages in groups can quickly pile up, especially those office communications that you must read, no matter what. Fortunately, there is a nifty feature on WhatsApp that reads all your unread messages and summarizes them for you.
This is done through WhatsApp Meta AI, where WhatsApp says this is a part of private processing where it doesn’t read your messages and all the processing happens locally on your device. This is also not enabled by default. You should go to Settings, and then Chats, and then enable Meta Private Processing.
Once you are done, you can open any group with unread messages and tap on the Unread Messages pill at the top, and you get a quick summary. This also works for individual chats.
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and go to any individual or group chat with unread messages

Step 3: Currently, it is only available in limited countries.
Translate WhatsApp Messages Automatically
This can be useful, especially if you have a contact in another country who doesn’t speak your language.
WhatsApp comes with a native translation feature where you can long-press a message and translate it into any language you want. The most useful feature is the ability to auto-translate all incoming messages from a specific contact. And it also supports two-way translation, which means the messages you are sending in return will also be translated into their languages. This is one of the useful features on WhatsApp that avoids the long wait barrier.
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and go to any chat you want to translate. Long-press on the message and click on the three-dot menu in the top right corner of the screen
Step 2: From here, tap on the language you want to translate from and choose the language you want to translate to. Remember that you need to download the language.
Step 3: If you want to translate all messages from the chat, enable the option that says translate all new messages in this chat.
Add a Personal Role Tag to WhatsApp Groups
There are times when, in WhatsApp groups, I have been mistaken for someone else. Fortunately, if you are in multiple groups and this happens to you, you can add your personal role inside groups so that users can see it and identify you before text. This also helps them to understand what your role.
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and go to the group profile you want to add the tag.
Step 2: Tap on Add Member Tag, add your member tag, and click on Save.
Turn Any Word Into a WhatsApp Sticker
More than 50% of my conversations with anyone are through WhatsApp stickers. And with my friends, I just communicate through stickers and rarely use text.
The best part is that WhatsApp also allows you to import stickers from third-party apps, and you can also create your own stickers now. While WhatsApp allows you to create your own stickers from your images, if you want to quickly highlight your text through stickers, you can go to the sticker tab and type your message, and your text is converted into a sticker. It is not only faster, but so seamless that you can just generate text-to-sticker in just a few steps.
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and go to any chat.
Step 2: Tap on the stickers icon and tap on the search bar inside the stickers section.
Step 3: Now start typing the text; WhatsApp automatically displays stickers with the typed text. You can simply tap on it to send.
Organize Chats and Groups With Custom Lists
WhatsApp lists are the most underrated feature, in my opinion. For those who are not aware, lists are like chat filters that currently appear on top of your WhatsApp chats and underneath the search button. You can create up to 52 lists.
The best use of lists is that they separate your personal chats from your work and also make a separate list for all your groups to categorize them. For instance, you can divide the WhatsApp chats or groups into friends or work.
The two biggest advantages I personally find are that WhatsApp’s “All Chats” view is generally cluttered with unwanted advertisements, especially in India. You can quickly switch to any list for a clean interface and see only messages from the chats you wish.
Here is how to create WhatsApp lists:
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and, if you see lists, swipe left and tap on it; if you don’t see lists by default, drag/swipe down from the chats to reveal them.
Step 2: You can give it a name and tap on Add people or groups. If you have the Plus subscription, you can also apply a theme and ringtone for all messages coming from this list.
Step 3: Next, add users or groups you want to add to the list and tap on Done. That’s it; your list will be created. You can just tap on the list to visit.
Set Custom Notification Sounds for Important Chats
WhatsApp notification sounds are handy; they quickly let you know that you have received a message. If you are at work and focused, but you also don’t want to miss critical notifications, you can set separate notification tones for specific chats. So, whenever you receive a notification from the chat, instead of the default notification, WhatsApp uses the notification you have set to notify you.
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and go to any chat for the group profile and tap on the Notification option
Step 2: In the notification settings, tap on the Notification tone and set a custom notification tone.
Add WhatsApp Chats and Groups to Your Home Screen
If you use WhatsApp for group or other personal communication that you often go to, you can directly add those specific chats or groups to the home screen and launch them directly from there.
Step 1: Open any chat on WhatsApp and tap on the three-dot menu at the top, then tap on More

Rewrite and Polish Messages With WhatsApp AI

Send HD Photos by Default
WhatsApp recently got an option that lets users share high-quality images instead of compressing them. Previously, to do that, I recommended sharing images as document files. Archive Marketing Messages Without Blocking Senders
I live in India, and here WhatsApp has become the main communication platform, even for business and marketing messages. There is no way to stop them, and the worst part is that if you try to block them, the company will appear on your feed with another number.
The most effective method is archiving those messages instead of blocking them. When you archive a message, WhatsApp hides it from your message chats and creates a separate archive page, which you can tap on top of your messages.
These will be hidden by default, even if you are on the main chat list. You will also not get notified of messages received from these chats, but you can easily view them if there is anything important.
Step 1: Go to the messages or content you want to block and long-press on it
Step 2: Click on the archive option at the top
Step 3: To view archived messages, tap on the archive option in the All Chats option, and you will be taken to all archived messages.
Edit Sent WhatsApp Messages
WhatsApp now allows you to edit a message once you send it. Currently, it allows you to edit the message within 15 minutes. If you accidentally share the message, you can simply long-press it, tap on the horizontal bar in the top-right corner, and tap on Edit to edit your message.
Remember that WhatsApp displays an “Edited” text to let the other user know, but it won’t display the previous version. If it’s more than 15 minutes, you can use the “Delete for Everyone” option.
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and go to the chat
Step 2: Send a message to edit. Long-press the message and tap on the pencil icon in the top toolbar
Step 3: Now edit the message and tap on the right option. That’s it. Remember that it only appears under 15 min
Protect Your WhatsApp Account With Two-Factor Authentication
Our post “How to Recover Hacked WhatsApp Account” still receives a lot of messages from people asking how to get back their accounts.
If you don’t want to be one of them, I highly recommend you enable two-factor authentication for your WhatsApp account. For those who are unfamiliar, two-factor authentication is an extra step that you need to go through when you are logging into WhatsApp. Along with the number OTP verification, you need to enter a six-digit PIN code to log in to your account.
So, even if hackers manage to sign in with your phone number through OTP, they still need to enter the two-factor authentication PIN to gain access to your account.
This is the easiest and most reliable way to add extra security that prevents your WhatsApp account from being hacked, unless a hacker also has access to that PIN. Remember that once you create a PIN, do not share it with others. And also remember the PIN, as WhatsApp frequently asks you to enter the PIN to secure your account.
Step 1: Open WhatsApp and tap on the three-dot menu at the top, then tap on Settings
Step 2: Scroll down and tap on the Account option
Step 3: Now scroll down and tap on Two-factor authentication
Step 4: Now tap on Turn on and follow the on-screen instructions to set a 6-digit unique secondary authentication code. Do not forget this PIN; it also asks to set a recovery email, so don’t skip this step.
Sign In Faster With WhatsApp Passkeys
WhatsApp also supports passkeys. For those who are unaware, passkeys are a new login method that uses your device credentials to log in to any account without using an email, password, or any other verification methods.

Nearly one in three Indian women aged 15-49 years is now overweight or obese, up from one in four women five years ago, according to data released by the Central government. The latest National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6) found that 30.7% of women aged 15-49 years were overweight or obese in 2023-24, compared with 24% in NFHS-5 (2019-21). Among men in the same age group, the proportion rose from 22.9% to 27.3%.
Speaking of the rising incidence of lifestyle-related disorders on fertility and pregnancy, which is prompting greater attention to health before conception, doctors and health practitioners are now increasingly focusing on the period before pregnancy, arguing that identifying and addressing health risks in both prospective parents could improve reproductive and pregnancy outcomes.
“The concept is not new to Ayurveda. The traditional system has described garbhadana samskara, a pre-conception regimen aimed at preparing prospective parents physically and mentally before conception. The approach is now being offered as a structured programme at the SDM College of Ayurveda and Hospital in Udupi, Karnataka, which has been providing pre-conception counselling and care to couples from different parts of south India,’’ Mamatha K.V., principal and senior obstetrician at the institution, said.
Describing this approach as the “conscious preparation for conception”, Dr. Mamatha said that the process involves assessment of the health of both partners, along with advice on diet, lifestyle, and other factors that may influence reproductive health. Pre-conception consultations can provide an opportunity to identify risks, review medicines, address nutritional deficiencies and encourage healthier lifestyles before pregnancy.
In Ayurveda, conception is described through four factors — ritu, the appropriate fertile period; kshetra, a healthy reproductive tract; beeja, the healthy sperm and ovum; and ambu, adequate nourishment. “Interventions are tailored around these factors, with dietary and lifestyle changes and, where considered appropriate, traditional therapies,’’ Shreyashri Suvarna, a physician at the hospital, said, adding that traditional interventions need to be individualised and clinically supervised.
