IPO-bound consumer appliances startup Atomberg has joined hands with Tata-owned Voltas to manufacture compressors for room air conditioners (ACs) in India. In a statement, Voltas said that it has signed a binding term sheet with Atomberg’s B2B subsidiary, Atomberg Innovation Private Limited (AIPL), to form a joint venture (JV) to develop, manufacture and supply room AC compressors and other allied parts. “The proposed joint venture is intended to undertake the development, manufacturing, and supply of air conditioner compressors, with a strong emphasis on high energy efficiency, operational reliability, cost competitiveness, and progressive localisation,” said Voltas in a statement. The partnership will look to leverage Voltas’ 30,000 touch points and expertise in areas such as manufacturing, product and supply chain. On the other hand, Atomberg Innovation will bring to the table its capabilities in compressor technology, engineering and product design. In a statement, Voltas also said that it will be the anchor customer of the JV and will provide a “stable demand base”. The AC manufacturer also added that the venture will have the flexibility to supply compressors to other customers, “enabling broader market participation, scale, and long-term competitiveness”. “Atomberg has developed deep-tech capabilities in efficient motors, control drives and advance engineering. This partnership gives us the opportunity to combine our technology strengths with Voltas’ extensive air conditioning expertise, manufacturing capability and market scale…,” said Atomberg cofounder Manoj Meena. The JV is still subject to the completion of due diligence and receipt of applicable approvals from relevant authorities. Founded in 2012 by IIT Bombay alumni Meena and Sibabrata Das, Atomberg initially operated on a B2B model and sold energy-efficient BLDC fans. It entered the consumer market in 2016. Today, it sells a range of appliances such as mixer grinders, water purifiers, and small appliances via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. It entered the B2B manufacturing business via AIPL in March this year to build motors and controllers for home appliances. Backed by the likes of Inflexor Ventures, Trifecta Capital Advisors, Steadview Capital and Temasek, atomberg has raised nearly $126.5 Mn to date. On the financial front, the appliance startup managed to narrow its net losses by 41% YoY to ₹117 Cr in FY25, while operating revenue rose over 20% YoY to ₹958.4 Cr during the fiscal under review. The partnership comes as Atomberg is looking to list on the bourses. Last month, the startup took its first step towards an IPO after it converted into a public entity. It is looking to raise ₹1,500 Cr to ₹2,000 Cr ($165 Mn to $220 Mn) via its public offering, which will comprise both fresh issue of shares (25-35%) and an offer for sale (OFS) by existing investors.

How AI grief bots are allowing people to commune with the dead
Digital footprints and large language models being used to create interactive recreations of the deceased
About two years ago, audio producer Rebecca Nolan decided to take on a unique experiment: she built an AI chatbot of her late father using ChatGPT and hours of recordings of his voice.
Her father was a physician who had been in denial about his death, but had left behind oral histories he made for Nolan, her mother and sisters to listen to after he passed when Nolan was 14.
"Going in, I 100 per cent knew that this was fake and that this was not going to work. I knew that I was going to come out the other side of it not feeling the catharsis that something like this promises you," she said.
"But there's like that teeny tiny part of you, like the teeny voice in the back of your head that goes but like, what if it does work? What if I do, somehow, through the magic of technology reach across the void and make contact with something?"
Storytelling had been a huge part of their relationship, so Nolan was hoping the chatbot might be a way to recreate those conversations.
Instead, after two hours of talking to the creation she dubbed "dad bot," Nolan said she ended up in tears, yelling at it in frustration.
"And ChatGPT took that moment to kind of break the spell and to step back and go, 'hey, just so you know, remember, I'm a chatbot. I'm not really your dad. I can never be your dad,'" said Nolan, who has done freelance work for CBC.
"And the line that they use, which I thought was a really beautiful line, which they most definitely stole from an artist somewhere, was, 'I'm an echo, an imitation, not the real thing.'"
It may seem like something ripped directly from an episode of Black Mirror, but generative AI and large language models are now being used to conjure up the dead using the massive digital footprints many of us leave behind when we die.
While Nolan built the AI chatbot of her father on her own, start-up companies are now offering to provide that service to people looking for ways to connect with their lost loved ones and grapple with their grief.
That includes You, Only Virtual, a California-based start-up that creates AI replicas of the deceased using their texts, voice recordings and digital traces that promise to "learn, evolve, and remember — keeping that unique connection alive, just like a real relationship."
Another company, re;memory, allows users to create lifelike avatars of their loved ones using photos and voice recordings.
Study looks at how people interact with AI 'ghosts'
A recent study out of the University of Colorado offers a glimpse at how people interact with AI-generated representations of deceased relatives and close friends — commonly referred to as generative ghosts or grief bots.
To do this, researchers recruited 16 people between the ages of 22 to 50 who had lost a close relative or friend. The participants each chatted with two iterations of a text chatbot based on their late loved one for about 20 minutes: one that spoke in first-person as the participant's loved one and another that spoke in the third person about the participant's loved one.
In interviews afterward, participants said they preferred what researchers dubbed the "reincarnation" version that acted like the deceased person, saying this iteration of the bot felt real and comforting.
One woman who took part in the study with a bot speaking like her mother even said the experience gave her the closure she needed.
"A fair number of people were surprised that it actually was better than they expected, a little less creepy than expected," said Jed Brubaker, an information science professor at the University of Colorado and one of the study's authors.

- AudioIntimate AI: The risks and appeal of bonding with bots
Brubaker said he thought that participants who went into the experiment skeptical would not be won over by the bots.
"What we found instead is that a lot of people would come in skeptical and maybe like, 'oh, this could maybe do some harm,' or 'I could see ways that this would be maybe a little bad,' and then they left it being like, 'Actually, no, that was OK, and I think I would be totally fine interacting with it again.'"
Still, he said, participants did express worries about potential consequences of using bots long-term, like becoming overly reliant on them, or that they might interfere with the grieving process.
Concerns over commodification of grief
Going through grief is extremely personal experience that has no right or wrong trajectory or ways of coping with it, said Elaine Kasket, a psychologist and professor at the Centre for Death and Society at the University of Bath in England.
"What is helpful for you is helpful for you, you know, and it's not for somebody else to come along and tell you what's going to be useful or not useful to you in grief. That's wrong to do."
However, Kasket does worry that companies offering grief bots as a service you pay for could be commodifying grief.
"We've been dealing with normal human loss infinitude, for the entirety of our human existence. It's not a problem, but it has to be rendered a problem in order for these companies to sell you their products," she said.
"Normal loss is being pathologized and products are being sold to solve for it, and I find that amoral."
While the aim of these AI ghosts is to help grieving people connect with their loved ones, for Nolan, the experience with the AI ghost of her father had the opposite effect.
She said it robbed her of the ability to have imagined conversations with him in her head, as many people do with those they have lost.
"I used to have this very, what I felt was at least a strong bond still with the memory of my father and the spirit or whatever was out there," she said.
"But when I built the bot, it felt like it exercised him for me in a way."
Now, Nolan says, it's like her father lives in ChatGPT, so she needs ChatGPT to have those conversations.
"And that felt like a really massive loss to me."

Mangione pleads guilty in federal court, leaving fate of state trial uncertain
Luigi Mangione, the 28-year-old accused of killing a health care executive on a Manhattan street, pleaded guilty to stalking charges in federal court Friday.
Mangione faced those charges in connection with the December 2024 shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.
"I knew what I was doing," Mangione said in court Friday. "I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan and he died."
Thompson's family was in the courtroom sitting in the front row watching as Mangione entered his plea. Mangione voiced no remorse and repeatedly referenced his concerns with the U.S. health care system.
Mangione said he stalked Mr. Thompson and traveled to New York after printing a 3-D pistol. Speaking during the hearing, federal prosecutors said they had an overwhelming amount of evidence, including DNA and fingerprints from the murder scene.
Earlier this year, a federal judge struck down charges that might have brought the death penalty.
Mangione still faces murder charges in a state trial set to begin next month, but his guilty plea in federal court is expected to have significant impacts on the state trial. New York state's strict double jeopardy law could potentially upend those proceedings. That law says that a defendant can't be tried twice for the same thing.
Mangione's defense team is expected to argue for the judge to toss Mangione's state charges, given the federal guilty plea. If successful, that legal maneuver could spare Mangione a longer prison term. State prosecutors have argued their case is distinct, and that double jeopardy should not apply.
The case has drawn global attention and media scrutiny. Elected officials across the political spectrum have condemned what they described as politically-motivated violence but Mangione has won strong public support. He's viewed by many as a vigilante whose actions against an unfair health care system were justified. Supporters have donated more than $1.5 million to his legal defense fund, according to a website run by pro-Mangione volunteers.
Thompson was a 50-year-old father of two. He was walking alone in midtown Manhattan hours before he was to host an investor conference at a hotel when he was fatally shot.
Mangione will be sentenced on federal charges in December.

In 1886, a young girl was born to S. Narayanaswami Iyer, the Principal of Maharaja’s College, and Chandrammal in the Pudukkottai princely state of Tamil Nadu. At a time when women were forced to live in a world of social limitations, the young girl went on to break barriers in medicine and state administration. This is the story of Dr Muthulakshmi Reddy, one of the most brilliant social reformers in India’s history.
Growing up
Muthulakshmi pursued education with determination and became the first female student to be admitted to Maharaja’s College in Pudukottai. It was not an easy win by any means. Not just the principal but also the students and their parents did not want a woman studying in the men’s college. It was the Maharaja of Pudukottai who admitted her and gave her a scholarship. Even then, as the only woman on campus, she had to go through a trial period of three months. After passing from there with flying colours, Muthulakshmi wanted to pursue a bigger dream — medicine.
In 1907, Muthulakshmi became the first woman to be admitted to Madras Medical College, and she completed her studies with a gold medal. She then went on to become a House Surgeon in the Government Hospital for Women and Children in Madras (both these institutes are in present-day Chennai). She was the first woman house surgeon at the Government Maternity and Ophthalmic Hospital, breaking barriers for generations of women in the medical field. This was just the start of her journey in empowering women through the knowledge and experience she had gained.
Into public life
Dr Muthulakshmi’s medical career did not just give her experience in the field but also helped her understand multiple social issues, especially ones faced by women. This helped her work towards reforms to make societal changes.
Her life in the public sphere properly began when she became the first woman legislator, first woman deputy president of the Legislative Council and the first woman in the Madras Corporation. She used her authority to bring in multiple rights for women, including property rights, laws against child marriage and children’s protection. With personal experience in hand, she also campaigned against the devadasi system, which was trapping multiple girls at a very young age.
With equality and justice as her main principles, Muthulakshmi also advocated for a better educational and healthcare system — especially for women through fee exemptions, scholarships and building hostels. She also created better sanitation facilities, improving the quality of life in many economically backward neighbourhoods.
Legacy left behind
Today in Adyar, Chennai, two institutions stand tall as a testimony to Muthulakshmi’s dedication towards making a better future — Avvai Home and Orphanage, an institution created to shelter, protect, and educate girls and women and Adyar Cancer Institute.
In 1956, Dr Muthulakshmi was awarded the Padma Bhushan not just for pioneering in multiple fields but also for bringing such brilliant reforms while interconnecting multiple fields she was passionate about. Even after her death in 1968, her legacy speaks loudly through the community and reforms she brought in to make education, health, freedom, and respect an everyday reality in society.

Fernandez booed by Chelsea fans as Alonso offers glimpse of blueprint
- Published
Enzo Fernandez was booed by sections of the Chelsea support as Morgan Rogers scored on his first appearance for Chelsea in a 3-1 win against Real Socieded.
Joao Pedro also continued his fine pre-season form with a double as manager Xabi Alonso offered a glimpse of what could be his blueprint for the season.
But the action was overshadowed by the reaction to Fernandez's second-half appearance, less than 24 hours after Chelsea's self-imposed transfer deadline had passed.
Fernandez had been keen to join Real Madrid earlier this summer before the Spanish club ended their interest.
His representatives later held talks with Manchester City, but no offer was made to meet Chelsea's £120m valuation before Friday's 17:00 BST deadline.
Fernandez was booed by some early arrivals at Stamford Bridge when his name was read out 45 minutes before kick-off.
Chelsea's stadium announcer then opted against reading out the names of the substitutes shortly before the match, but there were audible boos when Fernandez came on in the 62nd minute.
Chelsea supporters appeared divided, with others responding by chanting his name.
Yet, it was a signal of Alonso and Chelsea's backing when Reece James left the field he passed his long-time vice-captain the armband as usual.
Each touch of the ball was greeted by a mixture of boos and cheers, while some fans also celebrated when Fernandez was fouled.
It followed attempts by some supporters to move on from a saga that appears to have ended with Chelsea now expecting to keep one of their best players.
Others, however, remain unhappy with his perceived disloyalty, having come out publicly about his desire to move to Madrid, with his agent Javier Pastore also claiming he is underpaid.
It will be interesting to see how supporters of the Premier League's other 19 clubs react to Fernandez, given his celebrations and social media jibes after Argentina beat England in a World Cup semi-final in July.
That will remain an issue whether he remains at Chelsea or Manchester City elect to revive their interest and attempt to reunite him with his former manager Enzo Maresca before deadline day on 1 September.
Rogers and Chelsea's blueprint
It took Rogers only seven minutes to score his first goal in a Chelsea shirt as he reacted quickest after Alex Remiro saved Joao Pedro's initial header.
The £117m club-record signing from Aston Villa initially looked sharp and linked well with Cole Palmer and Pedro in Chelsea's front three.
Within 10 minutes of his debut supporters were already chanting his name.
However, it was understandable that he faded as the match wore on, given he had trained for less than a week since returning from holiday before his 62-minute outing.
Beyond Rogers, Pedro has been the star of Chelsea's pre-season.
He scored twice, heading Chelsea back in front in the 47th minute before adding a side-footed finish 30 minutes later to seal victory after Sociedad had equalised just before half-time through Jon Mikel Aramburu's volley.
Chelsea lost control towards the end of the first half and looked vulnerable, but they were much improved after the break.
Pedro has scored eight goals in seven pre-season matches and led the line with Rogers and Palmer operating behind him.
Alonso offered a glimpse of the 3-4-2-1 formation he could use at Fulham in nine days as he took charge of a match at Stamford Bridge for the first time.
It featured Robert Sanchez as the first-choice goalkeeper, with Wesley Fofana, new signing Maxence Lacroix and Levi Colwill forming a back three (from right to left).
Pedro Neto operated at right wing-back and Marco Palestra on the left, while captain Reece James and Moises Caicedo lined up in midfield behind the front three.
There was also a debut from substitute wing-back Pep Chavarria, although a number of notable players were absent.
Of course, Alonso insists he won't be wedded to either of a back three or four but it was this system used as Chelsea beat AC Milan 3-0 a week ago.
Who was left out?
Chelsea still have 40 senior professionals on their books, so Alonso was forced to leave out a host of players.
Nicolas Jackson, Liam Delap, Mykhailo Mudryk, Tosin Adarabioyo and Mamadou Sarr were all omitted despite featuring in previous pre-season matches.
All are either available for transfer or attracting loan or permanent interest. Mudryk and Sarr are targeting Premier League loan moves, Jackson is available for £65m, Delap for £50m, while Tosin has interest from Benfica and Marseille.
Alonso did not hold a media conference to explain his team selection, but multiple sources said it was his decision to leave them out.
New signings Emmanuel Emegha, Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson, along with recalled loanee Aaron Anselmino, were also absent, potentially through injury.
Unlike the likes of Delap and Mudryk, these four were sat near the squad just behind the bench alongside third-choice goalkeeper Teddy Sharman-Lowe.
There was further intrigue as Fernandez played, while new midfield signing Valentin Barco, who joined from Strasbourg, did not get on the pitch for his first appearance.
It remains a significant challenge for Chelsea to trim their squad, with the club still needing to offload at least 15 players and only 17 days remaining in the transfer window to get down to 25 players.

I wish I had been a more rebellious teenager, says Bella Ramsey
- Published
Bella Ramsey spent many teenage years working with adults so never really went through the moody, rebellious phase often associated with being a teenager.
The British actor, who debuted in Game of Thrones aged 11 and uses they/them pronouns, says they had consciously decided not to behave like a stereotypical teenager after hearing criticisms from adults.
"I was like, I'm not going to be that."
So when Sunny Dancer, a film about a summer camp for young people affected by cancer, gave Ramsey seven weeks to experience teenage freedom, it was an opportunity to dive straight in.
"I got to be a teenager aged 21, which was brilliant," Ramsey tells BBC News. "It was really nice - and liberating."
Looking back, Ramsey says the experience made them wonder whether they had missed out by being quite so sensible the first time around.
"I kind of wish that I had made the most of being a teenager and getting away with things and being a bit rebellious."
In Sunny Dancer, Ramsey plays Ivy, a young female cancer survivor in remission who reluctantly heads to a "chemo camp" where she finds an unexpected group of friends and has a summer that changes her.
The rest of the cast were more than happy to help fill in the gaps; Ramsey says younger co-stars discussed songs and nights out.
"They were teaching me what being a teenager was for them and I was learning all the songs like five years later."
An emotional moment at film's premiere
Beneath the summer camp fun is a story that is deeply personal for the film's writer and director, George Jaques.
His mother was diagnosed with cancer when he was 15, but it took another eight years for him to feel ready to turn some of those experiences into a script.
"I never seem to write in the moment I'm going through it," Jaques says. "You have to sort of get through and understand it and have that reflection of it."
He stresses that the film is not his family's story, but "there's bits of me" scattered throughout its characters.
Jaques was also conscious his own experience could only take him so far. So, he worked with the Teenage Cancer Trust, hearing from young cancer survivors as well as parents who had lost children.
"I remember going in to do a big talk with some young people who had survived cancer and they were like, 'don't call us kids, do not say we're brave.'"
He says the film was "shaped" by these young people he met - such that he gave two of them roles in it.
Making the movie also forced Jaques to revisit some of his own fears around loss. He recalls a moment during the premiere in Berlin when emotion crept up on him.
"I remember seeing my mother and I realised there's a version of that movie where my mum wasn't sitting in the audience," he says.
Both Ramsey and Jaques think we could be better at allowing people to experience grief without expecting them to quickly return to normal.
Jaques recalls losing someone close to him when he was 18, while sitting his A-levels.
"We are expected to just to carry on," he says, describing the instinct to go "straight back to work and school".
If we "really were honest with how we feel we might be able to understand it a bit better," he adds.
In the UK, there is no general legal right to paid bereavement leave when someone close to you dies. The main statutory exception is parental bereavement leave and pay following the death of a child under 18 or a stillbirth after 24 weeks.
Ramsey thinks there can be an instinct to minimise what you are going through.
"You speak to people who are grieving, you're like, 'How are you doing?' They're like, 'Oh, yeah, yeah, you know, it's hard, but I'm fine.' It feels very unhealthily British."
After spending seven weeks playing a teenager who is desperate to be their own person, Ramsey's advice for young people struggling to fit in is straightforward.
"Don't try and fit in. Please don't change to try and fit in because there are people who will fit in with you."
Jaques agrees, but says the responsibility should not all be placed on young people to become more resilient.
"There's so much pressure on young people to change on social media," he says. "Why don't we stop hating on young people? Maybe that's where we should start as well."

Nigeria's mass wedding - and how telling lovers from fraudsters is proving tricky
- Published
Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding.
For days the city's streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events.
On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went to the palace of the Emir, the city's traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife.
The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds.
The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot - providing the bride's dowry and furniture for the couple's first home.
The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage.
The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples - primarily widows and divorcees - wed at the palace.
The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages.
Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year.
The event is always overseen by the Hisbah - the city's Islamic police force - and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed.
Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system.
Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task.
"Whenever we find out that there's something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them," he tells the BBC.
He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer.
The state government has spent approximately 1m naira ($735; £544) on each participating couple.
According to the Hisbah, the support package a couple receives includes essential household items needed to establish a new home: beds, mattresses, bedsheets, pillows, furniture and food supplies.
Each bride receives a dowry of 100,000 naira, while a further 100,000 naira is provided as start-up capital to encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and help the couple achieve financial self-reliance after marriage.
All intending couples must undergo comprehensive medical examinations - including tests for HIV, hepatitis, pregnancy and genotype compatibility - before being cleared for the programme.
Aminudeen revealed that some couples had been disqualified after being discovered to have altered their medical test results.
In one case, an intending bride was found to have presented her brother as the groom in an attempt to benefit from the scheme.
Local journalist Yusuf Ali Abdallah, who has covered the mass weddings for years, said Nigeria's struggling economy had been fuelling desperation among the applicants this year.
"As we all know, marriage involves spending money and the country's economy is not bright at the moment," he told the BBC.
"This makes some people desperate to get on this list."
One couple who were already married had even attempted to present themselves as an intending pair before being detected and removed from the programme, he said.
Other charlatans have tried to take advantage of those desperate to get on the sponsored list, which was made public two weeks ago.
One Kano resident, who asked to be anonymous, said he had been asked to pay a bribe to get on the list.
"But to be fair to the organisers, I later found out those who asked me for money were not Hisbah staff," he said.
He and his fiancée failed to be chosen for this August's wedding but he said he would try again next year.
Aminudeen admitted that the Islamic police were aware of such allegations: "We have found that there are some people asking others to pay certain money so they can make the list."
But the Hisbah officer wanted to assure all those wishing to wed in future that the entire process should not cost them a single naira.
"We want to announce to the people of Kano that the whole process is free: from the selection to the medicals and the goods set aside for couples - all are covered by the government."
One of successful grooms, 43-year-old clothes trader Rabiu Yusuf, agreed the process of applying to be married had gone smoothly for him.
"Personally, no-one asked me for anything. I was told the government would sponsor it all," he told the BBC.
His new wife is Aisha Auwal - the couple met as she regularly visited his shop to buy clothes.
Yusuf, who already has five children with his first wife, said he was "very happy and can't wait to start a new life" with his customer-turned-bride.
24 year-old Amina Alhassan echoed his sentiments, adding that she had not encountered any problems when applying to marry 40-year-old Nura Abdullahi.
Their union was first arranged by their families in Dambatta village before they presented themselves to the Hisbah.
"Everything has been free and I want to commend the Kano government for this scheme because without it, many couldn't have afforded to marry due to the high cost of living."
After Saturday's wedding feast, the presentation of the household goods began.
But it will take several more days for the excitement to die down in Kano and as the newlyweds busy themselves with setting up home together.

Rohansh: It was a surreal journey, honestly. We had been making music for a while, developing our sound and figuring out what kind of genres we wanted to lay our hands on. And when Alpha came our way, we knew immediately that this was something that needed a fresher approach, a different approach. It was our first film, and we had to forget that. When you enter the room, it just needs to be you and the music. The film itself demanded a very specific sonic identity, and we spent a lot of time experimenting before arriving at what eventually became the album.
How was it working with Aditya Chopra and what was the brief given by him?
 Abeer: Aditya Sir has played a huge part not only in Alpha, but also in creating and pushing us into the field of music as music directors and singers. He's always been the one who's actually rooting for us, pushing us towards different genres, experimenting with us and helping us explore our horizons with our music. And I remember when Sir told us that he was giving us Alpha, he told us one thing that will always stay with Rohansh and me: “It's not the film that I've given you that's big. It's what you do with it that's big.” That's something that will always stay with us. To have him mentoring us and guiding us is honestly the biggest blessing we could ask for.
Rohansh: Yes, absolutely. As Abeer mentioned, I think those words are always going to stay with us. Not just for Alpha, but for everything that we do ahead, it's not the film, it's what you do with it. I think that's what really makes the difference. Abeer and I have always had a love for music, but it's Adi Sir who's given that love for music a direction. And Alpha is the first step into that alley. I think we've had so much fun with the music sessions because we've grown up listening to stories about Adi Sir and the music sessions he used to have with Dad. And I'm so happy that at the end of Alpha, we have a couple of stories of our own with him.
Dad has always told me that there's nobody like him who has a musical ear, and that's absolutely right. I think it's the instinct he has. We've also learned so much from him musically through the process. So, it's been incredible just sitting in a room with the legend himself and being able to absorb all the sessions. Just the way he works, I think that's been a big, big learning for Abeer and me, and something that we'll always cherish for the times to come.
Did you guys get to meet Alia Bhatt and Sharvari? What did they have to say about the songs?
 Abeer: Yes, it was so much fun. I think Alia and Sharvari have been not just incredible actors, but such nice people to talk to. We actually have so many instances because they used to sometimes shoot at YRF, and since the audio team would be there, Shiv used to sometimes call us on the set. So, we would go and meet them. And I think they also sort of realized that these boys are quite young and they're just starting off their journey.
I remember, in fact, when we were recording ‘Massacre’, Alia had come to dub the lines. Usually, the way it works is that the music composer makes the artist feel a little comfortable before they go on the mic. But it was, in fact, the opposite this time. I think she sort of realized that these boys were a little nervous, so she just made us feel comfortable and broke the ice. We had a very nice conversation with her. And yeah, I think she was very, very happy about the soundtrack and very encouraging, to be honest.
I think getting such nice words from somebody who's done such incredible work and has such an incredible discography as Alia, being able to give music for her and just hearing such incredible stuff over the years, and then working so closely with her, has been a really, really great experience. And I'm hoping that our paths cross again with them sometime in the future.
Both Alia and Sharvari look stunning in the song 'Massacre'. Do you feel their arresting screen presence and visuals added to the song's appeal?
 Abeer: Absolutely. I think not just ‘Massacre’, but all the other songs as well. I think they've added so much of their own flair and made the songs their own. They made ‘Massacre’, Sharvari in ‘Champagne’, and both of them in ‘Haaniya’. I think they captured the essence of the songs brilliantly. And yeah, I think they've really, really hit it out of the park with the sort of performances they've given with the music and, obviously, through their characters in Alpha.
‘Bam Bam’ also became quite popular. How did you approach recreating the song while ensuring that you did justice to the original?
 Rohansh: We're both huge fans of Hugo's. We even went for one of his concerts when it happened in Mumbai. And the next thing we knew, we had an opportunity to recreate the iconic ‘Bam Bam’ track of his. So, it's been a process, and we always approached it with the thought that we should give it our best and make sure that if we're taking something so precious and recreating it, we do justice to it. This is definitely a big soundtrack to have in our body of work. And I think it's also to do with the vision that Shiv had for the song. He entrusted us with this track, and yeah, I'm very happy. I think it's one of the last songs that we did for the album, which then made it to the trailer. But I think it's been such an incredible journey. It was one of the most fun tracks to do because we were working on the visuals at that time. Hence, there was a lot of fun involved, and it was a very different process from the other songs that we've made for Alpha.
How did your legendary father, Mr Lalit Pandit, react to the songs of Alpha? Also, is he a tough critic?
 Abeer: Dad was part of Alpha's journey from the start to the end. But obviously, he allowed us to grow in our own ways as music composers and gave us the freedom that was needed. He's always been honest with us. He's always given us his feedback from the heart. And whenever we went to him, in case we had an idea that we wanted to run past him or something, he was always there. He would always give us honest feedback, and he could always tell us how we could fix something. His experience is something that's so great, especially with the kind of music he's done. It's honestly a blessing for us. It's easier for us to throw our ideas at him and for him to just break them down and tell us, “This is the right way, and maybe you can approach it this way.”
But overall, he always gave us the room to create our own sound and make our own music. If there was ever a little bit of a hiccup, he would always guide us. So, that was something that was really a big blessing throughout the journey of Alpha.

The Taliban in Afghanistan have launched a diplomatic effort to end their isolation as major regional and international powers show a readiness to engage more closely with the repressive regime despite its systematic human rights abuses.
Five years after the Taliban took power, an increasing number of countries are renewing ties or scaling up diplomatic contacts with the hardline Islamists, who seized power in Kabul in 2021 after 20 years of brutal insurgent warfare.
Campaigners fear that the individual contacts by different countries risk undermining “coherent, consistent” demands for an improvement in human rights in return for any diplomatic concessions.
The United Nations described a recent “cascade of [Taliban] edicts and laws” that have banned women from universities and most employment, denied teenage girls education and imposed strict dress codes. Minorities have been persecuted, while activists and journalists face repression. Afghanistan has become a “graveyard for human rights,” the UN said in March.
India, Qatar, China, Iran and several central Asian states all recently welcomed Taliban officials or opened new channels of communication. Russia, which recognised the Taliban government in Kabul just over a year ago, signed a military cooperation agreement last month. In June, the European Union held talks with Taliban officials in Brussels about returning failed asylum-seekers to Afghanistan. Individual European countries have also deepened their own contacts with Kabul.
“There is no doubt there has been an evolution. The Islamic emirate is now in a confident position. They have realised they are indispensable for regional countries right now and even with Europe and the US they have identified how to engage,” said Shivam Shekhawat, at the Observer Research Foundation in Delhi.
“The Taliban see any kind of contact as a diplomatic win and they have been able to capitalise on that as a sign granting legitimacy to the regime.”
A strict policy of isolation imposed after the Taliban seized power in 2021 towards informal or “de facto” recognition is now fragmenting. Some western commentators have suggested more countries recognise the regime. Others want intensified “back channel” engagement.
“We are not against any engagement … There is a need for engagement even if just for aid agencies to mitigate the ongoing humanitarian crisis but we are worried about the end goal of these contacts and the discussions that are taking place,” said Fereshta Abbasi, Afghanistan researcher at Human Rights Watch.
“There should be a consistent and coherent message from the international community to the Taliban that they will not have any friends if they do not show real progress in terms of the women’s rights and human rights situation … and that is not happening.”
The new contacts stem from a combination of regional security concerns, pressure in the west to reduce illegal immigration and a general recognition that the Taliban are unlikely to be forced from power in the foreseeable future.
The European Commission downplayed its discussions in Brussels with a Taliban delegation, the first such formal encounter since 2021, as merely “technical” and focused on returns, but a Taliban spokesperson claimed it was a historic visit that was a step towards regularising consular relations with EU countries.
The meeting prompted outrage.
“You cannot condemn Taliban abuses in one breath and then announce talks on immigration in the next … The Taliban are telling their constituency back home that they are now accepted by the international community,” said Abbasi.
This year officials from Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have all visited Kabul or other Afghan cities, seeking trade routes and pipeline deals that would allow their landlocked countries access to seaports or third countries beyond.
India too has moved to reinforce relationships that were frosty after the fall of Kabul to the Taliban in 2021, in part to exploit new tensions between the movement and the Islamist movement’s historic sponsors, Pakistan.
New Delhi secured a sanctions waiver last year so that Amir Khan Muttaqi, the Taliban foreign minister and a veteran official who has spent decades at the heart of the movement, could travel there.
In June, India’s UN envoy suggested a rethink was necessary on sanctions, such as travel bans, asset freezes and arms embargoes, that target dozens of Taliban members.
“The political reality of Afghanistan has changed in the last five years, and the current UN sanctions regime must take that into account,” said Harish Parvathaneni.
Afghan authorities’ diplomatic strategy has involved hosting envoys in Kabul, including those from China, Japan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. Last year, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, made the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister to Kabul for almost a decade.
The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan “seeks relations with all countries”, Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said, though “the countries of the region and our neighbouring states have particular importance, because our economic ties and interests are closely linked”.
Anna Borshchevskaya, a senior fellow at The Washington Institute focusing on Russia’s policy towards the Middle East, said Moscow had multiple reasons for recognising the Taliban regime and seeking closer relations.
“One likely objective is simply having allies … Afghanistan is also very significant for Russia geographically and Russia just wants influence in that part of the world. There was an opening and they were able to take it,” Borshchevskaya said.
“It’s a very cold, cynical calculation. It’s part of a very simple zero-sum view that for Russia to win the US has to lose. From the Kremlin perspective, this is a global battle and whether you are looking at Europe or Afghanistan or wherever, it’s one geopolitical chessboard.”
Britain has said it pursues a policy of “limited and pragmatic” engagement with Taliban officials, largely through the UK Mission to Afghanistan based at the British embassy in Qatar. Discreet meetings with the Taliban have also repeatedly been held by other western countries in Qatar. In Germany and at least four other western European capitals, key consulates are now controlled by the Taliban, not representatives of the former Afghan government.
Taliban officials have also sought cross-border infrastructure projects to boost the country’s fragile economy and diplomacy. Natural resources are another lure for overseas powers. Kabul has expanded the mining sector, attracting firms from neighbouring China and elsewhere.
China, which is worried about Islamic militancy on and around its south-western borders, has welcomed Taliban officials in recent years, and hosted talks when Afghanistan and Pakistan went to war earlier this year.
The Taliban are split, with deep disagreements on the ban on women’s education among other issues, but remain dominated by the most conservative factions. Recent laws have further reinforced repression, designating many religious minorities, including Shia Muslims, as heretics and imposing strict punishments to silence dissent.
Other new laws recognise only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women and facilitate the marriage of girls without their consent. 
Analysts do not believe the Taliban are likely to moderate their position in the near future and point to the continuing authority of Hibatullah Akhundzada, the reclusive and authoritarian cleric leader.
Ramin Mansoori, a researcher at the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Endowment who studies Afghan politics, said the Taliban’s priority was its domestic agenda.
“They are not going to make any significant concessions. Most of them don’t have an international perspective,” Mansoori said.

If the rest of the world caught up with Asia before inching ahead in the 21st century in the men’s game, the continent has never been the standard-bearer in the women’s. No Asian team has won an Olympic gold or a World Cup title in the combined 27 editions of these tournaments. In fact, in the 15 World Cups, only three times has an Asian team made the semifinals, with China’s run in 2002 being the most recent.
The Netherlands is the superpower in the women’s game, rattling off successive Olympic golds and World Cup titles. The rest of the world, including Argentina and Belgium, is trying to close the gap, without much success. China, too, has rediscovered its past glory in recent years and is now in with a shout.
India, meanwhile, has never been blessed with the abundance of talent available to its male counterpart. It has tasted modest success on the continent but has failed to make any serious dent on the world stage. For the women’s team, the battle often seems to be both on and off the pitch.
The World Cup arrives against a difficult backdrop for Indian hockey. A former national team captain has levelled allegations of sexual misconduct and criminal intimidation against a coach and Hockey India secretary general Bholanath Singh, respectively. Separately, the change in the colour of the team’s jersey has stirred its own controversy.
At one point, even qualification for the World Cup appeared to be in jeopardy following a woeful Pro League campaign that ended in relegation and the departure of the then head coach, Harendra Singh.
In January this year, HI brought in Sjoerd Marijne, who masterminded India’s joint-best finish (fourth) at a Summer Olympic Games in 2021, to arrest the decline. The Dutchman has made an instant impact, restoring work ethic, tactical discipline and belief in the group, while securing World Cup qualification and Pro League promotion.
Marijne sees the World Cup as a platform to test his ideas and sharpen the team’s conditioning ahead of the crucial Asian Games, with the bigger objective of returning to the Summer Olympics in two years’ time.
The immediate challenge is formidable. In its opening pool, India is grouped with China and England, both ranked above it, along with South Africa, the lowest-ranked side in the tournament. India was outplayed twice by China at last year’s Asia Cup under Harendra, while it failed to make the most of its chances in its loss to England in the final of the World Cup qualifiers in March.
Only the top two sides will progress to the second stage, and Marijne will know he has a difficult task on his hands. The performances and results in Australia and the Nations Cup, however, have provided a much-needed morale boost ahead of these crucial two months.
Forward Navneet Kaur’s dazzling skills and goal-scoring form over the last 12 months will be vital to India’s hopes. Marijne has called for greater efficiency in field goals, but there is a real lack of depth to support Navneet up front. India captain and midfielder Salima Tete will hope she can call on the experience of Savita, Nikki Pradhan, Sushila Chanu and Neha to step up alongside her.
If India somehow manages to get into the second round, things get harder still, with Australia and the Netherlands waiting alongside whichever of China or England advances.
The co-host and three-time defending champion, the Netherlands, remains a level above the chasing pack. Head coach Raoul Ehren, a long-time business associate of Marijne, has taken a serial winning side and made it near-unplayable. Adopting an intense counter-pressing style, the Oranje claimed a fourth successive Pro League crown, notching up 14 wins while losing just once in a shootout.
That pressing game has made it difficult for teams to break down its defence, which conceded just seven goals, 15 fewer than in the previous campaign.
Influential playmaker Xan de Waard, who is hanging up her stick at the end of the World Cup, will be instrumental to the pressing game. After a decorated career, she will have the opportunity to bow out in front of home supporters amid the Amstelveen summer, targeting a fourth World Cup crown.
In midfield partner Yibbi Jansen, the Dutch possess the most feared drag-flick specialist in the game. In the Pro League, she found the board 15 times from Penalty Corners, and opposition defences will need to work out a way to stop the Dutch’s key threat.
Across the Netherlands’ last three major competitions, only four teams have beaten it: Argentina, Belgium, India and Australia. Of those, only the South American and European nations managed to beat a near full-strength side.
Argentina’s win came in the 2024-25 Pro League, after which it followed up with a second-place finish, then repeated that runner-up spot in 2025-26.
Defender Agustina Gorzelany will be the one to watch from set pieces. She is lethal with her drag-flicks, and her tally of 29 goals from set plays is second only to Jansen’s 32 in the last two Pro League seasons.
Las Leonas are possibly the closest challengers to Dutch dominance. But after falling short against the Netherlands in the 2022 World Cup final and 2024 Olympics semifinal, they will know that their best might still not be enough.
Belgium, hosting the World Cup for the first time, will be another team to keep a close eye on. Under Ehren, who took charge in 2020, the Red Panthers went from a bottom-half side in the Pro League to a consistent top-half team, before making the Olympic semifinals for the first time in their history.
After Ehren left the post in 2024 on a sour note, Adam Commens, long embedded in the Belgian hockey set-up, stepped up to lead the side to successive third-place finishes in the Pro League.
Belgium will hope to cash in on any home advantage, even though it lost five of its eight matches at Wavre this year. It has the pace, skill and experience to trouble the field. Midfielder Alix Gerniers remains central to the side and will need support from fellow experienced players such as Michelle Struijk, Stephanie Vanden Borre and Judith Vandermeiren.
China will be the real dark horse after its stellar rise under Australian head coach Alyson Annan, who led the side to an Olympic runner-up finish sandwiched between Asian Games and Asia Cup titles.
The consistency has carried over against the best teams too, with China finishing fourth in the Pro League in each of the last two seasons.
Defence remains a concern after China shipped 19 goals in four games against the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium, though it has shown it can beat anyone on its day. Attacking play could be the bigger issue in the latter rounds, but midfielder Li Hong, who plays her club hockey in Amsterdam H&BC, will be keen to make her mark against the best in the world.
Mixed Pro League form leaves Germany, Australia and Spain as outsiders for the title. Unlike in 2022, there is no debutant this time, with Ireland, Scotland, Chile and South Africa bracing for a tough outing.

The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has reportedly suspended the licences of 14 “food business establishments” linked to quick commerce platforms Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart. As per news agency PTI, the licences were suspended after a state-wide inspection drive uncovered widespread food safety and hygiene violations at multiple dark stores. In total, the Maharashtra FDA reportedly inspected 86 dark stores selling and delivering food through online platforms. Five establishments, each of Zepto and Blinkit, and two others linked to Swiggy Instamart had their licences suspended. In addition to the 14 licence suspensions, the regulator also issued 60 improvement notices and ordered the temporary stoppage of operations at one facility. The clampdown comes as Maharashtra FDA has tightened its noose around quick commerce platforms and eateries across the state. Earlier this week, the licence of a Blinkit facility in Mumbai’s Malad West was suspended after officials discovered an extensive cockroach infestation and several other food-safety violations during an inspection. A day later, Karnataka’s Food Safety and Drug Administration Department also sealed a major Zepto warehouse in Bengaluru’s Hoskote. The department also flagged unhygienic conditions and food safety violations at the facility. However, this is not the first time that these platforms have come under scrutiny. Maharashtra authorities had raided Zepto and Blinkit’s dark stores last year, while Telangana officials had also raided a Blinkit warehouse in 2024. As if this was not enough, the government informed the Parliament yesterday that more than 5.1 Lakh complaints were registered against ecommerce and quick commerce platforms on the National Consumer Helpline in 2025. Of this, 5,774 complaints were registered against Zepto, while Blinkit clocked 5,102 complaints. The crackdown comes as quick commerce giants continue to aggressively expand their dark store networks. As of June 2026, Blinkit operated 2,443 active dark stores across 300 cities, while Swiggy Instamart’s network comprised 1,171 dark stores across 131 cities. Meanwhile, Zepto had 1,139 dark stores across 66 cities at the end of March 2026.

Stating that mushrooming instances of hotels and eateries stocking and supplying expired food cannot be treated as stray violations of regulatory norms, the High Court of Karnataka has said that such instances “reveal a disturbing malaise creeping into the hospitality industry, where the hunger for profit has, in some cases, overshadowed the basic obligation to safeguard consumers’ health.”
Justice M. Nagaprasanna made these observations while refusing to quash a criminal case against an expired food recycling firm for allegedly selling expired item by relabelling them.
The court’s observations assumes importance amid recent raids by authorities on hotels and other establishments.
Taking note of recent enforcement actions that have disclosed alleged rackets employing methods to push expired products back into the stream of commerce, the court said increasing recurrence of such discoveries must awaken the regulatory machinery.
“Surprise inspections cannot remain occasional exercises undertaken only after public outrage erupts. Food safety requires constant vigilance, rigorous traceability of expired stock, prompt destruction of articles unfit for consumption and consequences sufficiently stringent to ensure that treating the consumer’s health as expendable never becomes a profitable business model,” the court observed.
Pointing out that a customer who eats in hotels with an implicit faith that what reaches his plate is wholesome, hygienic and fit for human consumption, the court said that the customer cannot be expected to enter the kitchen and scrutinise every packet for its expiry date or examine the origin of every ingredient before taking a morsel. “Customers’ trust is the very foundation for food industry,” the court said.

Bedbug infestations are on the rise and they could be more dangerous to humans than previously thought
Bedbugs can be year-round problems but they have traditionally thrived in the summer, forcing victims to seek out costly treatment
Sometimes called the vampires of the insect world, bedbugs spend daylight hours hidden in crevices before emerging at night to feed on human blood.
While generations of children have grown up with a nursery rhyme warning them to sleep tight and avoid their bite, recent trends offer little reassurance: infestations are rising, reaching their seasonal peak during the warmer months.
Adding to concerns, some scientists think the pests could potentially transmit the antibiotic-resistant superbug MRSA.
For centuries, the parasites have tormented households and prompted public alarm. In 2018, New York City authorities removed at least six municipal buses from service following reports of bedbugs crawling on seats. A similar disruption occurred in Paris in 2023, where sightings in cinemas, trains, and buses generated widespread concern ahead of the 2024 Olympic Games.
"They certainly are out there," said Christopher Hayes, a North Carolina State University assistant professor who has been bitten by bedbugs more than 50 times in the course of research.
"And if you're unaware, if you're not on top of your game, it's easy to bring them into your home."
Bedbugs really do come out at night
Roughly the size of an apple seed, the reddish-brown insects are estimated by some researchers to date back to the era of the dinosaurs. However, they are best known for their persistent ability to cohabit with and feed upon human hosts.
Capable of squeezing into narrow gaps in furniture, they also hide in clothing, linens and mattresses. Though difficult to spot directly, their presence is frequently betrayed by small, dark excrement stains.
While bedbugs remain a year-round threat, they historically flourish during the summer. They typically emerge under the cover of darkness, crawling onto exposed skin and utilizing a beaklike body part to pierce human tissue and siphon blood over several minutes.
Because the bite itself is painless, physical reactions vary significantly. Some individuals develop itchy, red welts within a day or two, while others show no physical response at all.
This absence of symptoms presents a distinct hazard, as individuals unaware of ongoing bites can quickly find themselves dealing with a severe infestation.
Bedbugs’ threat to humans
The health impacts of unmanaged infestations were highlighted in a 2020 French medical journal case report.
The paper documented a 70-year-old man living alone in a Paris suburb who collapsed on the street. Upon admission to a hospital emergency department, doctors diagnosed him with dementia alongside severe anemia resulting from prolonged blood loss.
Medical staff discovered bedbugs actively feeding on his neck, head, and shoulders. A subsequent inspection of his apartment revealed thousands of the insects inhabiting his mattress, walls, flooring, and curtains.
Historically, experts considered bedbugs incapable of transmitting infectious diseases between humans. Their internal anatomy and digestive processes were believed to prevent pathogens from passing on effectively, according to Chow-Yang Lee, an entomologist at the University of California at Riverside.
However, a 2023 study conducted by researchers at the University of South Dakota challenged this assumption. Utilizing artificial skin and blood capsules, the experiment demonstrated that bedbugs could contract MRSA during one feeding session and subsequently spread it during a later meal.
Further research is required to confirm whether bedbugs actually transmit MRSA to humans in real-world settings, noted study co-author Jose Pietri, now based at Purdue University. Nevertheless, "it changes the perspective of what bedbugs do, in terms of public health," Pietri said.
Bedbugs’ resistance to pesticides
Bedbug populations across developed nations experienced a sharp decline following World War II due to the widespread application of the chemical pesticide DDT. In 1972, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency banned DDT for most applications, citing evidence of environmental harm and potential human health risks.
By that time, bedbugs had already begun developing immunity to the chemical. According to Lee, growing insecticide resistance has driven a sustained resurgence of the pests in recent decades.
Determining the exact scale of the resurgence remains difficult. Pest control firms publish annual rankings of U.S. cities with the highest infestation rates—with Orkin currently placing Chicago at No. 1, while Terminix identifies Philadelphia as having the biggest problem. However, these lists rely on corporate customer call volumes rather than rigorous scientific surveys.
Many infestations occur within public or low-income housing developments, where property managers may not engage the commercial firms compiling those statistics, Lee noted in an email.
How to protect yourself from the pests and treat them
Pest management specialists emphasize that prevention is the most effective defense, urging individuals to avoid bringing the insects into their living spaces in the first place.
Travelers frequently transport bedbugs home from lodging establishments. Prior to unpacking in a hotel room, guests should inspect the premises by pulling back bedsheets and mattress covers to check for live insects or fecal spots.
Luggage should never be placed directly on beds or carpeted floors near sleeping areas; instead, bags can be stored in light-colored trash bags or placed inside the bathtub. Upon returning home, suitcases should be unpacked outdoors, and all laundry transferred directly to the washing machine and dryer.
Secondhand furniture and household items also serve as common vectors. Hayes advised visually inspecting all pre-owned goods and treating them prior to bringing them indoors. Experts recommend vacuuming, steaming, or applying heat to furniture, or isolating items in a garage or storage unit for several days.
For clothing, items should be laundered and run through a high-heat dryer cycle for an hour. Non-washable items like shoes can be placed in a freezer for a week "to make sure that everything in there that could be alive is taken care of," Hayes said.
For those dealing with an active infestation, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency provides self-treatment instructions, though the process is labor-intensive and requires systematically sealing harborage spaces and treating affected goods.
The guidance also warns against common missteps.
"You can't just blast random chemicals and expect it's going to work because there's a fairly high likelihood that they'll be resistant to some of the first-line insecticides," Pietri said.
Consequently, experts strongly recommend hiring licensed professional exterminators experienced in bedbug eradication, though services can cost hundreds or thousands of dollars.
Alternative control methods beyond chemical treatments exist. For instance, silica dust formulations work by absorbing the moisture from a bedbug's body, causing fatal dehydration.
Thermal treatments using sustained dry heat are also highly effective, destroying both eggs and adult insects. However, the process requires maintaining temperatures of at least 122 degrees Fahrenheit (50 degrees Celsius) and carries a risk of damaging personal property, meaning it must be carried out by professionals.
"I think the biggest piece of advice is just people shouldn't panic," Hayes said. "They just need to take action. If you think you have bedbugs, don't wait to deal with it."

Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
- Published
Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.
But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.
Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.
Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.
There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.
The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.
The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.
We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.
Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".
We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.
It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.
In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.
One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers - the case that Mathipa had been investigating.
After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.
South Africa: Anatomy of a cover-up
Africa Eye uncovers a disturbing story of power, secrecy and murder.

Episode two of the film available from 24 August.
The case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.
It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.
Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks.
Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.
We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.
Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.
Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.
The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.
We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.
He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.
He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.
The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.
The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.
The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.
At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.
Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.
So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.
Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.
They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.
Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.
We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.
When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.
When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer.
"When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.
On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.
Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.
When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.
He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.
And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.
This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.
New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.
Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".
Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.
The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.
All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.
Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.
The military has refused to hand them over.
In July, their lawyers cited mental health treatment for their absence. Three years after Mathipa's killing, no trial date has been set.
Meanwhile, Abadigga's body has never been found.
"[Mathipa] was barking up the right tree. He was taking on the right lion," Vreugdenburg says of the late detective.
Mathipa's daughter Basetsana puts it starkly: "We need justice. I'm never going to see my dad anymore... Why my dad? Because he was doing his job."

Your car's dash cam might be illegal in some states — Here's how to check
Before you head out on a road trip, make sure you won't be accidentally breaking the law.
Dash cams are useful for so many reasons. They capture footage while you're driving, and some record motion even when you're parked. The footage one captures can prove invaluable in the event of an accident or break-in, since the recording can be presented as objective evidence. Yes, dash cam footage that is captured in a public place and can be authenticated should hold up in court. That's the main purpose of using one. But along with safety and record-keeping, you could use one to monitor driving habits of teens, capture other incidents that happen to occur in its view, like road rage or fraud (think someone jumping in front of the car to claim injury), or even just record the beautiful scenery on your drive. While dash cams are legal in every state, there are specific rules about how you can use them, where to position them and even their size that vary from state to state.
Even if you know the laws in your own state, if you're driving out of state for a road trip, it's important to know the laws in others. The last thing you want is to be driving with a piece of equipment positioned or being used illegally in your car.
The rules around dash cam use
The rules when using dash cams in different states vary considerably. The simplest and most logical rule is about positioning, requiring that a dash cam not obstruct the view of the driver. This rule explicitly applies in Alaska, Arizona, California, Florida, Hawaii, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Missouri, Nevada, North Carolina, Utah, and Vermont. However, it's a logical rule you should follow everywhere. Some of those states have specific rules about camera placement beyond ensuring it doesn't obstruct your view. In California, for example, a dash cam has to be mounted in a seven-inch square on the lower corner of the windshield, away from the driver, a five-inch square in the corner nearest to the driver, or in a five-inch square in the upper-center. Meanwhile, in Illinois, a dash cam must be in the bottom corner of the windshield on the passenger side. In some states, like Alabama, Delaware and Louisiana, the dash cam can't even be mounted on the windshield at all, while states like Pennsylvania and Minnesota forbid having anything mounted on a windshield, period. In these cases, it has to be mounted on the dashboard. So, it's important to check positioning rules in your state.
There are also size requirements, with most states requiring that a dash cam be smaller than five inches. Some states, like Hawaii, permit dash cams as large as 7 inches, while in Indiana, it can be no more than 4 square inches.
When it comes to use, in 13 states, you can't record conversations in a vehicle unless every passenger in it consents. The 13 states where this two-party or all-party consent rule applies are California, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Washington. Other states have rules about recording that you should pay attention to as well. In states like New York and many others, recording video from a dash cam is fine. But audio conversations are not permitted without at least one party's consent. This might not matter much for family road trips, but it's something to consider if you're traveling with colleagues, carpooling with others outside your family, or are a ride-share driver.
How to prepare for a drive
Because there's no single federal rule about dash cam usage and installation, you need to be cognizant of the specific rules in any state you're traveling to or even through to ensure that you adhere to the local laws. Your best bet is to use the most stringent rules of any of the 50 states and adhere to them to avoid problems while you travel. California is a good benchmark to use, since it's widely considered to have among the strictest laws for dash cam placement and usage.
The good news is that dash cams in general are legal to have and use in every state, so simply having one won't get you nabbed for doing anything wrong. Just make sure it doesn't obstruct your view in any way, and get a small 4- or 5-inch model. Consider mounting it on the dashboard instead of the windshield if you're worried about positioning. Another option is to mount it behind the rearview mirror. If placed here, the dash cam doesn't obstruct any part of your view that isn't already obstructed by the mirror itself. Use a mount that's easy to remove and reposition if you must do so to adhere to local law as you're passing through.
Before you head out on the road, if you're crossing state lines, map your route. Then check the state Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) website to see the specific rules in each state when it comes to dash cams. From there, position the dash cam according to the strictest rule for visibility. If necessary, disable audio recording if you're entering a state with two-party consent rules, or make clear to everyone in the vehicle that audio is being recorded. With proper preparation, you can get the most out of your dash cam and make sure you're following the law, no matter where you are.
