The findings contradict the police’s official version. While Siwan Police stated that only four rounds were fired from an AK-47, Alt News verified at least nine rounds fired from AK-47 rifles at two locations, in addition to two separate instances of pistol fire. The footage also shows more than one police officer firing towards protesters.
Speaking to Scroll, injured Akash Yadav said he was shot by a policeman wielding a pistol and claimed he could identify the officer who fired at him. He also alleged that the police may have pressured him to change his statement. So far, however, action has been taken only against one constable.
Police Firing in Jehanabad on July 23
The firing in Siwan was not an isolated incident. Two days earlier, on July 23, police also opened fire while dispersing protesters in Bihar’s Jehanabad district during demonstrations over alleged irregularities in the NEET examination.
Alt News found videos of the incident recorded from two different angles, showing police personnel firing sub-machine gun carbines towards protesters. Political fallout
The Siwan firing quickly triggered a political storm.
Leader of Opposition in the Bihar assembly Tejashwi Yadav raised the issue on July 25, accusing the police of opening fire on students with AK-47 rifles. The following day, he visited the injured victims in hospital.
Samajwadi Party MP Akhilesh Yadav also questioned the use of AK-47 rifles against unarmed protesters, asking who had authorised the deployment of such a lethal weapon during the demonstrations in Siwan.
Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi later spoke to injured Akash Yadav over the phone and assured him of assistance. During the conversation, Akash said he had been shot in the shoulder, leaving one of his hands impaired. He also told Gandhi that he had lost his mother in childhood, lived with his father and had no siblings. Referring to the Siwan incident, Rahul Gandhi alleged that the state’s response to student protests had become increasingly violent and criticised the use of AK-47 rifles against demonstrators.

The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has taken action against a Parle Agro-linked Velocity Express warehouse in Mumbai after finding expired beverages and seizing stock valued at ₹99,970. The regulator has also suspended the licence of the facility near Chembur Naka in the Gadkari area, according to NDTV Profit. IAS Tukaram Mundhe-led Maharashtra FDA has stepped up its food safety drive. The confiscated products included expired batches of Appy Fizz, Frooti and Candy Juice. The FDA barred the expired stock from being sold, moved or distributed further. The inspection was conducted through the night by a team of eight FDA officials. The warehouse, situated in Prayag Nagar on LU Gadkari Marg in Chembur’s Washinaka area, was inspected from around 6 pm on August 13 until 5 am on August 14, according to reports. Following the seizure, officials sealed the warehouse and detained two vehicles used for transporting the products. Authorities said no food items from the facility would be allowed to be sold or transported until further instructions, the report noted. The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) carried out a statewide inspection campaign on Thursday, August 13, targeting food businesses operating through online delivery platforms. During the exercise, officials inspected 86 establishments across Maharashtra. The regulator ordered one business to stop operations immediately and served improvement notices on 60 establishments. It also suspended 14 food business licences with immediate effect. The suspended licences included five each associated with Blinkit and Zepto, two linked to Instamart, seven belonging to Bhagwati Store and one held by Swinsta Ent Pvt. Limited, according to an official statement. The inspection drive also covered milk and dairy products. Officials seized 698 kg of dairy stock worth ₹34,302, the FDA said. The department also initiated criminal action against the sale, distribution and transportation of prohibited products, including pan masala and gutkha. Ten FIRs were registered, nine people were arrested and banned food products valued at ₹46,76,631 were confiscated, according to the release. Moreover, officials seized around 1,270 kg of other food products, including milk and dairy goods, bakery products and edible oil, with an estimated value of ₹1,29,762. The FDA separately inspected 109 hotels, restaurants, dhabas and other food establishments. Improvement notices were issued to 49 businesses, while the licences of four food establishments were suspended, the department said. It mentioned the combined value of the confiscated products, covering both other food commodities and prohibited items, was ₹46,89,603. The department added that its special inspection campaign involved 15 raids. Separately, the FDA on Tuesday suspended the food-business licences of four Domino’s Pizza outlets run by Jubilant FoodWorks Ltd. after inspections found several violations related to food safety and hygiene. Fun, retro style that appeals to both teens and adults. Well-priced. UL-2271 and 2849 certified. Frame triangle is big enough to attach a folding lock.
TIRED
Seat is cheap-feeling and very hard. No suspension and no way to carry cargo. Range takes a huge hit on hills. No battery IP rating for water resistance. Not a “real” BMX.
Though I’ve since gotten used to it, every time I ride the electric blue Joe Rev 2 electric BMX, people stare. Their heads turn as they drive past, eyes narrowed. “Is that an adult riding a BMX bike?” I imagine the thought process going. “Why is it so fast? Why is it so big?” These are valid questions, and they all have the same answer: Because it’s fun.
In fact, my entire family has taken turns riding this bike all over town for the past four weeks, testing it up and down hills, taking it on grocery runs, and even staying out riding until the battery drained. The verdict? The Joe Rev 2 may not be the smoothest ride, but for the price, it’s a unique and worthwhile option for basic cruising and casual riding.
All Eyes on Me
Photograph: Kat Merck
California-based Retrospec specializes in affordable outdoor toys; primarily paddleboards, longboards, bikes, and no-frills ebikes like the foldable Judd Rev 2, which WIRED contributing reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani wrote “captures the vibe of being a 12-year-old kid and riding your bike more than anything I’ve ridden in some time.”
The entry-level Joe Rev was created in this same spirit—a full-sized, BMX-inspired frame with fun color options (electric blue, matte gray), 3-inch tan wall balloon tires, and those unmistakable handlebars. There are no apps or fancy readouts, no lights, and no shocks. Just five levels of pedal assist and a throttle attached to a single-speed drivetrain and 750-watt rear-hub motor.
Photograph: Kat Merck
“No cream, no sugar” is even printed on the chain stays, lest one forget the minimalist doctrine. On the plus side, this lack of bones allows the Joe Rev 2 to weigh in on the lighter side at 56 pounds.
This is the second iteration of the original Joe Rev, which is still available (for now) at the sale price of $1,200. The Rev 2 sports a bigger 500 Wh battery with a listed 60-mile range (up from 48 miles) and an updated display. Namely, a 2-by-2.5-inch LCD screen on the left handlebar displaying power level, battery life, and speed, as opposed to the original’s bare-basic hub with buttons.
The battery can be quickly locked and unlocked from the bottom of the frame with a key and charges from red to full green in several hours; it weighs about 7 pounds, so it’s easy enough to carry in a backpack, though at 18 inches long, it could be a tight fit if your bag is already packed.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
Teen Spirit
At one point during the testing period, my almost-14-year-old son, who is 5’ 10” and 145 pounds, took the Joe Rev 2 out on a full battery to see how long he could ride in our town of hills. We were all surprised to find he hit the red “recharge” light in about 20 miles. It shouldn't have been too much of a shock, given that the hills were steep, and he was using the throttle primarily. But it is a good reminder that, like all ebikes, the Joe Rev 2’s range will vary dramatically depending on rider weight, speed, and conditions.
Interestingly, there’s an ominous warning sticker on the Joe Rev’s frame that states no one under 16 is to ride this bike. It does have pedals and a maximum speed of 20 mph, making it a Class 2 ebike—legal in many, if not, most states for kids under 16.
When I asked Retrospec if there was anything specific about the Joe Rev 2 that would preclude younger teens from riding it, their rep told me the company “follows the most stringent regulations across the markets where their ebikes are sold. As a result, their minimum recommended rider age is 16. If local laws permit younger riders, such as a 12-year-old, it is ultimately up to parents or guardians to determine whether their child has the maturity, experience, and ability to safely operate an ebike.”
However, an adult-sized, mature 14- or 15-year-old could be a gray area. My son is allowed to ride the Joe Rev 2 occasionally, but not regularly. If you decide to go this route, know this bike was deemed acceptable by several teens in my orbit, though stylistically a couple notches below the e-moto-style frames popularized by brands like MacFox.
How It Rides
As is typical with ebikes, some assembly of the Joe Rev 2 is required upon arrival. Chiefly, attaching the wheels, pedals, and handlebars, for which it comes with a generously sized set of hex wrenches. The first night, it took a couple of tries to get the front wheel seated properly—there was a slight wobble during my husband’s inaugural ride around the block, but after further tightening, it has not resurfaced. The brakes are mechanical disc with 180 mm rotors, which also occasionally needed tightening, but otherwise caused no issues during the testing period.
My own first ride was on a flat surface, around the parking lot of my son’s former elementary school. I found that the five levels of pedal assist kick in quickly and almost forcefully; the throttle is an easy-to-use thumb switch located on the left handlebar. The frame feels like a good size for my height (5’ 6”), and the whole setup was easy to parse in just a couple of minutes.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Aside from the lack of suspension—you will feel every bump—my only major complaint is the seat. In fact, my butt still hurts as I write this from even a short ride yesterday. The Joe Rev 2's seat is hard, plasticky, and small—definitely worth swapping out if you’re going to be commuting on this or otherwise riding it daily.
My 5’ 8” husband rides the Joe Rev 2 to the grocery store several times a week, an activity he greatly enjoys, and over time we’ve found ourselves wishing there were an easy way to carry cargo, such as the ability to bolt on a basket or saddlebags. To be fair, though, I’m not sure it would ultimately be worth the reduction in range, though the bike does have a payload capacity of 350 pounds. We do, however, greatly appreciate the open space in the frame to attach a folding lock. (We went with the Seatlylock FoldyLock for $90).
One thing I have not yet been able to test is the water resistance. I live in western Washington state, where it rains nine months out of the year, and the Joe Rev 2's battery is mounted at the bottom of the down tube, where it could easily be splashed. There's no given IP rating for water resistance, so while I'm sure the battery housing can handle a light, occasional spray, riding the bike on a super-rainy day would make me nervous.
It also bears mentioning that if you're hoping for a real BMX bike with which you can do tricks, the Joe Rev 2 is not that. Insofar as being a BMX, the only quality seems to be the handlebars. Nothing about it feels nimble, and at this weight, you’re not taking it to the skate park—the only jumps and rail hops happening are in your imagination.
However, if you do happen to lose control of yourself and break something, the Joe Rev 2 is UL 2849 Certified for the electrical system and UL 2271 Certified for the battery, meaning that, unlike with many other internet-purchased direct-to-consumer bikes, your local bike shop may be able to repair it. Though this depends heavily on the type of repair needed; it’s worth calling to be sure.

Jharkhand student protesters intensified their agitation in Ranchi on Saturday, with leaders giving the Hemant Soren government until August 18 to address alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations or face a mass march towards the Chief Minister’s residence on August 20.
The protest by JPSC-JSSC aspirants has now entered its 22nd day, with students demanding the cancellation of the JSSC-CGL and JPSC 11th–13th examinations and an independent investigation into alleged irregularities.
Student leader Ravindra Paswan said the movement would enter a more aggressive phase if the government failed to respond to the demands. Invoking revolutionary figure Bhagat Singh, he said protesters were no longer willing to rely solely on peaceful demonstrations.
“Today, we are changing the course of our movement. We have had enough of Gandhian methods and peaceful protests. They simply aren't listening. We are now going to adopt the path of Bhagat Singh. We are prepared to face bullets, even if the government shoots us in the chest, for this cause. We will continue our agitation until our demands are met.”
Paswan said the protesters had issued an ultimatum to the government, demanding action by August 18.
“We are issuing an ultimatum to the government: meet our demands by the 18th. Cancel the JSSC results, scrap all exams conducted by the TDPL agency, and order a CBI inquiry into all of them.”
He warned that failure to meet the demands would trigger a larger mobilisation on August 20.
“If this is not done, lakhs of students and youths from Jharkhand will lay siege to the Chief Minister's residence on the 20th...”
The protesters are seeking cancellation of the JSSC-CGL and JPSC 11th–13th examinations. They have also called for a probe by the Central Bureau of Investigation or a panel of retired judges from outside Jharkhand.
Another student leader, Piyush Kumar, said protesters would begin burning effigies at district headquarters from Sunday.
“We are going to burn the effigies of the Hemant Soren-led Jharkhand government, Chief Minister Hemant Soren himself, Rahul Gandhi, and all the parties supporting them.”
Kumar also referred to the proposed August 20 Assembly gherao, describing the earlier protest outside the Vidhan Sabha as only a “preview” of the next phase of the agitation.
The protests have centred on allegations of irregularities in recruitment examinations and demands for greater transparency in Jharkhand's government recruitment system.
The agitation has also drawn attention to the condition of JLKM leader Devendra Mahto, who has reportedly been on hunger strike for 14 days.
Mahto has alleged that police prevented him from leaving Sadar Hospital to participate in the protest march. Videos circulating on social media purportedly show Mahto in a scuffle with security personnel while attempting to leave the hospital. The circumstances of the incident could not be independently verified.
Protesters say their demands extend beyond the disputed examinations and concern wider issues of equal opportunities and public confidence in the state's recruitment system.
The Jharkhand government has acknowledged concerns over the recruitment process.
In his Independence Day address, Chief Minister Hemant Soren said allegations surrounding recruitment examinations had shaken the trust of an entire generation. He assured students that claims of irregularities would be investigated impartially and that those found guilty would face legal action.
At the same time, Soren cautioned against declaring anyone guilty without evidence, saying any action must be based on facts.
“Merely apprehending the guilty is not the solution,” Soren said, stressing the need for systemic changes to prevent manipulation of examinations.
Soren outlined measures including a time-bound annual examination calendar, technology-secured examinations, timely publication of answer keys and OMR sheets, and multiple levels of accountability in the recruitment process.
With the August 18 deadline approaching, the Jharkhand government now faces the prospect of a significantly larger student mobilisation in Ranchi if the protesters' demands remain unresolved.

Barely 200 kilometres from Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, where students and youth of the country came together in thousands to demand educational reform in India, a notice was served on a university, declaring that most of its built structures were illegal and would soon be demolished.
The institute, Mohammad Ali Jauhar University (MAJU), located in Rampur, Uttar Pradesh, was established in 2006 by the Mohammad Ali Jauhar Trust, founded by Azam Khan, one of the founding members of the Samajwadi Party. Khan, a former MP and 10-time MLA from Rampur, was one of the most powerful politicians in the region until the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) came to power in 2017.
MAJU is recognised by the University Grants Commission (UGC) and holds minority institution status. However, its staff and student body comprise people from varied backgrounds and religious communities, vice-chancellor (VC) Prof Zaheeruddin and students themselves told Alt News.
On July 15, the Rampur Development Authority (RDA) issued a notice to the university declaring that 38 of its 40 buildings were illegal and would be demolished within 20 days. The university was told to carry out the demolition itself, failing which, the RDA would carry out the demolition while charging the university expenses. However, the demolition order was stayed on July 28 by the chairman of RDA and the Moradabad divisional commissioner, Aunjaney Kumar Singh, till August 10.
Only a day after the notice, on July 16, a ‘counselling camp’ was set up outside the university’s main gate, the VC said. On the same day, the UP Public Works Department (PWD) declared an internal road belonging to the campus as a public road while installing signage, he alleged.
On July 27, Alt News visited the 475-acre campus on the first day of the semester. The buildings — designed, according to the VC, in the image of the White House and Turkish mosques — looked grand but lifeless as several structures stood half-built with construction abandoned mid-way. An air of uncertainty loomed over the campus and on the faces of the very few students who were present.
Some students, who were protesting the demolition, told Alt News that a student delegation had met the DM and sought written assurance that the buildings would not be demolished until the matter was decided by the Supreme Court. The DM gave only a verbal assurance and declined to put it in writing, they said.
‘All Buildings Constructed Before RDA’s Jurisdiction’
Zaheeruddin, who served as pro-VC and chairman of the department of law at Aligarh Muslim University (AMU) before joining MAJU in April 2025, said that a prior show-cause notice had been issued on June 28 seeking a response from the university on the demolitions.
The university’s response was deemed unsatisfactory by the RDA, which called for a physical meeting on July 14, attended by registrar SN Salam and the institute’s legal counsel. The authority only heard their arguments for five minutes, and the next day, the demolition order arrived, said Zaheeruddin, adding: “This was completely unexpected for us. Our classes were running, admissions were fully underway. Compared to the past two years, more admissions were happening this year.”
The VC told Alt News the 38 buildings were constructed before 2016, when the university grounds fell under the gram panchayat, not the RDA. The RDA’s jurisdiction was extended to cover the land only through a notification in September 2024, he said, asserting that the authority is retrospectively taking action against buildings. “All buildings they have mentioned were constructed by 2016, when RDA had no presence in this area at all,” he said.
He further highlighted that multiple regulatory bodies — UGC, Bar Council of India, paramedical and nursing councils — have inspected and approved the university’s infrastructure over the years as part of their accreditation process.
Missing Paperwork & The 2019 Raid
The VC, however, did not want to show the approved maps to prove the buildings’ legality citing legal proceedings. “The matter is before both the divisional commissioner and the Allahabad high court. The university’s lawyers have advised against discussing legal specifics,” he said.
On the other hand, Salam, the registrar, offered a different explanation for the missing paperwork. He claimed that during a state-ordered raid in 2019, when police forces were deployed on campus, large quantities
of documents were seized. “They took so many documents, and we don’t know where they took them or find out which documents they took,” he said.
Salam recounted the 2019 raid, “As police and district officials raided the campus, the VC was confined to one floor, the registrar to another, the accounts staff locked elsewhere. There were media reports that around 8,000 books stolen from a 200-year-old madrassa had been recovered from the university. But when the matter reached court, only 26 books were produced.”
Both the VC and registrar claimed that during the raid, several books were destroyed, many of which were hand-written manuscripts. They also claimed that 42 large cupboards, purchased from Kolkata, with receipts and transport documents, were shown as stolen property. Alt News could not independently verify the claims made by the VC and the registrar on the 2019 raid.
The Sudden ‘Counselling Camp’
Exacerbating the adminstration’s and students’ worries after the notice was served, was the sudden counselling camp, allegedly set up the very next day to encourage students to enroll in other universities.
Among those at the camp were officials from Guru Jambheshwar University, Moradabad — a state university whose campus construction began in March 2024, currently operating from a temporary campus with just two rooms built, and teachers from Raza Degree College, Rampur. Their task, the VC said, was to inform prospective students that MAJU would soon be demolished and that they should apply for admission at Guru Jambheshwar University.
“I felt terrible, they were maligning us right in front of us, sitting outside our campus. I was shocked that government teachers were doing this and the district magistrate had set up the camp while we are still a functioning university,” Zaheeruddin lamented.
Arguing that the counselling camp amounted to contempt of court, he mentioned that the administration wrote to the Rampur DM citing a 2019 high court stay order that specifically ordered that students and staff of the university must not be harassed. The camp was removed after two days, on July 18 evening.
The Students’ Plight
When Alt News visited the campus, the students, now thrust into indefinite anxiety over their futures, were sitting in protest in front of the main gate, demanding that the RDA withdraws the demolition. “We are protesting since July 18 because RDA should withdraw this order. There are 3,000-4,000 students studying here, don’t snatch the pen from their hands,” said a 5th-year student from Panipat, Haryana.
Students echoed the administration’s account on the ‘pattern’ of state action which haunted their campus. Every year during admissions, they said, new action or rumours would surface, discouraging parents and prospective students. “Every year, fear is planted in children’s hearts that the university will be shut down,” said another student.
A student from Bareilly said his brother studied at MAJU between 2014 and 2017. After that, the perception in his area was that the university had already shut down. When he arrived for admission in 2015, he was urged not to enrol by several people in and around the area, with claims that the fees were too high and the university could collapse at any time.
The students further claimed that district officials attempted to curb their protest as the SDM arrived at the protest site on July 18 around 10 PM with policemen and asked the students to move their protest inside the campus, away from the main gate. District-level intelligence wing officials also called several parents, urging them to get their children to stop protesting, students alleged.
The students said they raised the issue with the district administration, which assured them that such pressure tactics would not be applied. Another protesting student mentioned that he had written twice to Saurav Das, the chief spokesperson of the Cockroach Janta Party, but had received no response at the time writing this report.
Alt News is withholding the names of the students who spoke to us in order to protect their identity.
RDA Officials Evade Queries
When we reached out to the RDA, we were re-routed through four different officials. We contacted RDA’s vice-chairman Ajay Kumar Dwivedi, also the district magistrate of Rampur, under whose name the July 15 notice was issued. His personal assistant, Ankush, directed us to the RDA secretary, Nitin Madan. The secretary, after answering some of our questions, directed us to the tehsildar, Ranveer Singh, who spoke briefly and redirected us to RDA assistant engineer Manoj Sisodia.
According to every official, only two of the 40 buildings had approved maps, obtained from the panchayat before RDA’s jurisdiction was extended to the area. The remaining 38, they said, had no approval from any authority — the Zila Panchayat, gram panchayat, or RDA. This formed the basis of the demolition notice, they said.
Upon being asked whether the matter could be resolved through compounding, a process where illegal construction is regularised by paying a fine and obtaining retrospective approval, Singh said it had been considered but rejected because the land use at the university site is not permissible under RDA’s current master plan. Sisodia, on the other hand, said that the university had never submitted a compounding proposal to RDA. However, the VC told Alt News that the institute believed that compounding was something RDA would initiate.
Further, we asked whether RDA had issued demolition notices to any other structures in the 62 villages that came under its jurisdiction since September 2024. Madan said “many have happened” without naming a single case. Ranveer Singh added “it keeps happening from time to time”, also offering no specifics. Sisodia eventually admitted that notices issued to other parties are “confidential and that the university’s case attracted attention only because it is a larger structure”.
“The university is in the wrong, but considering everything, the government, higher authorities, the courts, have taken their decision,” Sisodia said while acknowledging the dire condition of the students if the demolition is carried out.
The Azam Khan-Aunjaney Singh Connection
Parellel to all this runs another storied controversy between Azam Khan and Aunjaney Kumar Singh. During the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, complaints were filed by the then assistant development officer (panchayat), Anil Kumar Chauhan, and local BJP leader Akash Saxena against Khan for alleged hateful and provocative remarks against the then DM of Rampur, Aunjaney Kumar Singh, and other BJP leaders.
This led to Khan’s conviction in October 2022 with three years of imprisonment and his subsequent disqualification from the UP state assembly. His conviction was later overturned and he was acquitted by a higher court in Rampur.
Formerly an IAS officer of Sikkim cadre, Singh, hailing from Mau district in UP, notably has been serving as a government official in the state for 11 consecutive years now, and is presently on his sixth extension, which is set to end on August 14. Interestingly, in April last year, Singh accepted Khan’s plea against the imposition of Rs 20 crore fine in another case related to construction of MAJU.
According to Zaheeruddin, the demolition hearing, which was supposed to take place on August 3 at the court of divisional commissioner, has been postponed to August 10, bringing under scrutiny the apparent pendulum swing in the official relationship between Singh and Khan — from the district administration’s actions during Singh’s tenure as Rampur DM that culminated in Khan’s conviction, to subsequent administrative decisions that provided relief in matters concerning Khan’s university, and now the stay on the demolition proceedings.
The Unanswered Question
Beyond the missing approvals and the land use dispute, there is a deeper contradiction that neither the university nor the RDA addressed. During the April 2025 hearing concerning the Rs 20 crore labour cess fine, Khan had argued before the divisional commissioner that 10 of MAJU’s buildings were constructed by the UP PWD and UP Nirman Nigam using MP/MLA development funds.
Khan had then received relief after the divisional commissioner’s court nullified the cess fine imposed by the assistant labour commissioner (ALC) of Rampur. The same court, under the same authority of Singh, has now served a demolition notice to the institute. A pertinent question emerges: If state agencies built these structures with public funds, how did construction proceed without the approved maps?
Four government offices, multiple courts, contradictory bureaucratic positions and years of litigation have turned MAJU into a case study in administrative uncertainty. Whether the buildings ultimately stand or fall will be decided in court. Until then, it is not politicians or officials who bear the immediate cost of this prolonged impasse, but thousands of students who continue to attend classes while wondering if the campus they study in will still exist by the time they graduate.

Actor Arjan Bajwa has reflected on the meaning of independence, saying that personal freedom is closely linked to having the courage to make choices that may not always be understood by others. In a conversation on Independence Day, the actor spoke about taking unconventional decisions, dealing with criticism and remembering the sacrifices that made India's freedom possible.
EXCLUSIVE: Arjan Bajwa speaks on personal freedom to mark 80th Independence Day; says choosing your own path is an “act of courage and liberation”
Bajwa, known for films including Rustom, Fashion, Kabir Singh and Tamil film Bigil, as well as projects such as State of Siege: 26/11 and Demon Hunters, said choosing a different path can require considerable courage, particularly when it means going against what is expected. “To choose one's own path is, anyways, an act of courage because you are not following the herd and are trying to do something different,” he said.
According to Bajwa, unconventional choices can initially make a person appear out of place. However, he believes people's perception can change when they understand the reasons behind those decisions. “Maybe initially, people look at you as a black sheep or someone who's against the tide,” he said.
The actor added that standing by a decision can eventually inspire others to reconsider their own choices. “When one has chosen it for a good reason, the same people will follow you and call your act of choosing your path an act of courage and confidence,” Bajwa said.
Arjan Bajwa on moments of personal freedom
Bajwa said he has experienced situations in his own life where making a difficult choice or refusing to follow expectations gave him a sense of liberation. “Yes, of course, there have been many moments in my life where taking a strong decision, choosing a certain path, or even saying no when you are obligated to say yes has felt like an act of courage and liberation,” he said.
The actor was also asked about an Indian who has inspired him the most. While he acknowledged that India's history is filled with people from different fields who have influenced generations, he chose freedom fighter Bhagat Singh in the context of Independence Day. “India is such a great country that people from different walks of life have been inspirations for generations, so it's really difficult to pinpoint one person,” Bajwa said.
“But while I say that, since it is the month of Independence of India, I would say a heroic figure like Bhagat Singh has been an inspiration for our country and generations,” he added.
Arjan Bajwa remembers Bhagat Singh's sacrifice
For Bajwa, one of the most striking aspects of Bhagat Singh's story is the young age at which he chose to dedicate his life to India's freedom struggle. “A youngster making up his mind strongly and sacrificing his life for the country so that we deserve a better future and live with freedom and harmony is not an easy job or a regular person's state of mind,” he said.
The actor believes that remembering the sacrifices made by earlier generations is important to ensure that the freedoms enjoyed today are not taken for granted. While acknowledging that a single message cannot guarantee such awareness, he said remembering the cost of freedom is an important starting point. “Only if one message was enough for people to not take freedom for granted was possible,” Bajwa said.
He concluded by emphasising that the freedoms people experience today came after years of sacrifice and struggle. “What we have has been the result of a lot of blood, sweat, and struggle of our ancestors. So, let's keep their sacrifice in mind and not take every day, each moment of happiness, freedom, and positivity for granted in our lives,” Arjan said.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Indian Army to get kamikaze drones worth ₹1,577 crore amid push to be ‘global hub’
Given the growing impact of these systems on military operations, the drone purchases have been made under the ‘Buy Indian’ scheme.
The defence ministry on Friday signed two contracts worth ₹1,577 crore with Tata Advanced Systems Ltd and Nibe Pvt Ltd for loitering munitions (or kamikaze drones) and associated equipment to boost the Indian Army’s precision strike capabilities.
“The loitering munition system is critical equipment that can enhance the capability of artillery regiments and boost the overall operational effectiveness of the Indian Army,” the ministry said.
This comes as the army plans to induct tens of thousands of locally-made unmanned aerial systems and loitering munitions over the next five years to boost its battlefield capabilities, given the growing impact of these systems on military operations and how they have reshaped modern warfare as visible in ongoing global conflicts including the US-Israel war with Iran.

Global hub for drone manufacturing
“Procured from Indian vendors under the ‘Buy Indian’ scheme through a fast-track procedure, this initiative will further strengthen the vision of self-reliance in defence,” the ministry added while announcing the two deals.
The army’s requirement spans 80 different types of unmanned systems for specific roles including intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, precision strikes, munition dropping, air defence, jamming, mine warfare, data relay, and logistics, according to a Technology Roadmap for Unmanned Aerial Systems and Loitering Munitions unveiled in April. Defence minister Rajnath Singh earlier said India must take steps to position itself as a global hub for drone manufacturing by 2030.

The systems required by the army for surveillance include high altitude long endurance UAS (unmanned aerial systems), medium altitude long endurance UAS, high altitude pseudo satellites, and unmanned air littoral systems (UALs) for long/medium/short range surveillance, according to the roadmap.
The army is seeking loitering munitions to strike at long, medium and short ranges, drone swarms (for surveillance and strike), and FRV (first-person view) drones with strike capability. It also wants to deploy unmanned systems in special roles, including hunter-killer configured UALs, and systems with guided/unguided bombs. The roadmap aligns with India’s plans to raise a drone force under another roadmap, Defence Forces Vision 2047, which was released in March.

A-list festival acclaimed pics from some of Mexico’s most celebrated talent, many of them female and first-timers, make up this year’s line-up at the Morelia Film Festival (FICM).
Running October 16-25, the 24th FICM edition features such luminaries as actor-producer Diego Luna (“Andor”) in his fifth outing as a director in “Ashes,” which world premiered in Cannes and was picked up by Netflix for Latin America, Spain and Portugal. It’s co-produced by Animal de Luz, run by Inna Payan whose directorial debut “Liliana’s Invincible Summer” (co-helmed with Samuel Kishi) will stream on Netflix.
Also leading the pack of a dozen fiction features in competition for Morelia’s top Ojo Award, is Nicolas Pereda’s wry ‘Everything Else is Noise.” (“Lo demás es ruido”), acquired ahead of its debuts at the Toronto Film Festival (TIFF) and the New York Film Festival (NYFF) by U.S.-based distributor Pragda; Rodrigo Plá’s “The Newcomers” (“Los Nuevos”), a Patra Spanou pick-up soon after its world premiere at Locarno’s Kids Screenings and Fernanda Tovar’s feature debut “Sad Girlz,” snagged by Alpha Violet before its Berlinale debut.
Popular on Variety
A total of 96 feature-length and short films, helmed by filmmakers from 17 states across Mexico, will compete in their respective sections for El Ojo, a sculpture created by Michoacán artist Javier Marín, along with cash and in-kind awards.
Dovetailing with the festival’s aim for diversity and inclusion, women directed 40% of the pics in the Official Selection, while some competing films were directed by filmmakers from Indigenous communities.
“This has been one of the most fruitful years for the Mexican Feature Film section, which is a great source of pride for the festival. Interestingly, unlike in recent years, when we received between 80 and 100 fiction features, this year we received just 68. Yet the quality of those films made the final selection particularly challenging. We initially planned to select eight titles, but the exceptional quality and sensitivity of the work ultimately led us to expand the lineup to 12,” said Rafael Aviña, a member of the FICM selection committee.
This year’s fiction lineup sees some overriding themes. Several of the pics look back at Mexico in the 1990s, while others follow teenagers navigating contemporary issues in an increasingly complicated society where their horizons feel narrower than ever. The selection also includes more experimental films, as well as stories centered on childhood – an unusual focus to date for Mexican feature filmmaking.
Senior programmer and documentary programming coordinator Chloë Roddick also sees a robust year for Mexican documentaries. “In both [feature and shorts] sections, the real challenge for us this year was to narrow the selection down (12 titles in feature doc; 11 in shorts). The final selection reflects both the breadth of talent currently working on the documentary scene, as well as a plurality of stories, a strong interest in challenging structure and form and a diverse mix of voices – from first-time to more established filmmakers.”
“As in previous years we saw strong feature and short film representation from Mexico´s Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities and the final selection includes three films by Indigenous filmmakers: Ramon Llaven´s ‘El baile de las ánimas’ and the short films ‘Ni racaladxe’ ‘(a co-direction from Zapotec director Alma Yoari Cizana Lopez) and Hñähñu filmmaker Sara Stephany Padilla´s ‘Mascaras del tiempo.’”
“In the feature selection, films like Efrain Mojica and Rebecca Zweig´s Michoacán-set ‘Jarpieo’ premieres in Morelia after a healthy international festival run that included Sundance, Berlinale, CPH:Dox and True/False. Dano Garcia´s bold and genre-defying exploration of queer identity, ‘Mickey,’ premiered at SXSW, as did Otilia Padua Portillo´s immersive sci-fi portrait of Indigenous mushroom scientists, ‘Las hijas del bosque.’ First-time filmmaker Colette Ghunim´s nuanced and intimate portrait of her Mexican/Palestinian roots, ‘Traces of Home,’ exec produced by Melissa Barrera and John Leguizamo, bowed at DOC NYC.“
The documentary selection includes six more first features: Francisco Ohem’s Balkans-set “Los mariachis perdidos”; Pablo Vaca’s coming-of-age observational drama (with a twist) “Forensita”; ‘Yatra,’ Alejandro Rugama´s deeply personal exploration of sickness and isolation; Indigenous Chiapas-born filmmaker Ramon Llaven’s “El baile de las ánimas”; Vania Carolina Quevedo´s video-essay and ode to her baby daughter, “Mi sangre es petroleo” and Michoacán-born Mariano Renteria’s architectural opera ‘Odisea Nacional,’ which also participated in Morelia’s works-in-progress section, Impulso Morelia, in 2025.
Winning short films in the Fiction, Animation and Documentary categories, along with the Mexican Documentary Feature winner, will be eligible to vie for an Academy Award nomination.
Additionally, a selection of short films from this year’s crop will be invited to screen out of competition during the Cannes Festival’s Critics’ Week in 2027.
